“We will do whatever we can to make nothing even worse for you and try and explain every process.



“You will be at the heart of any inquiry should that take place in the future.”

News.title: Brit dad-of-two, 34, dies after ‘brutal & unprovoked’ attack on vacation at holiday hotspot as family pay tribute
News.content:
HOLS TRAGEDY Brit dad-of-two, 34, dies after ‘brutal & unprovoked’ attack on vacation at holiday hotspot as family pay tribute

A BRIT dad has died after suffering a “brutal and unprovoked” attack at a holiday hotspot, prompting a heartrending tribute from his family.

Scot James, 34, sustained devastating head injuries and spent 13 days in a hospital in Turkey, with his relatives setting up a GoFundMe to extend their stay.



A family friend reported that Scot had suffered a fractured skull and bleeds to the brain.

The fit and healthy rugby player – who played for Maesteg Celtic RFC near Bridgend in South Wales – was declared braindead on July 11.



He was flown home via air ambulance with his mother by his side and later transferred to the ICU in the Royal Glamorgan hospital.

His family described Scot as a “loving father, son, grandson and partner” and an “all-round loveable man”.



Sister Hannah said: “Peacefully with all his loved ones around him my beloved brother Scot passed away.

“We as a family got to spend and cherish his last few days with Scot and be by his bedside.

“But sadly yesterday afternoon Scot decided it was his time to go and us as a family was there to hold his hand while his life support was turned off and while he sadly passed away.”

She described the attack as “murder” and said the family would make sure the “perpetrator gets what he deserves for killing Scot.”

The family raised £7,500 on GoFundMe to extend their stay in Turkey, but issued an update following the tragic news about Scot’s condition.



Hannah said: “I’m giving you this update as initially this was set up to help cover the cost of the family staying out in Turkey.

“But as I’ve explained the circumstances have changed and now Scot has passed away.”

His local rugby club – which hosted a football tournament to raise funds for Scot – paid tribute on social media.

“We are deeply saddened to share the heart-breaking news that our former player, Scot James, sadly passed away yesterday,” said Maesteg Celtics RFC on Facebook.

“Everyone at the club is devastated by this news, and our thoughts go out to his family and friends at this difficult time.”



They added that Scot would be remembered as an “outstanding player” and a “friend to everyone”.

The Foreign Office have confirmed they are working with local authorities following Scot’s death.

An FCDO spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British national who died following an incident in Turkey and are in contact with the local authorities”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

An inquest is due to be opened by the South Wales coroner.

News.title: Crete wildfires live: Rethymno in flames amid mass evacuations on Greek islands
News.content:
Flames are tearing across Greek Islands, forcing the evacuation of entire villages on Crete, Paros and Andros as wildfires continue to sweep across Europe

Raging wildfires have taken hold across several Greek islands, forcing villages to be evacuated as firefighters struggle to contain the flames.

Wildfires in the Rethymno region of the south of Crete are burning "out of control on all fronts", with firefighting aircraft unable to be deployed due to strong winds. Thousands of people, including tourists, were evacuated overnight. Urgent evacuation orders have also been issued for parts of Paros and Andros.

Three firefighters have died in Greece, with two becoming trapped in a vehicle while tackling the flames in Rethymno. Meanwhile, Europe's emergency response chief warned that the entire continent could be engulfed as wildfires rage in France, Spain and Portugal.

"Italy will face risk at the beginning of August, and we will need to see what will happen with the Iberian Peninsula, because if [it is] there as well, we will have all Europe on fire," Maria Zuber, head of the EU's Emergency Response Co-ordination Centre, said yesterday.

News.title: Police seize 13 supercars caught driving 'anti-socially' down motorway
News.content:
Police seize 13 supercars caught driving 'anti-socially' down motorway

Lamborghinis, a Ferrari and a Porsche were among the supercars siezed by cops after reports of dangerous and anti-social driving on the M11 motorway

View 3 Images Thirteen high-performance cars have been seized by Essex Police (Image: Essex Police)

Police have seized 13 supercars, including Lamborghinis, a Ferrari and a Porsche, following reports of dangerous and anti-social driving on the M11.

‌



Essex Police were called to the motorway at around 4.20pm on Tuesday after the force received multiple reports from “concerned” members of the public about a convoy of high-performance cars travelling northbound.

‌



Witnesses said the vehicles were accelerating at great speed before slowing down suddenly, with drivers allegedly braking heavily and disrupting the flow of traffic, Essex Police said.

‌



The drivers were also accused of bunching together and using the hard shoulder to undertake other road users, the force added.

View 3 Images Lamborghinis, Audi R8s, a Ferrari and a Porsche were seized (Image: Essex Police)

‌



Officers pulled over the vehicles at Junction 8 and issued 13 warnings for anti-social driving.

Sergeant Will Willsher said: “The behaviour reported to us was not only anti-social but potentially placed other road users at serious risk, especially on a busy motorway during peak travel times.

View 3 Images Cops got reports from concerned members of the public about a convoy of supercars (Image: Essex Police)

Article continues below

“Roads Policing Unit officers acted quickly to locate the cars and take appropriate enforcement action. Speed limits are there to keep everyone safe and the law applies equally to all road users.”

A number of offences were identified for investigation and inquiries are ongoing, the force said. Anyone with information, video footage or dashcam recordings should contact Essex Police quoting incident 955 of July 28.

News.title: Diane Abbott returns to Labour Party after year-long suspension lifted
News.content:
Diane Abbott returns to Labour Party after year-long suspension lifted

Diane Abbott has returned to the Labour Party after her year-long suspension over an antisemitism row was lifted by Prime Minster Andy Burnham as Joani Reid also returns

View 4 Images Diane Abbott has been let back into Labour following her suspension from the party (Image: PA)

Veteran MP Diane Abbott has been readmitted into the Labour Party following her year-long suspension from the party.

‌



A Labour spokesman confirmed Ms Abbott - the longest serving MP in the Commons - was allowed back into the party’s ranks on Tuesday evening alongside another suspended MP, Joani Reid.

‌



Both have also had the parliamentary Labour whip restored, meaning they can once again sit as Labour MPs in the House of Commons.

‌



Ms Abbott, the first black woman to have a seat in the chamber, was suspended after she doubled down on comments about racism for which she has previously apologised.

View 4 Images Ms Abbott, Parliament's longest-serving female MP, was suspended in 2025 following an antisemitism row (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

Andy Burnham and Donald Trump on course for first major row after phone call confusion READ MORE :

A statement tonight confirmed: “The Labour Party expects the highest standards from our elected representatives and party members. The Party assesses any alleged breaches of such standards independently of the leadership and political interference.

‌



"Following a process conducted under Labour Party rules and approved by the independent review board, Diane Abbott and Joani Reid have been readmitted to the Labour Party and have had the Labour whip restored in the House of Commons. Diane Abbott has also apologised following the independent process coming to an end.

"All Labour elected representatives must be mindful at all times of their platform and the responsibilities that come with that privilege.”

View 4 Images Joani Reid has also had the whip restored after her husband was accusing of spying (Image: Facebook)

‌



Asked about whether she had regrets over the controversy, she told the BBC last year: "No, not at all." Ms Abbott went on: "Clearly, there must be a difference between racism which is about colour and other types of racism because you can see a Traveller or a Jewish person walking down the street, you don't know.

"I just think that it's silly to try and claim that racism which is about skin colour is the same as other types of racism. I don't know why people would say that."

In a post on social media tonight, the MP wrote: "Today, following a process conducted in line with party rules and approved by the independent review process I have been readmitted to the Labour party."

‌



She went on to say she had been "issued with a formal warning for a tweet I previously posted" - a referred to the Israeli Defense Forces as the 'Jewish Defence Force'.

View 4 Images The 72-year-old has been told she can sit as Labour MPs once again (Image: Thabo Jaiyesimi/SOPA Images/REX/Shutterstock)

"I used wording that conflates the actions of the state of Israel with the Jewish community. I am deeply sorry for any hurt caused by that conflation and apologise for any hurt caused by it."

‌



She added: "I have been and remain a lifelong anti-racist and remain deeply committed to opposing racism in all of its forms."

Ms Reid voluntarily suspended herself from the Labour whip after her husband was arrested on suspicion of spying for China.

The MP for East Kilbride and Strathaven, who was not personally under investigation or accused of wrongdoing, said she was "voluntarily suspending herself" from then PM Keir Starmer's party in March. Her statement came a day after news broke that her husband David Taylor was one of the three men arrested on suspicion of spying.

‌



The politician as said she will "not sit as a Labour MP" until a probe was concluded, and a spokesperson for the Labour Party said she was "co-operating fully" with the investigation.

Ms Reid, the granddaughter of trade unionist Jimmy Reid, served as a councillor in Lewisham for eight years before becoming an MP.

She too took to social media following the announcement, writing: "With my membership of the Parliamentary Labour Party restored, I am excited to play a full part in supporting our new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, his government, and in renewing Scottish Labour.

Article continues below

"I have never been part of a police investigation, as a suspect or as a witness, and I am pleased that this has now been recognised. The support I have received from colleagues across the political spectrum, my constituents and my local Labour Party has been steadfast. "I am also deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by me when it was politically easier to distance themselves. You know who you are – thank you."

News.title: Suffolk fire live: Nuclear plant monitors ‘unprecedented’ wildfire destroying rare bird habitat
News.content:
A wildfire is raging in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk where evacuations have been ordered - the blaze is close to three nuclear plant sites, and has burned an area the size of 140 football pitches

Hundreds of people were evacuated overnight after a wildfire erupted in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk, with firefighters still battling to bring it under control today.

Temperatures have soared into the 30s in southern England, doing little to help the huge emegrency response. The fire has now burned an area the size of 140 football pitches, posing a risk to holiday parks and the UK's largest nuclear power plant. Some 200 caravans were evacuated, with holidaymakers woken up by banging on their doors.

EDF says it is "continuing to monitor the situation" at the Sizewell B power plant, while staff at Sizewell C - a planned nuclear power station located 10 miles from the fire - say there is a "low risk".

There is also concern for wildlife in the area, after nature reserve RSPB Minsmere announcing its closure this morning. RSPB Suffolk area manager Adam Rowlands said the land was home to rare wildlife including nightjars - and it could take "more than a decade" for the habitat to recover.

The fire spread across Dunwich Heath due to a change in wind conditions overnight, and there are fears more changes could worsen the situation. Chief Fire Officer Jon Lacey said it was a "very dynamic and fast-paced incident", adding: "I wouldn't say the fire is surrounded and we're on top of it because it moves faster than we're able to deal with it."

Have you been affected by the fire at Dunwich Heath? Get in touch with us at livenews@reachplc.com

News.title: Parents issued dire warning about asthma medication during school holidays
News.content:
Parents issued dire warning about asthma medication during school holidays

Nurses and doctors, including those at Birmingham Children's Hospital, say when children return to school after the summer holidays, they often see a surge in life-threatening asthma attacks

Birmingham NHS Trust gives advice on children's asthma medication during school holidays

Children with asthma must continue using their inhaler throughout the school holidays — or risk their lives, experts have warned.

‌



Medics say they regularly a surge in asthma attacks in September because many parents are said to ditch or reduce - often mistakenly - the medication during the six-week holidays, particularly when the weather is warm. Those kids whom pause their medication in the summer break are four times more likely to be in hospital at the start of the term, doctors warn.

‌



Asthma, a lung condition which affects around one in every 11 children, causes various symptoms, such as coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. Mums and dads should also look out for complaints about chest or stomach pain.

‌



NHS Dr Ranj issues urgent asthma 'review' warning to anyone using blue inhaler READ MORE :

View 3 Images Parents are being issued with an urgent asthma warning as kids start the summer holidays (file image) (Image: Getty Images/Cultura RF)

In a campaign video, Louise Tipping, an NHS respiratory nurse at Birmingham Children's Hospital, said: “Asthma attacks tend to increase significantly in September after the school holidays, likely due to disruptions in medication routines during the summer break.

"However, by taking a few simple steps, parents can help their child to avoid asthma attacks and enjoy the summer as much as anyone else.

‌



“Even if your child is feeling well and has been running around all summer, it’s vital to keep on top of their asthma medication and ensure they’re taking their preventer inhaler as instructed by their GP or asthma nurse. This means they’ll have the best level of protection before they head back into the classroom.

“Follow your child’s personal asthma action plan and keep it handy so you know what to do if their symptoms are triggered. And, importantly, always be asthma ready. An asthma attack can be life-threatening, and you should make sure your child always keeps an in-date reliever inhaler (usually blue) with them.”

According to official figures from Asthma + Lung UK, there is a 348% rise in the number of five to 14 year-olds admitted to hospital with an asthma attack in September, compared to August.

‌



The latest data shows the largest increase is among five to nine-year-olds, with a 370% rise in the number of hospital admissions in September compared to the previous month. Meanwhile, among 10 to 14 year-olds, the increase is a staggering 307%.

The figures, which were recorded in 2024, showed how boys in the five to 14 year age range group are more likely to be affected compared to girls.

3 View 3 Images Nurse Louise Tipping has detailed the dangers of the end of the school year (Image: YouTube/Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Trust/@NHS_BWC) 3 View 3 Images An NHS video brings the issues into focus (Image: YouTube/Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Trust/@NHS_BWC)

Article continues below

Asthma & Lung UK backed the message, saying: "Every September, there’s a rise in the number of children in the UK who go to hospital because of asthma attacks. There are lots of reasons for this.

"Some children get out of routine during the summer holidays and do not take their preventer medicines as prescribed. This can lead to their asthma being poorly controlled when they go back to school. "It’s important to make sure your child is sticking to their medicine routine a few months before they go back to school. This is to give the medicine time to build up and protect them from an asthma attack when they start going to school again."

Asthma triggers when kids go back to school

News.title: Concertgoers trapped on sweltering tube for 90 mins after trespasser jumps on track
News.content:
Concertgoers trapped on sweltering tube for 90 mins after trespasser jumps on track

Crowds heading home from a Bruno Mars concert had flooded the Tube at Wembley and were left stranded for 90 minutes after a trespasser jumped on the tracks

View 2 Images Emergency services were called to remove the trespasser (stock) (Image: Getty Images)

Concertgoers were left trapped on a London Underground train in sweltering conditions after a trespasser jumped onto the tracks.

‌



Crowds heading home from a Bruno Mars concert had flooded the Tube at Wembley Stadium on Tuesday, July 28, when the chaos unfolded.

‌



Multiple passengers reportedly suffered heat exhaustion during the 90-minute ordeal, which saw the train get stuck at around 11:15pm before eventually reaching Finchley Road station at 12.45am.

‌



A social media post from the parent of an affected concertgoer said passengers were then left stranded in London after missing their connecting train home.

The user added that the nightmare journey left a number of people suffering heat exhaustion.

View 2 Images A TikTok user said passengers had been stranded due to a trespasser (Image: ssss__x/TikTok)

‌



Footage posted to TikTok showed the driver trying to reassure passengers, telling them: "I want to go home, just like you guys do."

Another clip showed passengers slumped on the floor while waiting for the train to move, reports MyLondon.

Transport for London (TfL) workers were forced to switch the current off on the track while emergency services were called to remove the person from the tracks.

Article continues below

Several people on board appear to have been attending the last of American pop star Bruno Mars' five shows at Wembley on his 'Romantic Tour'.

A TfL spokesperson said: "We apologise to Metropolitan line customers for the disruption to their journeys following the Bruno Mars concert on Tuesday evening.

"This was caused by a trespasser on the line, which meant the traction current had to be switched off while the emergency services worked to remove the individual involved."

News.title: 'Summer holidays quickly turned to horror in scenes from disaster movies as wildfire ravaged Suffolk'
News.content:
The smell of smoke fogs the air as sirens sound from passing fire engines and helicopters hover overhead.

The scene is reminiscent of a disaster movie, but it is all too real to residents and holidaymakers here in the area of Dunwich, rural Suffolk, where around 120 firefighters in 18 engines continue to tackle the 100-hectare blaze.

At least 47 people, including babies, as well as five dogs, a cat and a mouse, were evacuated from lodges and caravans at Cliff House holiday park, near Dunwich Heath, after the fire began at around 5pm on Wednesday night.

They were later taken two miles to a pop-up rescue centre at Westleton Village Hall, where dozens of kind-hearted locals fed and watered them before offering them lodging in their spare rooms.

‌



View 6 Images The scene of devastation as the wildfires spread (Image: SKY)

Among the evacuees was a mum-of-two on holiday from Southampton, who told how she and her family had to quickly evacuate their family-owned static caravan with their two young sons in their pyjamas with such haste they forgot to bring the children’s shoes.

The woman, who did not want to named, said: “It was scary. We just kind of grabbed them and left. They’re still in their pyjamas - no shoes.

"We first saw the smoke at around 7pm while eating our dinner. It very quickly with the change of wind took a very different direction. As soon as we left the caravan, we were straight out into the smoke."

‌



Other evacuees included midwife Jude Bayly, 73, from north London, who slept in her car after evacuating her caravan.

View 6 Images Families have been evacuated from homes and a caravan park (Image: Newsquest / SWNS)

She said: “I’ve never done such chaotic packing in my life. You don’t have any sense of order. I tried to sleep but we could just see the plumes of smoke getting nearer and nearer. You could see the red sky and the flames licking higher and higher. It was really, really scary. It’s so devastating as it’s such a beautiful area."

Rob Gordon, 56, from Spalding, Lincolnshire, was also among those evacuated alongside his wife and dog. The couple had been enjoying their holiday when police warned them they may have to leave.

‌



The delivery driver said: “Unfortunately, I’d had a couple of beers so I couldn’t drive us away. On site, we couldn’t see the smoke that much, but when the police escorted us out, the late evening sun was catching the smoke, which turned it bright red. It was apocalyptic.”

View 6 Images Evacuees were kept safe at a local village hall (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily mirror)

Evacuees were tonight being fed and looked after by volunteers at Westleton Village Hall. Among them was Barry Banks, 52, who has lived in the village full-time for the past five years.

He said: “We were fully open and operational for refreshments from about 10pm on Wednesday night and then we heard that people were being evacuated from the campsites up until about midnight, 1am.

‌



“We managed to get 47 people housed with the village. Everyone that turned up here was successfully housed. It was a mixture of accommodation, but I’d say about 80-90% was people’s houses. It was a great effort. We’re very proud.

“We arrived this morning to cook a full breakfast for everyone that was housed overnight.”

The fire has overtaken "a sizeable chunk" of the nearby RSPB Minsmere reserve, but officials last night played down fears it could reach the nearby Sizewell B nuclear power station.

View 6 Images The large heathland blaze on the Suffolk coast still rages (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

‌



However, they warned the fire is still travelling through forestry and admitted they are facing a challenge to put it out, which they expect could continue for between 24 to 36 hours.

Residents are now being told to keep their windows and doors closed and to stand by in case further evacuations are needed.

Suffolk Fire Service Chief Fire Officer Jon Lacey appeared at the rescue centre, where he spoke to residents and evacuees.

He admitted: "It's a very dynamic and fast-paced incident. I wouldn't say the fire is surrounded and we're on top of it because it moves faster than we're able to deal with it. It's very challenging. The flames are quite high."

‌



View 6 Images Smoke can be seen from miles with a major incident declared (Image: Billy Rogers / SWNS)

"The fire in terms of its size isn't getting significantly bigger, but it's travelling. We have seen it grow a little bit, with the warm conditions and the daylight conditions with the wind and it depends where the wind goes and what is in front of it as to how much bigger it will get."

Mr Lacey admitted it is too early to establish what started the fire and he cannot say when residents and holidaymakers may be able to return to their properties.

He added: "I'm devastated for the people who have had to relocate. I know it's really scary and quite worrying. We're flooding it with resources to do the very best we can for them.

‌



"At this rest centre you can really feel the community spirit and see how everyone is pulling together to help."

News.title: Egypt struck by explosive drones as yet more countries are dragged into Iran war
News.content:
Egypt struck by explosive drones as yet more countries are dragged into Iran war

Energos Winter, a US-owned floating storage and regasification vessel was targeted at the Mediterranean port of Damietta in Egypt sparking a blaze that spread to a neighbouring Greek-owned tanker

View 2 Images The fire that broke out aboard two energy vessels at Damietta Port was due to a drone, Egypt's government said (file photo) (Image: Damietta Port Authority/AFP via Getty Images)

A fire that broke out on two ships at the Mediterranean port of Damietta in Egypt was caused by a drone strike, the country’s government said.

‌



"No party has claimed responsibility," for the attack on the key liquified natural gas (LNG) hub, a statement said today.

‌



Investigations were continuing and authorities would "take the necessary measures to preserve Egypt's interests and national security," it added.

‌



A US-owned floating storage and regasification vessel, Energos Winter, was reportedly hit by a drone. The vessel caught fire with the blaze spreading to a nearby Greek-owned LNG tanker, the GasLog Salem.

Donald Trump drags Egypt into Iran war as US blitzes Tehran military targets READ MORE :

View 2 Images Iranian missiles on display above a banner depicting US President Trump at Azadi Square in Tehran (Image: ABEDIN TAHERKENAREH/EPA/Shutterstock)

Egypt’s oil ministry said no one was injured in the fires.

‌



The Egyptian Cabinet said today in its statement: “After the fire that affected two vessels at Damietta Port on July 29, 2026, was brought under control, preliminary investigations by the relevant authorities found that the incident was caused by a drone.”

Black smoke could be seen rising over the port in videos posted on social media. While there has been no confirmation where the drone came from or who was behind the attack, suspicion has fallen on Iran.

Iran and its allies have carried out similar attacks on tankers in the Gulf and the Red Sea as well as targeting energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries since the start of the war with the US and Israel.

‌



If Iran is behind the attacks this incident would be the first time Egypt has come under attack from the country. Implying that Iran or its proxies were responsible, US President Donald Trump told reporters on Wednesday: "It's a little more of the same. But it's going to be straightening out."

The strike on the US-owned vessel came hours after air strikes were launched by the US and Saudi Arabia on Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq accused of launching drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities.

At least 20 members of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), Iranian-backed Shia militias, were killed in the strike, the group said.

Article continues below

The killings came as the US carried out what it called a "heavy wave of strikes" over the course of Wednesday night.

News.title: Suffolk wildfire still growing and unpredictable, says fire service
News.content:
Homes and a holiday caravan park were evacuated after the fire broke out and there are fears for rare birds and wildlife whose home is the heath and nearby RSPB Minsmere.

The "large-scale, wind-driven" fire was declared a major incident on Thursday morning, due to the size and complexity of the blaze which was helped by south-westerly winds.

On Thursday evening, Suffolk's chief fire officer, Jon Lacey, said: "Eighteen fire engines and 120 firefighters are involved in the response, but difficult terrain and limited access routes are making it hard for crews to reach some areas of the wildfire."

He confirmed approximately 100 to 150 people had been evacuated from their accommodation.

An update on the fire service's website said it was being supported by firefighters from neighbouring brigades, with engines also being sent from London.

"We have also requested additional national support, including wildfire specialist appliances, officers, and tactical advisers," it said.

"Around 50 people have received support through the rest centre, which remains open.

"We expect the response to continue for at least the next 48 hours."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged to give the fire service "all the support it needs" to tackle the "very serious" heathland blaze.

Communities Secretary Angela Rayner praised firefighters for their "skill and dedication and bravery".

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has called for Burnham to host an emergency Cobra meeting to discuss the outbreak of wildfires in Britain, including in Suffolk.

News.title: Thousands evacuated in Crete as wildfires threaten tourist resorts
News.content:
Thousands of people have been evacuated on the Greek island of Crete as wildfires fanned by strong winds menace tourist resorts and villages.

Two firefighters died on the island on Wednesday when they became trapped while tackling a fire near Krya Vrysi in the Rethymno region. A third firefighter died on the Greek mainland, near the port town of Gytheio in the Peloponnese.

As gusts reached 125km/h (77mph) on the island, around 8,000 people were evacuated from their homes overnight but were later allowed to return.

Greece is among many European countries facing devastating fires and drought.

Several fires have continued to burn in Spain and Portugal, although Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez declared an end to the national emergency for wildfires in the Ãvila and Madrid regions.

In south-west France some residents have been able to return to their homes after a major wildfire in the Gironde region.

The fire raging in Crete broke out in the Rethymno region on Wednesday and has since spread rapidly, destroying homes and agricultural land. It remains one of the biggest fires currently active on the island and is still burning out of control.

News.title: Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'
News.content:
Richard Anthony, whose farm stretches over the Vale of Glamorgan and Bridgend county, said the ground on his land was as hard as a "rock" and had "no moisture at all".

The dry land has left Anthony unable to plant his crops, who added he had "never ever been in this situation" before.

"As soon as we've harvested the one crop, we plant in the next crop, but we can't do any of that now," he said. "I've never seen it as bad as this."

Our wheat deals are down between 20% and 30%. That is massive. we'll have to cope, we will survive, but the knock-on effect is huge."

Anthony said he is concerned that once the rain comes it will not stop, leaving him unable to plant next year's crops.

"It'll go from this to being too wet", he added.

National Farmers Union Cymru president Abi Reader has warned that the cost of the continuing dry and hot weather will have a financial impact on farmers.

"We're going to see costs for these farms rising, because they might be having to buy in extra feed for their livestock, or they might be spending a lot of money carting water," she said.

"We've been in this a long time now, and it's going to take a long time to recover, and absolutely everybody needs to remember that food security starts with water security," she added.

News.title: MP Diane Abbott readmitted into Labour Party after suspension
News.content:
The long-serving MP Diane Abbott has been let back into the Labour Party, following a year-long suspension.

In a statement, a Labour spokesperson said Abbott had "apologised" following an independent process and that she would be readmitted into the parliamentary party, meaning she can sit as a Labour MP once again.

Abbott, who was suspended in 2025 following an antisemitism row, said she had been "issued with a formal warning".

East Kilbride and Strathaven MP Joani Reid has also been readmitted to the party. In March, she said she had "voluntarily" suspended herself after her husband was arrested on suspicion of spying for China.

Responding to her readmittance on Thursday evening, Reid she was "excited to play a full part in supporting our new prime minister".

She added: "I have never been part of a police investigation, as a suspect or as a witness, and I am pleased that this has now been recognised."

A Labour spokesperson said the decisions about party membership had been taken "independently of the leadership and political interference".

Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, was initially suspended in 2023 over a letter to the Observer newspaper, external in which she said Irish, Jewish and Traveller people "undoubtedly experience prejudice" but "they are not all their lives subject to racism".

She was readmitted to Labour shortly before the 2024 general election however, in a BBC interview just over a year ago she said she did not regret the incident and defended her original remarks.

This led to her second suspension in July 2025 and since then she has been sitting as an independent MP.

In a post on X,, external Abbott wrote: "Today, following a process conducted in line with party rules and approved by the independent review process I have been readmitted to the Labour party."

She said she had been "issued with a formal warning for a tweet I previously posted", in which she referred to the Israel Defense Forces as the 'Jewish Defence Force'.

"I used wording that conflates the actions of the state of Israel with the Jewish community. I am deeply sorry for any hurt caused by that conflation and apologise for any hurt caused by it."

She added: "I have been and remain a lifelong anti-racist and remain deeply committed to opposing racism in all of its forms."

The post about the Israel Defense Forces was posted days before her suspension in July 2025.

Some Labour MPs had been calling for Abbott to be readmitted to Labour and more than 38,000 people had signed a petition backing her return.

Earlier, following reports in the Sun newspaper, external about Abbott's possible readmission, Jewish groups expressed concern.

The Board of Deputies said: "This is an early test of resolve for the Burnham administration.

"It is hard to conceive of the whip being restored unless there is clear and sustained evidence of genuine remorse, a proper understanding of why those comments were so hurtful, and an unequivocal recognition that antisemitism is racism.

"While people can learn from their mistakes, Diane Abbott's past record is not encouraging in this regard."

The Jewish Leadership Council said the prime minister "must explain how returning that whip to Diane Abbott is consistent with this zero tolerance approach to antisemitism."

News.title: British Airways flight called mayday on approach to Heathrow
News.content:
A British Airways flight issued a "mayday" distress call on its approach to Heathrow Airport earlier this month, according to a statement from France's accident investigation authority.

The call was made on an Airbus A320 flying from Dusseldorf airport in Germany on 6 July following two stall warnings on the aircraft, before it landed without further incident.

The UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it was "investigating a serious incident".

A British Airways spokesperson said the airline was assisting the AAIB with its investigation and was not legally able to comment further at this stage.

The French Air Safety Investigation Authority, the BEA, said that as the plane approached Heathrow, there was a data system failure which triggered a stall warning.

The crew then flew the aircraft in a different mode called "alternate law", which removes some automated flight protection systems. Another stall warning then occurred at 3,000 feet - which experts say was likely to have been just miles away from the airport.

The urgency call the crew had already made was upgraded to mayday, indicating imminent danger.

The BEA website attributed the statement to the AAIB, but the AAIB would not confirm it was from them.

They issued the following statement: "The AAIB is investigating a serious incident involving a commercial aircraft which occurred on 6 July on approach to Heathrow airport."

It said the investigation would be a correspondence investigation, meaning that no team would be sent to carry out field investigations.

Aviation safety investigator David Gleave said there are different forms of mayday calls, and to send an urgency message was "not unusual".

"You could have sick passengers on board who need urgent medical attentionâ¦ so it's up to the captains' discretion as to what they call, but its very unusual for it to be a significant failure on board the aeroplane."

News.title: Archbishop of Canterbury committed to £100m slavery fund
News.content:
This is Dame Sarah's first pastoral visit to Africa since being installed as head of the Church of England at a ceremony in Canterbury Cathedral in March.

Reparative justice has been one of the themes running through the Ghana leg of this trip.

At Cape Coast Castle, which came under British control in the 1660s, Dame Sarah was shown dungeons where slaves were held, and the so-called "door of no return" through which they were forced on to ships.

The archbishop said: "You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in and the way that they were treated.

"It completely throws you off balance and brings home the evil that was transatlantic slavery."

Above the dungeons sits a chapel, which she said was a "stark illustration of the way the church was involved in the slave trade".

The Church of England has previously apologised for its associations with the slave trade.

Its missionary arm ran slave-farmed plantations in the Caribbean to fund the spread of Anglicanism, individual members of clergy were slave owners, and the Church received large donations from slave traders.

News.title: Man impaled by a hiking pole treks 10 miles down mountain
News.content: David Cifaldi was hiking Montanaâs Granite Peak with friends when he slipped and was impaled by his trekking pole. Remarkably, the pole missed all major organs. Rather than call for a helicopter rescue, Cifaldi hiked 10 miles down the mountain on foot. As a wound care nurse, he immediately shifted into professional mode, assessing and managing his injury throughout the ordeal.

News.title: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil
News.content:
Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government.

In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister,, external Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"

This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil.

"If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country."

He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank."

"Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."

Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."

In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat.

"Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy.

"It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."

The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices.

Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".

Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency".

Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea.

"Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."

Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" - production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.

Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil and gas fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland.

In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge.

The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.

Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.

If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Levy, also known as the windfall tax.

News.title: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
News.content:
The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.

In a major blow to the Home Office, the court confirmed on Thursday that it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban which came into effect in July 2025.

While the full details of the reasons for the appeal are yet to be published, the BBC understands they relate to Huda Ammori's argument that the ban breaches human rights.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement the government would "robustly defend this appeal".

Officials at the court say the appeal will be expedited - which means it will be heard after the summer break. The eventual outcome of the case could have major implications for terrorism legislation in the UK.

The decision comes weeks after the end of the first major trial of members of the group which had caused more than Â£1m of damage to a defence firm near Bristol with an Israeli parent company. Four members of that break-in team were jailed, with one also sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.

Separately, more than 2,000 people are facing potential trial for protesting against the ban by declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group in mass demonstrations.

The battle over the banning of Palestine Action has now gone on for more than year.

Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper banned the group on advice from the police and security officials after an escalating spate of break-ins targeting Elbit, an Israeli-owned defence firm.

The High Court initially ruled that the ban was unlawful - but five judges on the Court of Appeal then overruled it, unanimously deciding the home secretary had acted lawfully and within her powers to proscribe Palestine Action.

That decision by the Court of Appeal will now be reviewed by the Supreme Court.

News.title: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on
News.content:
The current row began after Polanski shared a single post on Instagram that contained a carousel of 20 pictures.

The re-post was shared to Polanski's 713,000 followers, because he accepted a request to tag him as a collaborator, which on the platform makes him a "co-author," placing it on his page and into his followers' feeds.

Polanski said he had not noticed the offending image among the others on the post.

According to him, he had accepted collaborator tags for eight other posts from the same event in Bristol alone.

Reform UK leader Farage claimed the t-shirt amounted to incitement to murder and his party reported it to the police.

Neither the Metropolitan Police nor Avon and Somerset Police say the incident meets the threshold for further action.

But the political row has continued with Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick calling Polanski a "nasty piece of work", at a news conference earlier on Thursday.

Inside the Green Party, there has been some criticism of Polanski's behaviour online.

He has attracted positive and negative attention for the rate at which he posts, comments, likes and replies across multiple platforms including X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.

And this is not the first time a quick reaction has attracted controversy; last month he had to apologise to police after posting about their response to the Golders Green attack.

One senior party source said it was clear that due diligence had not been done on Polanski's social media output, and that moving forwards he needs "tight controls" to stay credible, while keeping a similar tone of engagement with his followers.

They pointed out that the speed and number of Polanski's interactions came with a "small upside" but a "colossal downside", and with the latest incident he had "shot himself in the foot at precisely the wrong time".

It comes as recent polling suggests the Green Party has lost ground to Labour, following Andy Burnham's election as Labour leader, and down from a peak earlier this year.

They added their concerns about a wider problem with the party's vetting on social media and of candidates, including around antisemitic posts in recent months.

Several candidates in recent elections have stood down over their social media activity, with two candidates arrested during May's local elections, and another suspended after being elected.

But Green Party peer and former deputy mayor of London Baroness Jones said the criticism of Polanski's Instagram re-post seemed to be "mainly from our opponents, not internal discussions".

She said that her party leader had "made a mistake", adding "we've all done it and got flak."

But she added: "His online presence is what makes him relatable".

Along with relatability, comes popularity: Polanski is the second-most followed UK leader on Instagram after Nigel Farage. The Greens surpassed other parties to become the most popular on the platform this year.

It is also seen as where a good portion of their voters spend time, as they are the most popular party among the under-30s, according to pollsters YouGov.

News.title: Bank holds interest rates but says it is ready to raise them if Iran war escalates
News.content:
The Bank of England has kept interest rates unchanged for the fifth meeting in a row but has indicated it could raise them if the Iran war escalates.

It expects inflation - the rate at which prices rise - to pick up due to volatile oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East conflict, although the peak will be slightly lower than previously thought.

The Bank voted to hold interest rates at 3.75% at its latest meeting.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey warned the future of UK interest rates depended on whether the US led war against Iran continues.

While major uncertainties remain because of the war, the Bank predicts the UK economy will grow this year by more than previously forecast.

Bailey told the BBC: "If we get a continuation of this conflict going on and oil prices stay above $100 a barrel... the odds are that interest rates will have to go up higher."

But he also said if a ceasefire, and memorandum of understanding, is established and sticks that would make a difference.

"So it depends on how the events in the Middle East, frankly, unfold. And sadly, we all know this is highly unpredictable," Bailey said.

"What goes on in the Gulf is not, I'm afraid, under our control."

Three members of the Bank's nine-member rate-setting committee voted for a hike, one more than the previous meeting - with that member explicitly citing the collapse of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding for their vote to raise rates.

However, speaking at an earlier news conference, Bailey said the Bank was not currently moving towards raising interest rates.

"Please do not leave this room thinking that the Bank of England is edging towards a hike, because frankly, there's nothing in what I said, and I think any of us have said along those lines," he told reporters.

If the Iran war continues and oil prices hover around $100 a barrel, then a rate rise seems likely. But many in the markets expect tensions to subside in the coming weeks, ahead of crucial elections across the US in the autumn.

News.title: Virgin engineer died after explosion in fuel tank
News.content:
A Virgin Atlantic engineer died of a traumatic brain injury after an explosion as he worked inside a plane fuel tank, an inquest heard.

Aircraft technician Georgie Buxton, 23, was injured during the incident at Heathrow Airport on 11 June and underwent various surgeries to his head and neck. He died at St Mary's Hospital on 7 July.

Senior coroner Lydia Brown opened and suspended an inquest into his death at West London Coroners' Court on Thursday, as she is waiting to see if any criminal charges are brought.

A criminal investigation has been launched by the Metropolitan Police who are working with the Health and Safety Executive. The coroner said she had no details of any potential charges.

Buxton was one of two Virgin Airlines' technicians who were examining a fuel leak on a Boeing 787 900 on 11 June at about 08:45 BST.

A spokesman for Aviation Policing told the court: "Both technicians wore breathing apparatus to protect them from any residual fuel fumes whilst inside the fuel tank."

The spokesman said there was "a non-combustion explosion" while Buxton was inside the fuel tank.

He added: "Georgie Buxton took the impact of that explosion to his head and torso causing him to lose consciousness and suffer catastrophic injury."

A forensic post-mortem examination, carried out at the request of the police, found Buxton had suffered a traumatic brain injury â a craniofacial trauma.

News.title: Four people die after busiest day for small-boat crossings this year
News.content:
Four people died trying to cross the Channel overnight after the busiest day for small-boat crossings so far this year saw 752 arrivals in the UK.

One man died after a vessel capsized off France's northern coast late on Wednesday, local officials said, with a one-year-old child among those hurt.

Seven hours later, three people were found dead aboard a small boat after launching from Dunkirk overnight, some 100km (62 miles) up the coast.

French officials confirmed their deaths as the Home Office reported that Wednesday saw the highest number of crossings in a single day this year, with nine boats reaching the UK.

Local authorities in France said the first boat capsized off the coast at Hardelot around 23:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday.

The man is thought to have been in his 30s or 40s, officials added. Six other people including the child sustained minor injuries.

Local officials said the vessel was a "taxi" boat - which cruise along the coast and pick up their paying customers who are waiting in the sea.

Security officials "neutralised" the boat and an investigation into the incident has been launched.

The second boat launched from the Dunkirk area overnight was spotted near a breakwater off the coast at 06:00, the French coastguard said.

Search and rescue officials subsequently found three unconscious people aboard. Their deaths were later confirmed by emergency medical personnel.

A UK government spokesperson said: "Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, speaking separately about small boat crossings on Thursday, said the UK had made "significant progress" on reducing the number of arrivals.

But, asked by reporters about US President Donald Trump's remark that the UK had a "huge immigration problem", Burnham said there was much still to do "to get those numbers right down".

News.title: Homes flooded and residents evacuated after quarry 'incident'
News.content:
Residents of a village on the outskirts of Cardiff were evacuated after flooding caused by a quarry "incident".

Roads have been shut in Gwaelod-y-Garth, with reports of water up to 5ft (1.5m) deep in some homes on Thursday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to the scene and people were advised to avoid the area.

The Breedon Group confirmed there had been an "incident in its quarry".

"Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities while engaging with the local community as we respond to the situation," the company said.

News.title: England on track for record heat-related deaths this year, UKHSA estimates
News.content:
England is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

In a preliminary assessment, it said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.

An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the 24-27 May heatwave and a further 2,124 with the one from 21-28 June. Definitive figures are expected in early 2027.

Both spells broke Met Office UK monthly temperature records, with 35.1C (95.2F) recorded at Kew Gardens on 26 May and 38.0C recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.

The current record for heat-related deaths was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths were recorded.

Report author Dr Ross Thompson, from the UKHSA, said "while the figures are interim, they suggest that, if we experience more periods of hot weather this summer, we could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record".

Thompson added: "These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people's health.

"This is particularly true for those who are more vulnerable including older adults and people with underlying medical conditions."

He said "as the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme", adding that it is vital the country is prepared to deal with higher temperatures.

Earlier this week parts of the UK sweltered through another heatwave that peaked on Wednesday, with temperature reaching 35.2C in Writtle, Essex.

Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for some on Thursday and into the weekend, but likely not in the driest areas.

News.title: Missing child, 5, dies after being found in water
News.content:
A missing five-year-old child has died after being found in a body of water.

West Mercia Police said officers had responded to reports of a missing child in Badsey, Worcestershire, on Wednesday evening.

The child was found unresponsive in the water and a short time later was pronounced dead.

The force said they were believed to have drowned and called it "an incredibly tragic incident", adding there was no third-party involvement in the death.

Officers said they would not be identifying the child's sex out of respect for the family.

West Midlands Ambulance Service said they were called at 18:50 BST, sending an ambulance, two paramedic officers and the Midlands Air Ambulance Critical Care Car to the scene.

A spokesperson said: "On arrival we discovered one patient, a young child.

"Ambulance staff and police worked quickly to treat the patient, but sadly, it became apparent nothing could be done to save them and they were confirmed dead at the scene."

One of the nation’s oldest wine distributors has blamed Americans' lack of drinking for its bankruptcy.

The Republic National Distributing Company announced Sunday that it had filed for bankruptcy to “explore potential sale transactions in court and implement an orderly wind down of our remaining operations.”

The company, which distributes wine and spirits around the country, said its decision to file for bankruptcy “was not made lightly.”

“Over time, our industry has evolved, consumer preferences have shifted and the wholesale environment has grown increasingly challenging,” the company said in a statement.

A Gallup poll released last summer found that just 54 percent of adults say they drink alcohol, the lowest number in the nearly 90 years since the analytics firm has collected the data.

open image in gallery One of the nation’s oldest wine distributors has blamed Americans' lack of drinking for its bankruptcy ( Getty Images )

“This coincides with a growing belief among Americans that moderate alcohol consumption is bad for one’s health, now the majority view for the first time,” Gallup wrote in a release of its findings.

Of those who do drink, beer is more popular. Thirty-eight percent of U.S. drinkers said they drink beer most often, compared to 30 percent who said liquor and 29 percent who said wine.

National wine sales are down to their lowest level in more than 20 years as Americans are drinking less and many young drinkers are turning to canned cocktails or nonalcoholic beers, according to The New York Times.

In California, which produces roughly 80 percent of the country’s wine, vineyards are being burned on purpose because it’s often cheaper to discard the grapes than harvest them with a surplus of unsold bottles, the Times reported Thursday.

open image in gallery Just 54 percent of Americans say they drink alcohol, according to a poll ( AFP via Getty Images )

The Republic National Distributing Company, which got its start before the Prohibition era, may not survive the decline of drinking more than a century later.

The company said it has already made changes over the last several months that “preserved over 5,000 jobs and allowed our businesses in those markets to continue serving their customers and suppliers.”

In late May, the Reyes Beverage Group acquired Republic National Distributing Company’s operations in Arizona, Colorado, Florida, Hawaii, Louisiana, Maryland, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, Virginia and Washington, D.C.

open image in gallery In California, vineyards are being burned on purpose because it’s often cheaper to discard the grapes than harvest them with a surplus of unsold bottles, according to a new report ( Getty Images )

Nearly a year before, Republic National Distributing Company decided to shut down its operations in California.

“We’ve made the difficult business decision to withdraw from California which affects many of the roles in the state,” CEO Bob Hendrickson told BevNET in June 2025.

“We are complying with all regulatory obligations and are committed to handling every transition thoughtfully and smoothly and ensuring everyone is treated fairly and respectfully. We are grateful for the support of these employees and will do our best to support them during this time.”

The bankruptcy process will allow the company to continue to work with entities that “have expressed an interest in acquiring our other markets,” Sunday’s statement read.

“We thank our suppliers and customers for their patience and support. We are incredibly grateful to our associates for their dedication and commitment to our company, our suppliers, our customers and each other,” the company said.

New citizenship approvals in the Chicago area are on track to decline by more than 80 percent this year, after the city saw one of the Trump administration’s largest and most aggressive military-style immigration crackdowns in late 2025.

In a typical year, the Northern Illinois District Court is home to about 20,000 to 30,000 new approvals, peaking at nearly 33,000 in 2022, according to an ABC 7 analysis of federal data.

This year, just 3,765 people have become citizens, the outlet found.

"When I saw the numbers that you had shared...I was floored,” local immigration attorney Kathleen Vannucci told the station.

"The administration does not want to see high numbers of new citizens, and so I think this is a result of what their overall goal [is]," she added.

open image in gallery New citizenship approvals fell steeply in 2026 around Chicago, after the city was the site of a massive immigration crackdown last year ( Getty )

“For years, the Biden administration prioritized rubber-stamping aliens’ applications for U.S. citizenship with minimal vetting. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, under the leadership of President Trump, is implementing rigorous screening and vetting processes across the country,” USCIS spokesman Zach Kahler said in a statement to The Independent. “USCIS will not take shortcuts in the naturalization process.”

The Trump administration has pursued a range of actions to make it harder to become a U.S. citizen, including attempting to pause most asylum cases, stripping temporary protected status from people inside the U.S., denying more citizenship applications, and pushing to make new applications feature higher fees and a harder civics test.

The White House has also pursued once-obscure or unheard-of measures, including denaturalizing existing citizens, reinstating “neighborhood investigations” for applicants and campaigning to eliminate the constitutionally protected right to birthright citizenship.

In the case of the Chicago area, these legalistic changes played out while the administration sent masked federal agents into city streets over the fall as part of the controversial 64-day “Operation Midway Blitz.”

Agents were accused of using excessive force, carrying out racial profiling, launching tear gas without warning, aiming rubber rounds at reporters, then deceiving a federal court about their conduct, which the administration denied.

open image in gallery The Trumpa administration was accused of using excessive force during the Chicago-area ‘Operation Midway Blitz’ ( @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social )

Ahead of the operation, Trump threatened that the city was about to “find out why it’s called the Department of WAR,” and posted an AI image of him in a fake movie poster for “Chipocalypse Now,” a reference to the classic Vietnam War film Apocalypse Now.

The White House also pushed to deploy the National Guard on Chicago streets over the objection of local officials, though the Supreme Court ultimately blocked the plan.

In Chicago and beyond, the Trump administration has sent immigration agents near spaces previously considered off limits under “sensitive locations” policies, such as schools, hospitals and religious settings.

Critics of such tactics warn they keep even legal immigrants from accessing important community spaces and government institutions.

As The Independent reported last year, deportation fears have turned once-thriving immigrant neighborhoods into “ghost towns.”

Donald Trump appeared Thursday to be on the verge of tanking one of his own nominees as his battle with reluctant Republicans in the Senate continued, perplexing many on Capitol Hill.

The president’s fixation on preserving the terms of a settlement deal the courts have seemingly already rejected is just the latest angle of a months-long feud he has engaged in with several members of the Senate Republican caucus. But those terms, which include the creation of a $1.776 billion “weaponization” fund for the Department of Justice and granting him and his family immunity to IRS audits seem to be a crucial sticking point for the president.

And that could cost him the appointment of one of his closest and most valuable political operatives.

The president wrote on Truth Social Thursday that he may pull the nomination of Todd Blanche until two Republican senators currently opposed to his confirmation, Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, leave office at the end of the year.

Unstated, however, was the political reality: This is a death sentence for Blanche’s nomination.

open image in gallery Sen. Thom Tillis and another Republican spurned by Trump, John Cornyn, are leading the effort to block Todd Blanche's confirmation ( Reuters )

Republicans are projected by most election models to lose one if not more seats in the Senate this upcoming midterm cycle, and it’s highly unlikely Blanche will ever get a more favorable playing field than he has now.

Asked by The Independent why the White House and Justice Department weren’t agreeing to the counter-proposals offered by their side, Tillis replied that it was clear the president hoped to revive the fund Blanche has verbally declared “dead” on several occasions.

“Well, I guess it means that he wants to revive it at some point later on,” said Tillis.

“Why aren't we taking this off the table? It's not helping the president's popularity,” added the North Carolina Republican. “It's not helping our candidates who are up for election. Nothing good is coming from this. And Blanche recognizes it.

“The president's getting bad advice. He should listen to Blanche and others who think if it's dead, it should be rendered completely dead.”

As the president wages war with Tillis and Cornyn on social media and in comments to reporters, it seems clear that, at a minimum, his own personal animus for the two senators is preventing the president from achieving any kind of progress in the GOP-controlled Senate at a bad time for Republicans. Staring down the midterm deadline, the chamber is eyeing what it can pass before the lame-duck session begins, including government funding legsislation ahead of a September deadline.

Meanwhile, the eyes of voters are on Washington in greater numbers as the midterms inch closer and closer. Further signs of a dysfunctional Republican congressional majority in either chamber could further worsen the party’s chances of protecting those majorities in November.

Republicans in both chambers eye the terms of the Trump/IRS settlement agreement as a detriment to their re-election efforts. They openly say the effort to establish the so-called “slush fund”, which they argue could benefite Jan. 6 rioters, stinks of corruption.

open image in gallery John Thune has become the target of Trump's ire over the SAVE America Act ( AFP/Getty )

But Trump, according to multiple accounts of those close to him and with knowledge of his thinking, is not concerned about protecting Republican majorities and especially the careers of members whose votes he cannot control. He’s spent months publicly pressuring Senate Majority Leader John Thune to pass voter ID legislation, the SAVE America Act, and has been making his frustrations about the Senate leader clearer even as Thune tries to hold on to power.

“He gets obviously frustrated with me,” Thune said in an interview with Politico, claiming that he and Trump “get along” despite the criticism.

“Math is math, arithmetic is arithmetic,” said Thune. “And part of it, too, is the active role he played in some of these primaries.”

“He thinks I can wave the magic wand,” he added. “I wish it were that easy.”

Cornyn, speaking to MS Now on Thursday morning as a planned committee vote on Blanche’s nomination was postponed, said that the president had not spoken with him and “could fix this [situation] in a minute”. He added that a phone call from the president would be helpful to clear up their disagreements.

open image in gallery John Cornyn warned reporters that he and Tillis were not the only Republicans willing to stand up to Trump over the 'slush fund' ( Getty )

That phone call looked unlikely by the afternoon, as the president returned to attacking Cornyn and Tillis on social media.

“John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting,” said Trump on Truth Social. “Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention.”

Tillis, responding to a question from The Independent, asserted that he’d never asked the president for his endorsement and added that Trump would’ve received “a Tillis reply” had he ever threatened him directly with support for a primary opponent. Cornyn and another Republican senator, Bill Cassidy, were ousted this cycle by Trump-backed primary opponents. Tillis chose not to seek re-election last year after a public break with Trump, and as it was clear he’d face a Trump-backed opponent were he to run.

And Cornyn, in his own comments to reporters, insisted that the resistance to the “slush fund” would not dissipate within the GOP caucus with his and Tillis’s departure from the chamber.

“I mean, we were having a perfectly good conversation with Todd Blanche. I think he's a smart guy, a good lawyer, and we just wanted to confirm what he already swore to. And now the president's pulled him back, thinking that well, he can out wait Tillis and me,” said the Texas senator.

“But ... there are more than just two people who have reservations about the weaponization fund and about the scope of the settlement agreement.”

Even the most devoted cat owners wonder at some point, perhaps waking up in a cold sweat in the middle of the night, whether their cat really loves them. Dog people like to smugly point out dogs’ long history as humankind’s best friend.

But research shows cats’ reputation as a cold and aloof pet is undeserved.

Because of their evolutionary ancestry, domestic cats are, by their nature, more independent than dogs. The wild ancestors of our cats didn’t live in social groups as canines do. However, during the process of domestication, cats developed the ability to form social relationships not just with other cats, but also with people.

While they may not rely upon people to feel safe as dogs do, many cats show affection towards their guardians and seem to highly value the company of their human companions. Their attachment to humans is partly influenced by their experiences of being handled by people as a kitten.

Cats behave towards humans in the same way that they respond to their feline friends, so the secret of whether your cat feels bonded to you lies in their behaviour.

open image in gallery Their attachment to humans is partly influenced by their experiences of being handled by people as a kitten ( Getty Images )

1. Look out for scenting

The ability to communicate with other cats over long distances and when no longer physically present was an advantage to their wild ancestors. Our pet cats have retained this “supersense” and rely heavily on this form of communication .

In particular, cats use scent to identify members of their social group or family, by sharing a group scent profile. Cats have scent glands on their flanks, head and around their ears, and often rub their heads against people and objects that are familiar and comforting.

Does your cat rub its head or side against your legs? The soft sensation you feel against your calves is actually your cat identifying you as a friend and is a huge compliment.

open image in gallery Does your cat rub its head or side against your legs? The soft sensation you feel against your calves is actually your cat identifying you as a friend and is a huge compliment ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

2. Watch how they greet you

One of the most obvious signs that your beloved pet is fond of you, is the way that your cat greets you. When cats greet members of their social group they show signals to indicate friendship and a desire to move closer. Cats also show these signals to humans.

A tail held in the upright flagpole position shows a friendly intention (the feline equivalent of a wave), indicating familiarity, trust, and affection. Some cats also use an upright question mark shaped tail to greet someone they like, or to motion that they want to play.

Cats sometimes intertwine their tails as a sign of friendship and the human equivalent of this is to wrap their tail around your calf.

Rolling over and exposing their vulnerable under belly is another gesture that a cat has ultimate trust in you. However cats prefer to be petted on the head and neck area, so this is not usually a request for a belly rub.

Attempts to stroke a cat’s belly will often result in a hasty retreat, or even claws. The chirrup or trill greeting is a melodious sound that cats make when saying hello to preferred individuals. So if your cat sings to you in this way, be assured they are pleased to see you.

That familiar feeling when your cat hits the back of your knee can also be a sign that they feel an extremely close bond to you. The feline version of a high-five, the head bump is usually saved for a cat’s closest feline friends and most trusted humans.

3. Look for blinks

Your cat might also be secretly signalling their affection in the way they look at you. When cats encounter strange humans or other cats they don’t know, they usually greet them with an unblinking stare. But they are more likely to slowly blink at cats they have a good relationship with.

Research suggests slow blinks are associated with a positive emotional state and can be a sign of trust, contentment and affection, similar to a human smile. If you wish to return the compliment, blink and your cat might blink back. This is nice a way to bond with your cat if they aren’t keen on being touched.

4. They get up close

Cats are very protective of their personal space and don’t like unwelcome guests to invade it. If a cat allows you to get close to them, that suggests a close bond, particularly where the contact is frequent or long lasting.

Curling up on your lap for a nap is a sign of deep trust. Grooming only happens between cats with a warm relationship, so licking your hand or face can be a show of endearment, even though those barbed tongues may not feel all that gentle.

Ancient DNA from Chilean mummies offers the firmest evidence yet that European colonization introduced smallpox to the Americas.

Before its eradication in 1980, largely due to vaccination, smallpox stood as one of humanity's deadliest diseases. It historically claimed the lives of about one-third of those infected, often leaving survivors with deep, disfiguring scars.

While outbreaks ravaged Asia and Europe, the virus eventually reached the Americas. Colonial writings and missionary reports extensively documented its catastrophic impact, killing millions and decimating Indigenous populations who lacked prior exposure.

The new scientific evidence comes from an analysis of Chilean mummies, which provides the strongest genetic link yet to the virus as it existed outside the Americas. This offers a clearer understanding of how smallpox reached remote populations through colonization, explained geneticist Shigeki Nakagome of Trinity College Dublin.

Researchers found evidence of two smallpox infections in ancient DNA from the leg bone fragments of an adult man and woman ( Reuters/Will Dunham )

In the new study, Nakagome and colleagues examined 13 bone samples previously collected from an archaeological site at Camarones, in northern Chile.

Researchers found evidence of two smallpox infections in ancient DNA from the leg bone fragments of an adult man and woman.

From dating the remains and peeking at the genes, scientists concluded the two likely died between 1492 and 1631. Scientists also compared the genes in this version of smallpox to other versions and fit it neatly between European strains from medieval times and later versions. This was important molecular evidence, suggesting that the strains of smallpox infecting people in the Americas evolved first from Europe.

“Nobody would ever question that smallpox came to this hemisphere from colonization, but this proves it,” said Patricia Foster, a biologist at Indiana University. She had no role in the new research, which was published Thursday in the journal Science.

Exactly which population brought smallpox to the Americas from the Old World remains unclear, said the study authors. European settlers came in different waves to the Americas following the explorations of Christopher Columbus in the Caribbean in 1492 and Amerigo Vespucci along the South American coast about a decade later. The disease also could have passed through Africa as part of the introduction and expansion of the slave trade.

These smallpox infections in South America were identified in an area with no previous record of the disease, opening new questions about how the virus got so far south — possibly spreading along Indigenous trading networks that had long pre-existed the arrival of Europeans.

Studying various strains of the virus also allowed scientists to pinpoint how it evolved, turning off certain genes to become more effective at its deadly mission.

In addition to confirming the history of smallpox, the research also shines a light on the human cost. The two sick individuals studied were between 18 and 35 years old, and the disease is likely what killed them.

The findings point to how devastating the disease was across the Americas, wiping out entire populations and leaving them vulnerable to European conquest, said study coauthor Constanza de la Fuente Castro, a biological anthropologist at the University of Chile.

“It wasn't just cultural or demographic. It's literally written into biological evidence that we can still recover and read today,” de la Fuente Castro said.
