Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. Ukraine has offered Poland assistance in investigating the scene, he added. Earlier in the morning, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command (DORSZ) said that air defence radars had detected at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine overnight whose trajectories could have posed a potential threat to Polish airspace. An unidentified object was detected in Polish airspace at 3:40 a.m. travelling westward, DORSZ said. An F-16 fighter jet was dispatched to identify and intercept it. At 3:46 a.m., before the object could be clearly identified, it disappeared from the radar. An Mi-24 helicopter was then sent to the area of the last radar detection to verify the indications. Its crew located what was believed to be the crash site. W trakcie rosyjskiego zmasowanego ataku rakietowego na zachodnią Ukrainę doszło do naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej. The prime minister added that Polish forces had been prepared to shoot down the object had it continued flying in a way that posed a threat. “This initial information clearly indicates that the relevant services, the military, our pilots, and our aircraft acted very quickly and efficiently. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A newly sworn-in judge of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has said he will refuse to sit on the court until four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year, but blocked by the president, are allowed to take their seats. It is the latest development in a months-long dispute between the opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki and the government, which considers the TK to be improperly staffed and therefore illegitimate. Although Nawrocki swore in Sławomir Patyra, who was appointed by the ruling majority in parliament in June, as a TK judge on Tuesday, he continues to refuse to swear in four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year. Po złożeniu przysięgi Patyra ogłosił, że zamierza odmówić orzekania. To gest solidarności z czwórką sędziów, od których prezydent nie chce przyjąć przysięgi https://t.co/jdbKusQ3H9 — OKO.press (@oko_press) July 28, 2026 Shortly after his swearing-in ceremony at the presidential palace on Tuesday, Patyra arrived at the TK headquarters in Warsaw, where he was accompanied by four other judges appointed by parliament this year, including two whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. There, he announced that his decision not to sit on the court was a matter of loyalty to the constitution and his belief in judicial ethos. “I cannot imagine taking an oath today to uphold the constitution, only to start breaking that constitution tomorrow,” he said. Patyra told journalists that he would “submit a declaration of refusal to adjudicate” due to his solidarity with judges who are “unlawfully deprived of the chance to participate in the work of the tribunal”. He added that, along with the other judges chosen this year, he is “fully mobilised to restore the Constitutional Tribunal to its proper, constitutional, systemic form”. Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK, the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, TK’s chief justice Bogdan Święczkowski has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again later in the month, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. After repeated requests, Nawrocki finally decided last week to invite Patyra to the presidential palace. The president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, noted that “there were some doubts” but “the president dispelled them” and added that Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”. Nowo wybrany przez Sejm Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej uchwałą z dnia 11 czerwca 2026 r. sędzia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Sławomir Patyra złożył wobec Prezydenta RP ślubowanie. pic.twitter.com/VLMRAIg1Yj — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki says that 40 MPs and one senator aligned with him will form their own parliamentary group, deepening a split in the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) after a dispute over party direction and loyalty declarations. The move marks the most serious internal challenge in years to PiS, which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023, and follows months of tensions between Morawiecki’s more moderate faction and party conservatives who have pushed the group in a hard-right direction. Once formally established, Morawiecki’s caucus would become the third-largest bloc in the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament. Powstanie klub parlamentarny „Rozwój Plus”. Morawiecki zdecydował#PAPInformacjehttps://t.co/IftRdgpIPw — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 29, 2026 One of Morawiecki’s allies, Marcin Horała, told reporters that the creation of the caucus did not mean they were leaving PiS, but “simply setting up a parliamentary group so that we can get on with our work”. He noted, however, that PiS’s parliamentary group “has stopped treating us as its members”. Morawiecki, meanwhile, said that his group remained ready to cooperate with PiS as a “second lung” of the party’s broader political camp, but suggested that the group was moving in a different direction. He said that parts of PiS’s messaging were increasingly influenced by “dissidents and schemers” as well as hardline factions, including Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), a nationalist group that was previously a junior coalition partner of PiS and often clashed with Morawiecki when he was prime minister. Reacting to Morawiecki’s announcement, party chairman Jarosław Kaczyński said the former prime minister had carried out a planned split of the party despite his efforts to reach a deal. “Until the end I made efforts to reach an agreement, unfortunately Mateusz Morawiecki clearly had his own political plan in mind, carried out on the basis of a split in PiS,” Kaczyński wrote on X. The announcement follows a dispute that began after Morawiecki launched his Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) association in April. The former prime minister insisted the association was intended to complement PiS with a pro-development agenda rather than rival it. However, critics within PiS viewed it as an attempt by Morawiecki to build an alternative power base that could eventually evolve into a separate party ahead of the 2027 parliamentary election. Seeking to end the standoff, the party ordered PiS lawmakers to resign from all outside political associations by last Thursday, or face “consequences” including “the loss of membership in PiS”. On Friday, Kaczyński said that “around 30 MPs” had failed to comply and had therefore effectively resigned from the party, adding that Tuesday’s meeting of the party’s political committee would simply confirm this fact. Poland's right-wing opposition PiS party is set to split after a more moderate faction of over 30 MPs loyal to deputy leader @MorawieckiM refused to sign a loyalty pledge demanded by leader @OficjalnyJK, who says that means they have effectively resigned https://t.co/TuqYpGI5ak — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 24, 2026 On Tuesday, the party announced that instead, the committee had referred the cases of 44 members, who either failed to submit the required declarations or submitted them on the wrong form, to the party’s disciplinary officer for individual review, delaying a final decision. “From a formal and legal perspective, Mr Mateusz Morawiecki has not yet been removed from the list of members,” PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek said on Tuesday. PiS disciplinary officer Karol Karski told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) he would examine each case individually. “I am open to speaking with each of them so they can present their positions,” Karski said. “At this point, I can initiate proceedings against the individual in question, refer the case to a peer disciplinary tribunal with a motion for punishment – this could include a temporary suspension or expulsion from PiS.” PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, the party has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll at a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. The national-conservative opposition PiS party has named its candidate to be prime minister if it wins next year’s parliamentary elections. Przemysław Czarnek is a hardline conservative who played a prominent role in PiS's campaign against "LGBT ideology" https://t.co/sSJLON00hW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2026 They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Adam Szłapka, the spokesman of the current more liberal government, said Braun was “the ultimate playmaker in this whole game”, who had helped push far-right rhetoric into the political mainstream. “The worst thing about this whole situation is that Poland’s largest opposition party has, in effect, started to adopt Grzegorz Braun’s agenda from A to Z,” Szłapka told broadcaster TVN24. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has ruled that a new regulation allowing the registration of foreign same-sex marriage certificates in Poland was partly unconstitutional, saying it went beyond technical administrative changes and conflicted with the constitution’s definition of marriage. The regulation, introduced by the digital affairs ministry after rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), was due to take effect on 23 August. The government, which considers the court to be improperly constituted, says it will not implement the ruling. The government has issued a regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriages to be entered in the civil registry The decision comes in response to an EU court order and marks a major change in a country that does not allow same-sex unions under domestic law https://t.co/2an5mGtnHl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 22, 2026 Polish law does not allow same-sex couples to marry or enter into civil unions, and a bill that would have granted such limited rights to unmarried couples was recently vetoed by the opposition-backed president. Until this year, same-sex couples who married abroad were also unable to register their marriage certificates in Poland. After the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise such marriages, the digital affairs ministry changed civil status forms. Instead of separate fields for “man” and “woman”, the new templates use “man/woman”, allowing registry offices to record both opposite-sex and same-sex marriages. Lawmakers from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, however, challenged the regulation, arguing that the digital affairs minister had exceeded his powers because the changes were not merely technical but affected the legal definition of marriage. The tribunal, which is widely seen as being under PiS’s influence, agreed. The tribunal said the new forms allowed relationships that do not match the constitution’s definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman to be recorded as marriages. It said regulations can only implement existing laws and cannot change matters reserved for the constitution or parliament. The tribunal also said that registering a foreign marriage certificate cannot produce legal effects that conflict with the basic principles of Polish law. It added that changing the constitutional definition of marriage would require amendments to the constitution and related laws. Some legal experts argue that, while the constitution states that a “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman… shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” that phrasing does not rule out other legally recognised unions receiving state protection. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Shortly after the ruling, government members said they would not comply with the tribunal’s decision and that the regulation would enter into force as planned. “The illegal Constitutional Tribunal is once again attempting to obstruct a state that is enforcing the law in force and the rulings of European courts,” digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said. “The transcription of foreign same-sex marriage certificates is and will remain legal,” he said, adding that 184 same-sex couples had so far had their foreign marriage certificates transcribed. Katarzyna Kotula, the government official responsible for equality issues, said the TK ruling on the issue of transcriptions “has no legal force whatsoever”. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. For a long time, the government refused to appoint new judges to the Constitutional Tribunal as the terms of the previous judges expired, with some vacancies remaining unfilled for over a year. In recent months, the government has resumed appointing new judges, but President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, is refusing to administer the oath of office to some of them. A decision to designate a village as a protected monument has sparked fierce opposition from residents, who have vowed to “fight until the end” against measures they say will limit their ability to renovate and build on their properties. The village in question, Ostaszów in southwestern Poland’s Lower Silesia province, was established in 1936 by Nazi Germany as an agricultural settlement of around 42 farms. At the time, the region still belonged to Germany. The Lower Silesian Provincial Conservator of Monuments argues Ostaszów has “unique, homogeneous historical architecture” requiring state protection, but local officials say that the way the decision was made, despite opposition from residents, shows “the voice of local communities has no significance”. After World War Two, most of Lower Silesia, including the village, became part of Poland. The village’s architecture has remained largely unchanged, with its residential buildings connected to barns, forming unique cohesive farmstead units. Around 250 people live there. Earlier this year, the residents were told proceedings had begun to add the village to the register of protected monuments, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The provincial conservator said on Friday it had reached a decision. “The unique, above-standard historical, scientific and artistic value of Ostaszów as a monument cannot be questioned,” it wrote in a statement. It noted that a study by a team working under the culture ministry had found that the village was the only preserved settlement of its kind in Lower Silesia. Residents and local officials said they planned to appeal against the decision, arguing it would create additional bureaucracy and interfere with property owners’ ability to decide on building and renovation work. “We have a years-long legal battle ahead of us, but we won’t give up. We will fight until the end. We believe that decisions about the 42 homes in Ostaszów should be made by their residents, not by harmful officials,” residents wrote in a statement quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “In a cardboard state, the voice of local communities has no significance – only orders and bans count. Our future is to be decided by a heartless official from [the Lower Silesian capital of] Wrocław who does not even have time to meet with the victims of his decisions,” said the village head, Sylwia Mazur. Wieś Ostaszów wpisana do rejestru zabytków. Mieszkańcy będą się odwoływaćhttps://t.co/ZxmH2lbHnb pic.twitter.com/cPdL73PXIH — Dzieje.pl (@dziejepl) July 26, 2026 The conservator noted, however, that until the appeals process is concluded, construction works cannot proceed. It added that it planned to cooperate with locals to “develop principles of renovation and investment procedures in accordance with the regulations on the protection of monuments”. It also urged residents not to spread “scandalous narratives” about the decision leading to an “open-air museum, the impossibility of renovation, and the blocking of investments”. It said other villages in Lower Silesia were subject to similar protections without hindering their development. Gazeta Wyborcza cited some residents saying that the launch of proceedings in January had already forced them to pause work on their properties. Others complained that the decision will increase renovation costs due to strict conservation requirements. The Opole Provincial Conservator of Monuments said that, as of 2021, some 86 villages across Poland had been added to the register of monuments because of their historic layouts. World.title: Poland enters race to host EU-backed AI gigafactory
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has joined the European Union’s plan to build artificial intelligence (AI) gigafactories with a view to hosting one of the bloc’s new computing centres. Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski said Poland had completed a key legal step by joining the joint procurement process. The move enables Poland to bid for one of seven AI gigafactory projects planned under the EU programme, potentially attracting investment of more than 10 billion zloty (€2.3 billion) while giving businesses, researchers and public institutions access to advanced AI computing capacity. “On behalf of the Republic of Poland, I have signed the Joint Procurement Agreement, which means that Poland joins the AI gigafactory initiative,” Standerski told daily Rzeczpospolita. Under the proposed model, AI gigafactories will be designed, financed, built and operated by private consortia selected through a European tender organised by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). In the first procurement round, EuroHPC JU plans to select seven projects comprising four medium-scale facilities and three large-scale sites. Poland is bidding for a medium-scale project, which would initially provide computing capacity equivalent to at least 25,000 AI accelerators before expanding to at least 75,000. The EU and its member states will support the projects by committing to purchase computing services during the initial years of operation, providing demand certainty for investors. “Poland and the EU will each buy 17% of the power, and the remaining two thirds will be made commercially available by a private consortium; Poland will commit to purchasing its own pool for five years,” Standerski said. Standerski also told the newspaper that companies’ interest in the project is “enormous”. “This means that, from the very first day the gigafactory is operational, part of its computing capacity will already have been sold,” he added. Poland’s government will spend 1.9 billion zloty (€437 million) equipping the majority of schools with so-called AI labs before the start of the next school year. The money will fund laptops, AI software and interactive displays, among other equipment https://t.co/outNQIGCv0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Standerski said the government would not designate a site for the facility, with the final location to be determined by the winning consortium through the European procurement process. He said the government had previously identified 10 locations across Poland capable of hosting. Last week, the deputy minister also said Poland was preparing to sign an agreement with the Czech government, under which cooperation would involve mutual purchases of computing capacity between the two countries. He also said Lithuania had committed to a one-sided arrangement to buy computing power from a Polish AI gigafactory. Częstochowa will become the first city in Poland to use the Polish Large Language Model to support the use of AI in providing municipal services. The government also pledged to purchase AI services worth €100 million between 2028 and 2033, with a matching contribution from the European Union. According to the government’s timetable, the European procurement process is expected to begin later this year. World.title: Prague Pride Strengthens Security Measures Following Berlin Attack
World.content:
Security will be tightened at this year’s Prague Pride festival following a deadly attack at a similar event in Berlin.

Czech police are preparing additional measures to protect participants in the week-long festival, which begins Monday.

The measures will also reflect changes to this year’s festival route and venue.

Prague Pride is moving its main festival area from Letná Plain to Štvanice Island. The traditional Saturday parade will also follow a new route, starting in the lower section of Wenceslas Square, continuing through the historic center and ending at Štvanice.



Organizers will begin the parade with a minute of silence on Wenceslas Square to remember the person killed in the Berlin attack.

“Thousands of people standing in silence will be a reminder that we will definitely not remain silent about violence motivated by prejudice,” Prague Pride director Kamila Fröhlichová said.

This year’s Prague Pride will feature more than 100 cultural, educational and social events. Dozens of associations, institutions, companies and individuals will organize programs at venues across the capital.

While many events will focus on the lives and experiences of LGBTQ+ people, the festival will also address wider questions surrounding human rights and civil society. A full program is available on the Prague Pride website.

Prague Pride was first held in August 2011. Its inaugural edition was met with strong opposition from conservative groups and politicians, who described the parade as obscene and accused its organizers of promoting what they called an “ideology of homosexuality.”

Then-President Václav Klaus was among the most prominent critics, arguing that society needed to oppose what he described as the spread of homosexuality.

Protests continued in subsequent years but gradually declined in size and intensity.

World.title: Prague Opens Air-Conditioned Space in City Centre to Help Beat Heat Wave
World.content:
People looking for relief from the heat in central Prague can use the air-conditioned ground floor of the Škoda Palace in Jungmannova Street on Thursday and Friday.

The city has opened the space to the public as temperatures across the Czech Republic are expected to rise well above 30°C. The building will be accessible from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on both days.

Visitors can sit on benches and chairs, refill their water bottles at drinking fountains and use the toilets. Drinks and snacks are also available for purchase.



The measure comes as the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute has warned of very high temperatures in parts of the country. Forecasters are advising people to drink regularly, stay out of direct sunlight where possible and avoid strenuous physical activity, particularly during the afternoon.

The Czech Republic is facing several days of intense heat, with Friday expected to be among the hottest day of the current spell. Temperatures above 35°C are possible in some areas.

Individual Prague districts are taking similar steps. Prague 3, for example, plans to make air-conditioned areas in its town hall, information centre and Žižkostel available to the public when temperatures are forecast to exceed 35°C. Visitors will be able to sit down, drink water and take a break from the heat.

The city says the cooling spaces are intended to provide temporary relief during the hottest periods, particularly for people who may struggle to cope with high temperatures.

World.title: Revolut Opens Private Market Funds to Czech Investors
World.content:
Revolut is expanding its investment services in the Czech Republic, giving retail customers access to funds focused on private equity, private credit and infrastructure.

The new products will become available in the Revolut app from July 31. The fintech has signed distribution agreements with four major asset managers — Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group — which collectively manage more than $2.8 trillion in assets.

The move gives Czech retail investors access to parts of the private markets that have traditionally been aimed largely at institutional investors.



Private market investments have often required substantial minimum commitments, frequently above €100,000, or around CZK 2.5 million. Revolut’s new offering is designed to lower that barrier and allow customers to add private assets to portfolios that may already include stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds.

Investments will be available directly through the Revolut app.

The funds will be offered through the European Long-Term Investment Fund framework, known as ELTIF 2.0.

How ELTIF 2.0 works

The structure is intended to provide investors with greater flexibility than traditional private equity funds, where capital can remain committed for several years and withdrawals may not be possible during that period.

The products offered through Revolut use an “evergreen” structure. This allows investors to put money into funds with existing portfolios rather than waiting for a traditional investment cycle to begin.

ELTIF 2.0 also provides scheduled liquidity windows during which investors can request the redemption of their holdings, subject to the conditions of the individual fund.

That does not mean the investments are as liquid as publicly traded shares. Private market assets remain difficult to sell quickly, and investors should expect to hold their money for the long term.

Revolut already offers Czech customers access to a range of traditional investments, including US and European stocks, ETFs, bonds and commodities. The addition of private market funds expands the investment options available through the same app.

World.title: From Old Town to Main Station: Tourist Charged €150 for Short Taxi Ride
World.content:
A tourist has reported an alleged taxi scam in Prague, claiming that a journey from Old Town Square to Prague Main Railway Station ended with an unexpectedly high fare and a disputed payment.

The incident reportedly took place on July 25 at around 16:15. According to the complaint, the driver charged CZK 980 for the ride, an amount the passenger said was far higher than the expected price for such a short distance.

The tourist claims that the driver refused to accept payment by card and requested cash instead.



“I paid him 100 Euros for the fare. He just took the note, swapped it and lied to me saying what I gave was 100 in Czech currency, and demanded me to pay the remaining 50 euro taxi fare,” the tourist said in his complaint.

“So I paid the initial 100 euro that was swapped, plus the 50 euro taxi fare.”

According to the passenger, the total amount paid for the ride was therefore €150 (over 3,600 CZK). He said he was rushing to catch a train to Bratislava and was unable to resolve the dispute at the scene.

The tourist also claimed that no receipt was provided after the payment. According to his account, the driver said an invoice would be sent by email, but it was never received.

The case has been reported to the relevant authorities, while details of the incident have also been shared online to raise awareness among other visitors.

Travellers are also encouraged to use established taxi applications or services recommended by hotels, restaurants, and official tourist information centres. Paying by card and confirming the expected price in advance can help avoid disputes.

World.title: Babiš Warns Czechia Could Become Net EU Payer by 2029 as Contributions Surge
World.content:
The Czech prime minister also said Brussels is likely to permit a larger budget deficit as Prague seeks funding for hospitals, highways, and other domestic investment.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has expressed alarm over the country’s rapidly increasing payments to the European Union, warning that the Czech Republic could become a net contributor to the bloc as early as 2029.

Following talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerová, Babiš said Czech payments into the EU budget had risen by 22 billion crowns (€911 million) this year alone.

“I was shocked by how much we are paying into the European Union,” he said, as cited by Echo24. “If in one year we are told that we will pay 22 billion more, that is a lot.”



Officials currently expect the Czech Republic to become a net contributor to the EU budget for the first time in its history in either 2029 or 2030.

Babiš was also asked about next year’s state budget deficit. When asked whether it would exceed this year’s planned shortfall of 310 billion crowns (€12.8 billion), he replied, “Don’t test me. I don’t know what the deficit will be.”

Schillerová said a reliable estimate would only be possible after the Finance Ministry publishes its updated economic forecast next month.

The government has informed the European Commission that it expects next year’s structural deficit to reach as much as 2.9 percent of GDP, compared with 2.4 percent this year. According to Schillerová, Brussels has provisionally accepted the higher ceiling.

“We have to invest in hospitals, highways and bypasses,” he said, justifying the overspend but maintaining that the deficit should remain significantly below 400 billion crowns (€16.6 billion).

Planned spending includes psychiatric hospitals, surgical facilities, oncology centers, highways and city bypasses. The government also intends to maintain defense expenditure at 2 percent of GDP.

World.title: Hundreds of Czech Castles and Chateaus to Offer Free Entry on Two Special Days
World.content:
Visitors will be able to explore more than 100 state-managed castles, chateaus, monasteries, and other historic landmarks across Czechia free of charge on August 30 and September 27.

The initiative follows a spring pilot program that granted free admission to selected state museums and galleries. According to the Ministry, strong public interest in that campaign encouraged officials to extend the concept to historic monuments managed by the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ).

The free admission will apply to the standard sightseeing route at each participating site, along with selected additional visitor circuits where available.



Tours will operate under normal conditions, meaning visitor numbers will remain limited and capacity restrictions will continue to apply.

The National Heritage Institute is expected to publish a complete list of participating sites, opening hours, reservation requirements, and visitor information on its website in the coming days.

The latest initiative builds on an earlier trial introduced this spring.

Between April and June, visitors were granted free entry on selected Sundays to five of the country’s largest state museums: the National Museum in Prague, the Moravian Museum in Brno, the Silesian Museum in Opava, the National Technical Museum in Prague, and the Technical Museum in Brno.

According to the Ministry of Culture, attendance at those museums nearly doubled during the pilot period, with the Silesian Museum recording the largest increase in visitor numbers. Selected state galleries also participated in the program earlier this year while officials assessed the financial impact of waiving admission fees.

The ministry has said one of its long-term objectives is to help restore visitor numbers at cultural institutions to levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.

World.title: On this Day, in 1419: the First Defenestration of Prague
World.content:
Six hundred years ago, an angry crowd stormed Prague’s New Town Hall and threw several royal councillors from its windows.

The attack, known as the First Defenestration of Prague, took place on July 30, 1419, and is widely regarded as the event that ignited the Hussite Wars—a conflict that transformed medieval Bohemia and left a lasting mark on Czech history.

Yet the violence that unfolded that summer day had been years in the making.

Its roots lay in the teachings of Jan Hus, a Czech theologian, university lecturer, and religious reformer who became one of the most influential figures of the late Middle Ages. Hus openly criticized corruption within the Catholic Church, particularly the sale of indulgences and the growing power of the church hierarchy. Rather than viewing the Church as an institution led by the pope and bishops, he argued that the true Church was the community of faithful believers.

Summoned before the Council of Constance in 1415 to defend his beliefs, Hus was arrested despite receiving a promise of safe conduct. After refusing to renounce his teachings, he was convicted of heresy and burned at the stake.



His execution outraged many across Bohemia. While members of the nobility saw it as the unjust killing of one of the kingdom’s own, Hus’s followers spread his ideas far beyond Prague through a network of priests and former university students. The capital, home to Charles University and the Bethlehem Chapel where Hus had preached, became the center of a rapidly growing reform movement.

Bohemia’s political circumstances also allowed the movement to flourish. Neither King Wenceslas IV nor the Archbishop of Prague took decisive action to suppress it, allowing religious tensions to deepen over the following years.

By the summer of 1419, the situation had reached a breaking point.

On July 30, radical Hussite preacher Jan Želivský led a religious procession through Prague after delivering an impassioned sermon. Although the march may have appeared spontaneous, historians believe the confrontation had been carefully prepared. Some participants reportedly arrived carrying concealed weapons, expecting violence.

The procession made its way to Prague’s New Town Hall, demanding the release of Hussite supporters imprisoned there. When the councillors refused, the crowd forced its way inside.

The assault was led by Jan Žižka, a military commander who would later become one of medieval Europe’s greatest generals. Several councillors were seized and thrown from the building’s windows. Although the fall itself was not fatal for everyone, those who survived were beaten to death by the waiting crowd below.

For medieval society, the act carried a powerful symbolic meaning. Publicly casting powerful officials from an elevated position represented the dramatic downfall of those who had abused their authority.

The defenestration did not, by itself, begin the Hussite Wars, but it made peaceful reconciliation increasingly unlikely. Just weeks later, King Wenceslas IV died, leaving the throne to his brother Sigismund, whom many Bohemians blamed for failing to protect Jan Hus at Constance. Relations between the Hussites and the crown rapidly collapsed, and in 1420 the first crusade against Bohemia was launched.

The wars that followed lasted more than a decade. They devastated much of the kingdom but also produced extraordinary military victories under Jan Žižka and established the Hussites as one of medieval Europe’s most formidable fighting forces.

The First Defenestration of Prague remains one of the defining moments in Czech history—a single act of violence that turned years of religious unrest into a revolution whose legacy can still be seen throughout the country today.

World.title: Czech Company Enters Fortune Global 500 for the First Time
World.content:
A Czech company has entered the Fortune Global 500 ranking for the first time in history.

Energy and industrial group EP Group (EPG), controlled by Czech businessman Daniel Křetínský, placed 179th in the latest edition of the prestigious list of the world’s largest companies by revenue.

The ranking, published annually by the U.S. business magazine Fortune, evaluates companies based on their total sales. EP Group reported revenues of $75.387 billion, equivalent to around CZK 1.6 trillion.

To put the figure into perspective, the Czech state budget expects total revenues of CZK 2.118 trillion this year.



EP Group’s portfolio includes stakes in major companies across Europe, including British postal operator Royal Mail, Slovak energy producer Slovenské elektrárne, German retail chain Metro and French energy giant TotalEnergies.

With its debut in the ranking, EP Group has also placed Prague among the headquarters of the world’s largest corporations. The Czech capital is now one of 242 cities worldwide where at least one Fortune Global 500 company is based.

Only 14 other countries in the Fortune Global 500 ranking have a single representative, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Poland, Austria and Thailand.

EP Group is also among a very small number of newcomers. Only 13 companies worldwide entered the top 500 this year for the first time, while another 11 returned after previously dropping out of the ranking.

The company’s rise reflects the growing importance of energy, infrastructure and industrial businesses in the global economy.

US companies dominate the ranking

American companies continue to lead the Fortune Global 500, with 141 firms making the list — the highest number since the global financial crisis in 2008.

World.title: Leading Chinese commercial vehicle brand FOTON available in Hungary! – photos, video
World.content:
Author: György Sipos

Since its founding in 1996, FOTON has grown into one of the world’s leading commercial vehicle manufacturers: in 30 years, it has conquered the markets of nearly 150 countries, and has held the market leader position in China for 21 consecutive years.

FOTON available in Hungary

Today, it is one of the world’s top-selling commercial vehicle brands, boasting the broadest model lineup. This event is also a historical milestone: Hungary is the 10th European country where FOTON is officially entering the market. This is not only a significant event for the Hungarian commercial vehicle segment, but also a new chapter in FOTON’s global expansion.

Source: György Sipos/HellóMagyar/DailyNewsHungary

At the event, I was able to personally get to know FOTON‘s full freight transport portfolio, as well as the business opportunities behind the brand. For me, one of the highlights of the day was the real off-road test drive of the TUNLAND models.

Source: György Sipos/HellóMagyar/DailyNewsHungary

Getting behind the wheel as a layman, I was absolutely blown away by how effortlessly the Tunland models handle, even under difficult off-road conditions. Although I am personally a lover of classic cars, it is undeniable how much modern technology simplifies driving—practically under any conditions. Since I’ve had very little to do with off-roaders, I would have easily gotten lost among the abundance of functions and buttons without the instructor’s guidance, but after a short introduction, the vehicle felt so familiar, as if it had been mine for a long time.

Source: György Sipos/HellóMagyar/DailyNewsHungary

Although today’s car prices can often be shocking, I must say that Foton has entered the scene with a highly competitive offer. However, I didn’t find the most impressive model among the off-roaders, but among the light commercial vehicles in the form of the Cavan C1: in exchange for an affordable price, you get an electric van that is not only highly practical, but also exceptionally well-equipped.

Source: György Sipos/HellóMagyar/DailyNewsHungary

Generous pricing

Technically speaking, this model is a real treat: it is not a conversion of a diesel van, but is built on a dedicated electric, low-floor platform co-developed by Foton and Bosch. For a starting price of HUF 9,990,000 net, you get a remarkably modern vehicle equipped with a weight-adjustable suspension seat. Depending on the version, it offers a cargo volume of 7–9 cubic meters, while its 105 kW motor and CATL battery enable a WLTP range of up to 333 km, plus it can be charged at an impressive 125 kW from a DC station.

If you missed: Fuel prices in Hungary rise at slowest rate in the EU

Although Foton is not a new brand globally, it is still a newcomer to the Hungarian market. Because of this, buyers might initially view it with understandable reservations, as there are no long-term local experiences regarding its reliability and durability yet. However, the manufacturer offers extremely generous warranty terms. For instance, the Cavan C1 comes with a 3-year general warranty with no mileage limit, 5 years or 200,000 km for the powertrain, and 8 years or 400,000 km for the battery, which won me over at first glance. If they can maintain this level of quality, the Chinese brand could have a bright future ahead in Hungary.

World.title: Extreme heatwave can force many trains out of service in Hungary
World.content:
Hungary’s rail operator has warned that several trains may be withdrawn from service in the coming days as extreme heat pushes the network to breaking point. Temperatures above 40C are causing serious technical failures across the system, with MÁV saying some FLIRT multiple units have already been disabled after their batteries overheated during the late-June heatwave.

Many trains may shut down during the peak of the heatwave

The problem is particularly inconvenient because the trains’ protection systems intervene automatically in such cases. Once the batteries overheat, charging is disabled, meaning the unit cannot be put back into service after stopping. At the end of June, roughly 30 FLIRT trains were rendered inoperable in a short space of time. Later entries in the government’s heat-alert bulletins also noted that FLIRT units had been taken out of service because of battery overheating.

What is more, the train cannot move again until the outside temperature falls to an acceptable level. In other words, passengers can be left stranded on board even when the air conditioning is no longer working, since that too requires electricity.

MÁV is now seeking a long-term solution together with engineers from Stadler, the manufacturer. The batteries have been inspected, the necessary replacements carried out and spare units secured. An emergency operating procedure has also been introduced for extreme heat, reducing the strain on the trains while technical staff continuously monitor their condition.

Failures cannot be ruled

The next step is to test heat-protection measures designed to reduce the thermal load on the battery compartment, as well as to trial a new battery-charging module. If successful, this could provide a fleet-wide solution.

Meanwhile, the government is continuing to monitor the condition of the railway tracks and the temperature of the rails because of the heat, and speed restrictions are imposed where necessary.

If you missed: Paks NPP shutdown date revealed, PM Péter Magyar says Hungary may face energy crisis

According to MÁV, further FLIRT failures cannot be ruled out as long as temperatures remain above 40C for extended periods. The current measures therefore reduce the risk, but do not yet amount to a final solution to the problem.

World.title: Getting to Budapest Airport by taxi will be very inconvenient from August but anger mounts over new rule – updated
World.content:
It will become a great deal more inconvenient to reach Budapest Airport, as fury mounts over a new rule. We updated our article with Budapest Airport’s reaction.

Reaching Budapest Airport by taxi: new rules spark fury

Budapest Airport Zrt., the company operating Budapest Liszt Ferenc International Airport, will abolish from 3 August 2026 the five-minute free transit allowed to Budapest taxis through the car parks on its premises, the Budapest Taxi Association said in a statement sent to MTI on Thursday, adding that the operator should suspend the measure until a solution acceptable to all can be found.

In practice, the association said, scrapping the five-minute free passage would mean taxis having to pay parking fees every time they drop off or pick up passengers. It warned that, as a result of Budapest Airport Zrt.’s decision, a significant number of cabs would only be able to set passengers down and collect them at the taxi rank 1,100 metres from the terminal building’s main entrance.

Will the Magyar government intervene?

The taxi organisation told the operator that immediate implementation of the change would lead to a severe deterioration in service quality, and on that basis asked for the decision to be suspended until a suitable solution for all parties could be worked out. Budapest Airport rejected the request for a delay, the association said.

In its statement, the Budapest Taxi Association urged the government, which holds an 80 per cent stake in Budapest Airport, to call on the airport operator to suspend implementation until the necessary legislative, regulatory and technical changes have been made to allow the transition.

Update: Budapest Airport operator rejects taxi association’s requests, open for dialogue

According to Budapest Airport, scrapping the five-minute free entry for taxis registered in Budapest from August is intended to create a level playing field among service providers. The operator said local taxis had until now enjoyed a privileged position, as all other licensed passenger carriers had already been able to use the area for a fee, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

Budapest Airport is introducing a practice already in use at several international airports, aimed at ensuring a more transparent and fairer sharing of the costs of infrastructure use. It says the move should also help to optimise capacity, improve traffic management and enhance passenger safety. The operator added that the system would not mean extra costs for taxi drivers, as it waited for an increase in the city’s base fare to offset the airport access charge.

Watch out: Budapest taxi fares to increase from Saturday

Taxi drivers, however, argue that the change would impose a payment obligation on every pick-up and drop-off, and that a significant share of cabs would only be able to collect or set down passengers at the taxi rank, some 1,100 metres from the terminal’s main entrance. The Budapest Taxi Association said this could seriously damage service standards and has called for the suspension of the change. Budapest Airport refused, but indicated that it was open to fine-tuning the system at a later stage.

The operator stressed that one five-minute free entry per day will still be available for airport car parks, and that a separate pick-up point and other short-stay, free parking options will also remain in place.

World.title: Breaking – Paks NPP shutdown date revealed, PM Péter Magyar says Hungary may face energy crisis
World.content:
For the first time in the Paks nuclear power station’s 42-year history, production is expected to shut down completely within 24 to 72 hours because of the Danube’s record-low water level, Péter Magyar, the prime minister, said on his Facebook page on Thursday afternoon.

Paks NPP shutdown date revealed

That means 2,000 megawatts will be knocked out of Hungary’s power generation by Monday at the latest, even as soaring heat drives up demand for electricity among households and public institutions, he added. According to water management forecasts, the Danube is set to fall further in the coming weeks, meaning a restart of the plant is certainly not expected in the short term, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

He said that water-management forecasts indicate the Danube’s level will continue to fall over the coming weeks, so a restart of the nuclear power plant is definitely not expected in the short term.

The prime minister said he wanted to reassure everyone that, although such a shutdown has never happened before, it poses no danger and that every step is being taken in full compliance with the strictest safety regulations.

Péter Magyar talks about critical energy-supply situation

He said that the full shutdown of the Paks plant, the failure and shutdown of the Danube Power Station on Wednesday, and consumption rising close to record levels could, by Monday at the latest, produce a critical energy-supply situation unlike anything Hungary has ever faced in its history.

Against an average summer evening demand of 6,000 megawatts, Mavir, the Hungarian transmission system operator, expects consumption to rise by 20 per cent in the peak period between 5 PM and 10 PM over the coming days because of the extreme heat.

Danube water level extreme low at Paks. Photo: MTI

He stressed that the national energy supply is currently secure, but that in the coming days “this unprecedented situation will require solutions we have not had to use before”. He added that the extraordinary circumstances would require coordinated work and exceptional unity.

The government is preparing a series of layered security measures for the coming days. First, it will mobilise available domestic power-generation reserves and secure the necessary electricity imports. At the same time, large industrial consumers will be asked to reschedule production and voluntarily reduce consumption: on the government’s instruction, Mavir will from Thursday call on several dozen major users of the high-voltage grid — including battery factories, cement plants, chemical works, car plants and other facilities — to curb their electricity use during the critical time window. Unnecessary energy consumption in government buildings will also be reduced, he said.

Request to the public repeated due to unprecedented situation

The prime minister repeated his request to the public that, where possible, people should move any electricity-intensive activities outside the evening peak period, between 5 PM and 10 PM, particularly the charging of electric vehicles and the use of air-conditioning units.

“Because of the severity of this unprecedented situation, we are asking everyone — including large consumers and the public — to act responsibly. It is in all our interests to avoid unplanned shutdowns and a system collapse, unexpected but already experienced in Western Europe and the Balkans,” he said.

He also said that a pre-prepared security system was available in the form of a rotating power-cut regime. This would be decided on by Mavir on professional grounds and would only be used if power-generation reserves, imports, voluntary reductions by large consumers and additional technical measures together were still insufficient to maintain balance on the national grid.

Péter Magyar also said that hospitals, social institutions and services essential to the functioning of the country would receive priority protection and attention.

Necessary legislation prepared

At the same time, the government has begun preparing the necessary legislation to handle the expected emergency energy crisis, so that it can intervene — if necessary on a compulsory basis — by ordering the scheduled, temporary disconnection of certain large consumers in order to safeguard Hungary’s energy security.

He added that it is the system operator’s job to maintain the balance between electricity generation and consumption at every moment, while the government’s task, in cooperation with the Defence Administration Office, Paks Nuclear Power Plant Ltd, Mavir and MVM, is to coordinate the activities of state bodies, energy companies and wholesalers, as well as large consumers, and to keep the Hungarian public informed in good time.

Record-low water levels

Due to the low water level of the Danube, a full shutdown of the Paks NPP, and with it the cessation of electricity generation, will become unavoidable within the next 24 to 72 hours, MVM Paks Nuclear Power Plant Plc. said on its website on Thursday afternoon.

In its statement, the company recalled that the Paks plant, which provides close to half of Hungary’s electricity generation and has a capacity of around 2,000 megawatts, is cooled by the Danube. Water is needed to cool the condensers, or units.

The Danube’s water level is currently 28 centimetres below the previous record low set in 2018, which was itself more than one metre lower than the 100-year minimum water level taken into account when the plant was designed more than 40 years ago, the company said.

Record-low water level in Budapest. Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

There is sufficient water to cool the units, but the intake pipes of the pumps needed for this are positioned higher than the present, and still falling, water level, meaning they can no longer perform their task. Technical work to lower the intake pipes has already begun, and within a few years the plant is expected to be able to continue producing power even at lower water levels than at present, it said.

The plant stressed that it is prepared to manage the emergency situation arising from a full shutdown. Procedures have been drawn up to deal with low-water conditions on the Danube, which are divided into four stages; the plant is currently at stage three. On the basis of forecasts, there is a realistic chance of stage four being reached, the statement said.

Less water required for cooling

Once all the plant’s units have been shut down, the cooling of the idle reactors must still be ensured. That requires five cubic metres of water per minute, compared with 100 cubic metres per second needed by units in operation.

Because water forecasts have changed several times within the same day, the plant can currently give only an estimate for the timing of a full shutdown. According to its calculations, the shutdown would have to be carried out within 24 to 72 hours.

The company also said it was prepared for the possibility of further extreme drops in the Danube’s level. In that case, Pajtás pumps installed in cooperation with the National Water Directorate would ensure that sufficient water remains available to keep the idle units cooled.

If required, 12 of the Pajtás pumps can operate continuously, with four more held in reserve and a further 13 on standby. The necessary operators and maintenance staff, spare parts and fuel are also available, it said.

Historic heat, drought: Paks NPP may be switched off, Hungary’s power supply could be pushed into crisis, industry may grind to a halt

Safety ensured

Even in the event of extreme low water lasting for weeks, the units would be kept in a safe condition, and once the appropriate water level is reached, generation would be restarted immediately and in stages. Depending on the water level, the units could be brought back online within a few days, the company said.

Continuous upgrades at the Paks plant have made it possible for the facility to generate electricity even when the water level is 120 centimetres below the design level.

But persistent, extreme drops in water levels will require further improvements in future. Those developments have already begun, and according to the plans, electricity generation will continue without disruption within a few years even at significantly lower water levels, the company said.

Information affecting the plant’s operations will be published on its official website and official Facebook page, where the announcement of a full shutdown will also be made.

The plant has asked the public to help maintain Hungary’s electricity supply security through responsible and economical use of power.

Large industrial energy consumers may make voluntary cuts in their electricity usage

Hungarian transmission system operator MAVIR, acting on orders from the government, will call on several dozen large industrial energy consumers to make voluntary cuts in their electricity usage, Prime Minister Peter Magyar announced in a post on social media on Thursday. He said MAVIR will contact cement factories, car and battery manufacturers, chemical plants and other large plants to cut their electricity consumption in the critical hours from 5:00 in the afternoon to 10:00 in the evening.

The PM said the government is preparing legislation so that it can intervene on a mandatory basis if necessary for the scheduled, temporary shutdown of some large consumers. Magyar said that at the latest from Monday, a critical energy supply situation that Hungary has never faced in its history could occur. “An unprecedented situation requires unprecedented solutions,” he added. On a normal summer day in the hours between 5:00 in the afternoon and 10:00 in the evening electricity demand averages 6000 MW but MAVIR estimates that the peak could now be some 20pc higher, Magyar said.

The prime minister noted that growing demand coincides with a 2,400 MW drop in Hungary’s energy output. Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plant will be shut down completely as water levels on the Danube, used to cool the NPP, fall, and the gas-fired Dunamenti Power Plant is malfunctioning. Magyar also called on households to be conscious and self-restrained in their electricity usage and said that despite the cuts in output, the situation is manageable.

The PM noted a rotational shutdown system is available, applying it is the decision of MAVIR. It will only be used if power plant reserves, imports, self-limitation by large consumers and other technical means are not sufficient to maintain the balance of the national grid. Magyar said that hospitals, social institutions and the provision of services essential to the functioning of the country enjoy special protection and attention.

World.title: German airline deceived major Hungarian city? Huge scandal brewing, debts piling up
World.content:
Just days before the parliamentary election, on 30 March, Levente Magyar, the deputy foreign minister, was still praising the scheduled flights relaunching from Pécs-Pogány after an 18-year break, under the German airline operator SkyHub Airlines. It took only a few months for the company to all but collapse, and now Pécs may be left chasing its money. The scandal has caused a stir locally, although the city leadership insists it thoroughly vetted SkyHub at the time and that the failure is not its fault.

German airline operator went bankrupt quickly

At a meeting of Pécs City Council’s Legal and Procedural Committee on 22 July, members had to consider a bleak proposal. According to the document, Skyhub, which operated the Pécs–Munich scheduled service, had become insolvent, meaning not only had the route already been suspended, but there was now little prospect of recovering the funds invested by municipal institutions and companies.

Read our previous article concerning the issue – Scheduled flights return to rural Hungarian airport

According to the document signed by Deputy Mayor Csaba Ruzsa, only two months after the service launched on 30 March, the German company informed the municipality on 27 May that, because of payment difficulties, it would stop flying on all its routes from 10 June. “Skyhub requested the opening of insolvency proceedings in Germany on 2 June 2026, about which Irány Pécs Nonprofit Ltd received official notification on 9 June 2026,” it added.

The German firm owes a great deal

The route operated only 21 times between the two cities, with very low load factors, even though at the end of March the deputy foreign minister had spoken in upbeat terms about the return of scheduled services as a sign of the rural airport’s future rapid development.

Instead of a success story, however, there has been a total flop. What is more, Pécs taxpayers’ money — a total of 774,000 euros, or more than 280 million forints — was transferred to Skyhub under various titles by municipal institutions. Some of that money can no longer even be recovered; only roughly a little less than half may be claimable. The committee approved the proposal, but also decided to launch an investigation. The head of the municipally owned Irány Pécs company, a partner of the German firm, has been asked to explain why it previously regarded the rapidly failing company as a reliable partner.

The arrival of the first scheduled flight at the airport in March. Source: Facebook/Magyar Levente

On this point, the Pécs municipality said the German company had undergone an exceptionally strict due diligence process at the time. Through its press office, the city leadership said the Skyhub PAD GmbH & Co. KG company commissioned to operate the service had been subjected to extremely rigorous vetting before the contract was signed. Nor, it added, did anything point to the risk of insolvency: within a single year, the company had increased the number of its investors from 40 to 100 and was also under contract with, among others, Lufthansa’s official partner airline, the Danish Air Transport (DAT), the city told MTI.

Regional airports in trouble

The airport in Pogány, a small settlement south of Pécs, was opened in 2006. Capable of receiving small and medium-sized aircraft, typically 50- to 100-seat passenger planes, it has since been used largely for hobby flying, while Magnus Aircraft Zrt, a small-aircraft manufacturer, has operated a production base on the site since 2018.

Over its 20-year history, the airport has handled scheduled services on three occasions, but each time the carrier abandoned the route for financial reasons.

Record summer for Wizz Air: 1,200 daily flights and new rules for travellers!

Austrian Airlines operated the Pécs–Vienna route for about six months in 2006 before cancelling it because of poor load factors. The Maltese airline Universal Air carried passengers between Munich, Malta and Corfu from spring 2024 until summer 2025. Skyhub launched the Pécs–Munich service at the end of March this year. According to the proposal, the aircraft operated at an average load factor of 40.6 per cent, although from May Lufthansa’s connecting Munich services also became available from Pécs via direct booking.

Transport Minister Dávid Vitézy said at a government spokesperson’s briefing in early June that regional airports were facing an operational crisis, and that efforts were under way to find a solution.

World.title: Foreign nationals held in custody in Hungary over assault on police officer and transporting drugs
World.content:
The Szekszárd District Court on Thursday remanded an Israeli national in custody, suspecting him of transporting drugs to the Ozora Festival, the Tolna County Prosecutor’s Office told MTI. Furthermore, the Siófok District Court has sentenced a foreign national to a two-year suspended prison term and expelled him from Hungary for three years after he assaulted a police officer on 1 July.

Israeli national in custody

The prosecution said the measure has been ordered for one month, on the grounds that there is an increased risk of flight and concealment in the case of a suspect accused of drug trafficking who has no ties to Hungary, and that he could jeopardise the taking of evidence if left at liberty, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

The prosecutor’s office added that police stopped the 27-year-old man in Tolna County on Sunday evening as he was travelling to the Ozora Festival in a hired car with German registration plates. The vehicle was searched, and officers found a significant quantity of drugs, mostly so-called party drugs, which the man allegedly intended to sell at the event, according to the statement.

Police officers doing house search – illustration. Photo: police.hu

Foreign national convicted over assault on police officer

The Siófok District Court has sentenced a foreign national to a two-year suspended prison term and expelled him from Hungary for three years after he assaulted a police officer on 1 July in Balatonőszöd, the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office said on Thursday.

If you missed: Israeli man stabbed at Hungarian festival

Citing a final judgment delivered by the court on Monday, the prosecution said the man, in his twenties, had driven away from a petrol station in Siófok without paying, prompting police to try to stop him. Ignoring their repeated orders to pull over, he fled at speed, but in Balatonőszöd he reached an area from which he could go no further.

Lake Balaton near Siófok. Photo: depositphotos.com

The prosecutor’s office said the police removed the man from the vehicle, but he resisted arrest and punched one of the officers in the face several times, causing bruising. Officers eventually used a stun gun against the man, it added.

The court found the driver guilty of violence against an official person.

World.title: Budapest’s renewed bike-sharing scheme Mol Bubi to kick off in days
World.content:
The revamped Mol Bubi bike-sharing scheme will be ready to launch fully in a matter of days, Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) said on Thursday.

Renewed Mol Bubi scheme to kick off soon

In a statement to MTI, the company said the public bike system had passed its test period with flying colours, with more than 1,200 users sharing their experiences. Most respondents gave the new generation of the service a positive assessment: overall satisfaction with the system stood at 4.48 out of five, while the new app received a rating of 4.25, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

Some 86 per cent of testers said they would definitely or probably continue using Mol Bubi after the full launch. Electric bikes proved the biggest hit. According to feedback, the main advantages of the system are electric assistance, an easily adjustable saddle, and the speed and simplicity of use.

There was also positive feedback on the new app. Users liked its simple, clear interface, the option to reserve bikes, and the way it quickly and conveniently supports pick-up and drop-off. Respondents said the new app makes the system significantly easier to use.

Additional suggestions and developments

Several suggestions have already led to specific improvements. The statement cited changes to the app’s speed, the display of rental history, and certain map functions.

Photo: BKK

If you missed it: Budapest’s iconic green bikes are back: New MOL Bubi launches with e-bikes, bigger fleet and free trial rides

Some users said the pedalling on the traditional bikes made it harder to reach higher speeds, and that they therefore felt the bikes were less dynamic than in the previous system, the company said. It added that a key consideration in designing the new Mol Bubi was that less experienced cyclists should also be able to travel around the city comfortably and safely, without any particular physical strain, which is why the bikes are primarily tailored to the needs of everyday, short urban journeys. At the same time, based on the feedback received, the BKK is examining options for fine-tuning the drivetrain and gearing.
