Independent analysts believe the amount could be even greater, considering US officials said $US11.3 billion was spent in the first six days of the conflict alone.

Nate Swanson, director of the Iran Strategy Project at the Atlantic Council and former State Department representative on the Trump administration's Iran negotiating team, said the true cost of the war so far was "certainly much higher".

"That number really only accounts for the munitions spent, it does not account for damage to US facilities," he told ABC's Radio National Breakfast.

" We have worn down US munitions in ways that were never really anticipated. "

The US is burning through Patriot missile interceptors to defend against Iranian attacks in the region. (AP: Sebastian Apel/US Department of Defense)

In late June, soon after the US and Iran agreed to a 60-day ceasefire, the US Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated the conflict had cost the US Department of Defense about $US40 billion.

Iran could mark 'end of an era' for US military Five months into a war Donald Trump said would last only weeks, the Iran conflict has so far cost the United States tens of billions of dollars.

It estimated $US26 billion went towards munitions alone, with a "high use" of expensive, sophisticated weapons.

"The thing that probably surprises me most was just how big a chunk of the cost was in munitions, particularly the high-end, expensive munitions," the report's co-author Mark Cancian, senior adviser with the CSIS Defense and Security Department, said.

The non-profit think tank highlighted the heavy use of powerful air defence interceptors such as Patriot missiles, the Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) and SM-3s.

THAAD interceptors have been in high use to defend against Iranian missile attacks. (Reuters)

The US has relied on the sophisticated interceptors to defend US assets in Gulf states, which have been a main target of Iranian drones and missiles attacks.

Concerns have been raised about depletion rates for items such as Patriot and THAAD interceptors, stocks of which a CSIS report this week found were running significantly low.

CNN reported that "three sources familiar with the matter" confirmed the CSIS estimates were "close to internal government figures".

A US official also told America's ABC News the figures roughly reflect estimated usage rates.

The US was also using large numbers of long-range ground attack munitions such as Tomahawk and Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles (JASSM).

More than 1,000 of each of the missiles were estimated to have been fired, costing about $US1.5—$3.6 million each, according to CSIS analysis.

Tomahawks are in high-demand globally and only a few hundred are manufactured a year.

Price tags for big-ticket items

Figures in the graphics below are based on CSIS estimates released before the breakdown of the June ceasefire and do not factor in weapons' usage since heavy bombings resumed earlier this month.

Trump administration officials have not provided broken-down figures.

The CSIS says its methodology combines Department of Defense initial cost releases, order-of-battle data, allied Gulf partner reporting, and "historical employment patterns".

US Patriot air defence missile interceptor cost and estimated Iran war use, according to a June 23 report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). (ABC News graphic: Kylie Silvester)

The Patriot is considered one of the most advanced air defence systems in the US arsenal.

The mobile surface-to-air missile defence system was designed to be used against aircraft, ballistic missiles and cruise missiles.

During the Middle East war, Patriots have also been used to intercept cheap Iranian attack drones launched at US allied-Gulf countries.

Eighteen countries operate the Patriot air defence system, including Ukraine, which is in desperate need of more interceptors to defend against Russia's missile attacks.

THAAD missile interceptor cost and estimated Iran war use, according to a June 23 report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). (ABC News graphic: Kylie Silvester)

The THAAD mobile system was specifically designed for ballistic missile defence.

It can hit targets at ranges of 150 to 200 kilometres, focusing strictly on intercepting ballistic missiles in their final stage.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE), which has faced extensive Iranian missile and drone attacks, said THAAD systems had played a crucial role in achieving high interception rates.

The US produces about 100 THAAD interceptors per year.

US Standard Missile 3 interceptor cost and estimated Iran war use, according to a June 23 report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). (ABC News graphic: Kylie Silvester)

The SM-3 ship-launched interceptor is designed to destroy short- to intermediate-range ballistic missiles during their mid-course phase in space.

It travels at hypersonic speeds and is capable of intercepting missiles outside the Earth's atmosphere.

Unlike conventional systems, it does not carry an explosive warhead, instead using "sheer force" to destroy its target, according to manufacture Raytheon.

The ship-launched Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) interceptor, which costs about $US4 million per unit, has also been used extensively extensively against Iranian threats such as ballistic missiles and drone swarms.

Iran's cheap arms tip balance

Iran does not have a modern air force, instead it has been using stockpiles of thousands of ballistic missiles and Shahed attack drones to wreak havoc on its US-allied Gulf neighbours in waves of strikes.

A look at Iran's ballistic missile program Iran has spent decades building the largest and most diverse ballistic missile stockpile in the Middle East and is refusing US demands to put limits on the weapons program.

Its one-way attack drone costs between $US20,000 and $50,000.

Iran has not disclosed the price of its various ballistic missiles.

Some analysts estimate Iranian short-range Fateh-110 missiles could cost only a few hundred thousand dollars each.

The Shahab-3, a frequently-used medium-range ballistic missile, is estimated to range between US$1 — 3 million.

Iran has spent decades building up its ballistic missile stockpiles. (Reuters: WANA/Majid Asgaripour)

Expensive US interceptors have been some of the only effective options to defend against Iranian attacks.

Throughout most of the conflict, the US and its allied regional partners have said about 80 to 90 per cent of threats were being intercepted.

But the US military has increasingly shifted to selective interception due to cost and inventory constraints.

"Diminished stockpiles may force the United States and its coalition partners to take more risks with interceptions," the authors of a CSIS report this week wrote.

" There are no good alternatives to Patriot and THAAD for ballistic missile defence. "

Expensive US interceptors are being used to take down cheap Iranian drones. (AP: Iranian Army)

Malcolm Davis, senior analyst in defence capability at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), said modern warfare was using "missile systems at a voracious rate".

And Western militaries could no longer get by with the mentality that "qualitative edge will always allow us to win".

"If we haven't learned from the lessons of Ukraine and past wars, then it's our own silly fault," Dr Davis told the ABC.

"We've gone down the wrong path by assuming, firstly, that quality gives us an automatic edge.

"And secondly, quality means we don't need to have a lot of weapons."

Damage in the Fujairah oil industry zone caused by debris after the interception of an Iranian drone in the United Arab Emirates. (Reuters: Amr Alfiky)

Need for low-cost solutions

A number of US media outlets reported US President Donald Trump paused the latest spate of attacks earlier this week, in part, due to concerns raised by officials about the vast expenditure of sophisticated and difficult-to-manufacture weapons.

Trump vows to hit Iran 'hard' in expletive ridden warning In a phone interview with Fox News, the US president reportedly said the US would "beat the f****** s***" out of Iran in response to the surprise strikes.

Mr Trump dismissed the reports.

A main issue flagged is the depleted stockpiles could create "a risk to US readiness to fight a war against China in the western Pacific", according to CSIS analysts.

Mr Swanson from the Atlantic Council said tens of billions of dollars in additional funding requested by the Pentagon would be prioritised to replenish weapons stocks.

"They need these funds actually to replenish what we had," he said.

" You can't rule out a forever war, but the reality is they [the US] can't even sustain what they've done so far. "

The Pentagon is accelerating defence production with new multi-year mega contracts awarded to major US weapons companies.

The US Army signed a record $US58.6 billion Patriot missile deal with Lockheed Martin this week.

Earlier this year, Lockheed was also awarded a contract worth $US35 billion to quadruple production of THAAD interceptors.

US weapons manufacturers are benefiting with massive contracts announced to replenish Patriot and THAAD missiles. (Reuters: Kacper Pempel)

Manufacturing lead times for critical weapons range from about two to more than four years.

Dr Davis said militaries, including Australia, needed to prioritise investing in low-cost interceptor capabilities that could be mass produced.

"Our thinking is based around these exquisite, boutique, very expensive solutions that will only be able be afforded for a very small number of missiles," he said.

"We can't be continuing on this trajectory if we want to win the next war. We have to fundamentally shift direction.

"I'm not saying we never produce systems like Patriot or THAAD, but we have to also compliment that with large numbers of low-cost systems that we can produce rapidly."

World.title: 'Life-saving' Australian-first veterans court to launch in SA
World.content:
A dedicated court for veterans which advocates hope will be a "life-saving" initiative will sit for the first time in Australia next week.

The South Australian Veterans Court (SAVC) Pilot Program will act as a specialist therapeutic court to connect eligible veterans with rehabilitation and support services prior to sentencing.

Advocates said the establishment of the court was in response to a recommendation from the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide.

The pilot is intended to run for 12 months and sit for half a day each month at the Elizabeth Magistrates Court in Adelaide's northern suburbs, a court spokesperson told the ABC.

The new court will act as a specialist therapeutic court for veterans. (ABC North Queensland: Rachael Merritt)

The spokesperson said the program would "recognise the unique nature of military service and its impacts on veterans and their families".

"It will also enable the court to approach sentencing decisions informed by a participant's rehabilitation progress and the circumstances associated with their military service," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said a veteran facing summary or indictable charges in any of Adelaide's magistrates courts could seek a referral to the Veterans Court, but only after entering guilty pleas to the most serious and majority of charges.

At their first SAVC hearing, the spokesperson said a "preliminary triage" would be conducted to assess the offender's veteran status, the connection between their service and offending, as well as their willingness to engage in rehabilitation.

A Griffiths remand would then be granted, meaning the veteran would participate in treatment and rehabilitation before sentencing, and would have regular court reviews to monitor progress.

The court spokesperson said all of the state's magistrates could preside over the SAVC and that some magistrates who had previously served in the ADF had expressed interest.

Addressing needs from the Royal Commission

The program was developed through an initial collaboration between the SA Department for Correctional Services (DCS) and Defence Kidz, which supports the children of defence families.

Chris Tilley is the senior advisor for Veterans Services at DCS, and a veteran who served for eight years in the Australian Defence Force (ADF) as an infantry soldier, including at Afghanistan and East Timor.

Chris Tilley will be sitting in the courtroom when it gets underway. (Supplied: DCS)

Mr Tilley said recommendation 88 of the royal commission recognised a specific need to "support veterans who are incarcerated, both during and after their incarceration".

"We're in a really unique position here in South Australia in that we have a population that is both large and small enough to be able to facilitate some really interesting initiatives," Mr Tilley said.

" It's not about treating veterans special, it's about community outcomes. "

Mr Tilley, along with a representative from Defence Kidz, Open Arms and the Department of Veterans Affairs, will be sitting in the court.

Defence Kidz chief executive Hayley Boswell said the idea for a specialist court came from "grassroot" origins.

"Chris Tilley and I were literally sitting in parliament having a chat about veterans incarceration and we're just brainstorming about how can we better support our veteran community," she said.

Defence Kidz CEO and lawyer Hayley Boswell hopes the Veterans Court will bring greater support for the families of veterans navigating the justice system. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

Ms Boswell, who is also a lawyer, said the program would link veterans to tailored mental health and behavioural support they may not have ordinarily accessed.

"There's a lot of veterans who are not signed up with DVA that just don't know these services exist … I think it's going to save lives, genuinely," she said.

"As a solicitor, we were always told don't disclose if your client is a veteran and so they would not be afforded support because people wouldn't know that they were veterans.

" There's a perception in the community through lawyers that when they were sentenced that the veteran should know better. "

Breaking a 'revolving cycle'

Senior criminal defence lawyer and Law Society of South Australia member James Caldicott said major indictable offences, such as drug, violence or sexual offences, would not be able to be diverted to the Veterans Court.

James Caldicott hopes the program will be expanded interstate. (ABC News: Tim Morris)

But the court would hear other serious offences which are usually dealt with by magistrates courts.

"There can be very serious or significant domestic violence related matters that could potentially be triaged through the South Australian Veterans Court program," Mr Caldicott said.

"That shouldn't be seen as diminishing the serious nature of the offending generally, and there will still be sentencing penalties representable of the offending conduct to an individual."

Mr Caldicott said the pilot program would be regularly reviewed and hoped it could also be established in other states and territories.

A 'positive step forward'

Veteran Ricky Skiathitis served as an infantryman in the ADF, including touring Afghanistan and East Timor, and knows the challenges of re-adjusting to civilian life after service

As the project manager for Andrew Russell Veteran Living, he has used his experience to provide emergency accommodation for veterans who are at-risk or experiencing homelessness.

Veteran Ricky Skiathitis welcomes the development of a dedicated Veterans Court. (ABC News: Rachael Merritt)

He welcomed the establishment of the court and has described it as a "positive step forward".

"I think the biggest one would be breaking the cycle, we don't want to keep repeating or [seeing] repeat offenders," he said.

"Wraparound support for the right person at the right time is only going to provide a positive housing outcome or a better outcome overall."

The SACV will sit for the first time on August 3.

World.title: Australia's old friend wasn't at the Glasgow velodrome, but the old enemy was
World.content:
The crowds at the 2026 Commonwealth Games have varied in size and spirit.

Particularly at the Scottish Event Campus, not far from the city centre, casual fans will wander down and get a taste of the action if they've got time on their weekend.

It's school holiday time in Glasgow too, so plenty of families looking for a way to occupy the kids have made their way into the various arenas.

You may never get the chance to watch again, so a spot of 3x3 basketball or bowls, accompanied by some frankly excellent tunes and an overpriced carton of chips, is a decent way to spend four hours.

Aussie sprint stars through to 200m finals, gold rush at the velodrome Australia's track cycling squad claims three golds on the first day of competition at the velodrome, as Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis fly into their second finals of the week.

That's especially true when the weather has been so dreary to start the Games.

But on a day when it dried out at last, thousands made a decidedly purposeful pilgrimage to the velodrome at the Glasgow International Arena, just next to the home ground of Celtic Football Club.

This was not something you happen upon. This was something you go to. This was the moment Scotland had been waiting for at the arena named for one of their favourite sons, Sir Chris Hoy.

Ironically, before every race it was a pre-recorded Sir Chris (the real thing might have caused a riot) and fellow Scottish icon Duncan Scott telling the crowd to quiet down — or "haud yer wheesht", as Scott said — for the starter's buzzer.

But even Hoy — the six-time Olympic, 11-time world and two-time Commonwealth cycling champion — couldn't have contained his house when it was Scotland's Neil Fache (along with pilot Aaron Pope) who won the first gold of the track cycling program for these Games in the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

Scots Neil Fachie MBE (left) and pilot Aaron Pope won the first gold medal of the cycling program in Glasgow. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Australian Kane Perris won Australia's first medal in that event alongside pilot Luke Zaccaria, and earlier in the day, Tara Neyland had picked up Australia's first world record in any event at these Games when she clocked 4:49.648 in qualifying for the C4-5 4,000m individual pursuit.

She later went on to win gold, but only after the women's team pursuit squad started what the cycling team hopes will be a gold rush in Glasgow.

Trailing New Zealand at the halfway mark of the gold medal race against New Zealand, the team of Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks, Alyssa Polites and Felicity Wilson-Haffenden put away their schedule and just started racing.

"That's my happy place. When we start racing, that's when I'm happiest. When the board goes away, and the hand signals come out, that's when I come into my own," 21-year-old gun Wilson-Haffenden said.

Women's team pursuit gold marked the start of what promises to be a big Games for Australian cycling. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"Just pedal. I was riding 50-cent coins by the end, the pedals weren't going around smooth but giving as much power as I had, grit the teeth and get to the finish line."

England pipped their men's counterparts, and Jessica Gallagher was unable to defend her Birmingham gold in the tandem B sprint final after a tyre failure caused a nasty crash with the New Zealanders in the second race.

But, as pilot Jacqui Mengler-Mohr put it: "It's not how many times you fall, it's how many times you get back up."

Silver medallists Jessica Gallagher (right) and Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr (left) had a nasty fall as they won tandem B sprint silver. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

And getting back up was exactly what the men's team sprinters did, going one better than the women's team and taking down their English rivals in the final.

They never looked like getting caught over the 1,000m race as Leigh Hoffman won a title as the leader of a new-look team with 23-year-old Danny Barber and 22-year-old Ryan Elliott.

The revamp came after the defection of Olympic gold medallist and sprint superstar Matthew Richardson, whose name Elliott wouldn't even utter when talking about the rivalry with Team England.

"I think it's definitely grown a lot since the swap and defection," he said.

"Between the GB guys maybe a bit less so but definitely between the defector himself."

Australian defector Richardson out of Games after fall Matt Richardson, a three-time Olympic medallist in Paris for Australia before he sensationally defected to the land of his birth, has been ruled out of the Commonwealth Games.

He wasn't the only departure after the team's gold medal at the Paris Olympics, with Matthew Glaetzer retiring and Tom Cornish pivoting to endurance events, making way for Elliott and Barber.

"There's a big change in the roster after Paris, and everyone's question then is: how well can our system back up? What's their depth?" he said.

"Us as the younger guys coming through wanted to prove we have depth in Australia and we're here because we're hungry."

Hoffman said he enjoyed riding with teammates who were 100 per cent in it for Australia.

Ryan Elliott, Danny Barber and Leigh Hoffman won team sprint gold in their new formation. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"It would've been great if he stayed with Australia but his heart was obviously never always in it, so good riddance," he said.

Richardson is no longer coming to Glasgow at all due to an ugly fall during a keirin race in Japan just days ago, with Hoffman disappointed he and Barber won't get a crack at him in the individual event.

"I would have loved for him to come here and race and see how I and Danny stack up against him," Hoffman said.

"I'm upset he's not here, but that is what it is. … I've got plenty of other fish to worry about."

England, Wales, Scotland, Australia and New Zealand are some of the world's strongest track cycling nations, with Malaysia's Azizul Awang and Nicholas Paul from Trinidad and Tobago threats for Hoffman and Barber.

But the good news is Hoffman isn't going anywhere.

"We checked his passport and his lineage," Elliott said.

"So he's good."

World.title: Record-smashing El Niño to deliver Australia a spring of droughts and fires
World.content:
El Niño is strengthening across the Pacific Ocean at an alarming rate and could annihilate all previous records in the modern era.

The rapid warming of our largest ocean is supplying additional heat into the Earth's atmosphere, contributing to a summer of extreme heatwaves and fires across Europe and North America.

But with El Niño still months away from peaking, its impact on global weather will intensify through the back half of 2026, including in Australia, raising the prospect of our hottest spring on record and a heightened risk of drought and fires.

Pacific heading to historic El Niño warmth

El Niño refers to a period of warmer-than-normal waters in the eastern and central Pacific Ocean along with the associated changes to the atmosphere, a state that can linger for up to 12 months.

According to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM), there have been 27 El Niño years since 1900, and both observations and forecasts indicate the 2026 El Niño is tracking into uncharted territory.

El Niños are usually evaluated by the Niño 3.4 index, a simple measure of the water temperature compared to average in a box along the equator.

A tongue of warm water along the equatorial Pacific is now deeply in El Niño territory and is affecting weather patterns across the globe. (ABC News)

After starting the year at about -1 degrees Celsius, the index has soared to nearly +2C, easily the fastest developing El Niño since 1900, and even accounting for climate change, the signal from the Pacific is the strongest on record for late July.

However, a typical El Niño does not peak until at least November, and leading global modelling, including the BOM's in-house model, are predicting further warming of the Niño 3.4 index to around +3.5C by mid-to-late spring.

Considering the highest ever monthly Niño 3.4 figures are +2.6C from January 1983 and +2.65C from November 1902 (using the ERSST v5 database) , the 2026 El Niño, therefore, has the potential to not only hit +3C for the first time, but comfortably evolve into the strongest on record.

Australia faces a scorching spring and summer

So why does a tongue of abnormal water temperature matter in the middle of the Pacific?

Climatologist and meteorologists pay so much attention to El Niño because the shift in marine heat and currents leads to sweeping changes through the overlying atmosphere

Australia is especially vulnerable due to our proximity to the Pacific.

Past events have contributed to some of our hottest and driest years on record.

And while El Niño might not peak for another four to six months, its greatest impact on Australia is likely to be felt sooner.

One of the most reliable markers of change in our region is the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), a calculation of the pressure difference between Darwin and Tahiti.

Its current value, shown in the graph below, has already dived to nearly -30, well beyond the El Niño threshold of -7, and the lowest in more than 40 years.

A deeply negative SOI indicates high-pressure is dominating Australian longitudes while lower than normal pressure is established over the central Pacific.

And since winds blow from high to low pressure, the typical easterly trade winds which bring tropical moisture to Australia from the Pacific have been reversed, so it is no surprise national rainfall has fallen off a cliff during the past few weeks.

With this pattern now established for the remainder of the year, the prospects for a wet second half of 2026 are poor, and the latest BOM seasonal outlook from August to October heavily favours reduced rain across eastern states.

The next three months is unlikely to bring significant rainfall to most Australia as El Niño continues to deepen. (ABC News)

Another driver of Australia's weather variability may also prevent rain this spring, a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), which is basically the El Niño of the Indian Ocean is also showing signs of emerging.

But while rainfall is likely to remain below average, our temperatures are almost guaranteed to stay well above normal.

Modelling is tipping a mean national temperature in spring about 2C above the 1961 to 1990 baseline.

This could make it Australia's hottest spring on record, challenging the current anomalies of +2.08C from 2024.

The map below shows the chance of spring having temperatures in the top 20 per cent of years, and it is nearly a sure bet for the southern half of the country.

The BOM's modelling is forecasting well above average temperatures during the coming months, that could easily challenge records for this time of year. (Supplied: BOM)

While rainfall during El Niño years typically returns to average by January, the effect on temperatures lingers into the new year, and while it is still beyond the lead time of forecasts, at this stage the most likely outcome is a summer of extreme heat.

But it is the combination of high temperatures and low rainfall, which is the greatest concern, since the two work together to dry out soils and enhance bushfires.

One positive though, is unlike the lead up to Black Summer, most of the nation is not in the middle of a long and severe drought, so we should not automatically assume devastating bushfires will be widespread.

How El Niño impacts global weather

El Niño 's footprint extends well beyond the Pacific.

The shift in marine heat and currents leads to sweeping changes through overlying pressure and wind patterns, which then has a downstream impact on both rainfall and temperatures as far afield as Africa and Europe.

Average global sea surface temperatures have already reached record levels for more than a month, but the mass of oceanic warmth also acts like a heater, transferring immense amounts of thermal heat into the atmosphere.

Thanks to the background influence of climate change, strong El Niño events therefore frequently send global air temperatures to record highs.

It is no surprise the planet's hottest year, 2024, coincided with the back end of the last El Niño, but with this year's episode already stronger, global temperatures are on a trajectory which may even see 2027 nearing the 2C warming above pre-industrial levels for the first time.

World.title: Kangaroo Island's seal population under threat from H5 bird flu
World.content:
The H5N1 bird flu has spread to Kangaroo Island, forcing marine experts to ask what can be done to protect species susceptible to the virus, such as the sea lion population.

Wayne Boardman from Adelaide University's School of Animal and Veterinary Sciences says the pros and cons of any intervention need to be weighed up.

"The issue now with bird flu being found on Seal Bay is that it's almost certainly going to go from the birds into the sea lions," Dr Boardman said.

"We've known from historical events in South America that sea lions and fur seals and the southern elephant seals down in Heard Island are particularly susceptible to this virus."

Wayne Boardman from Adelaide University's School of Animal and Veterinary Sciences. (Stephen Opie)

About 5 per cent of the species' entire global population lives at the site, and experts fear what the virus could do to the population of around 12,000 animals.

One strategy could involve treating the species for hookworm, an infection prevalent in pups.

"This hookworm infection is passed on from the mother to the baby via the milk, and so as they get this hookworm infestation it causes anaemia and general weakness," Dr Boardman said.

"In the face of another virus coming or a virus coming into this sort of situation, then you know those animals that are particularly weak or a bit under condition might be even more susceptible."

However, treating the pups is a "contentious question".

"We wouldn't know whether it would improve their ability to fend off [the bird flu] virus, but certainly the virus is very pathogenic, very virulent against sea lions and seals," he said.

"But if it [treatment] gives them just a little bit of extra help, then that might be a good thing.

" The thing that you need to consider with that is the disturbance that you might cause to those animals … is the benefit going to outweigh the cost of doing it? "

Another possible step is a mammalian bird flu vaccine, which is being trialled in the United States.

"The idea was to actually trial it on these northern elephant seals in captivity to see whether it would confer immunity and to then see if it was feasible to potentially use it in the Hawaiian monk seals," Dr Boardman said.

"I think it would be a really good thing to consider in the not too distant future, if not retrospectively."

Sea lions breed every 18 months. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

However, again Dr Boardman stressed that there would need to be lots of steps before that could happen.

"At what point do you say we need to risk it versus we've got animals that are dying left, right and centre?" he said.

"It's a very hard one, and I know generally speaking that the authorities would not really want to use an untried vaccine unless there was really good evidence that it might have some effect."

What has been done?

Beach tours at Seal Bay have been temporarily paused to help protect the local sea lion population. (Caroline Horn)

One step authorities have taken is issuing a pause on beach tours at Seal Bay.

Tourists are still able to visit and observe the sea lion population at Seal Bay, with boardwalk tours still open.

Exceptional Kangaroo Island owner Craig Wickham. (Caroline Horn)

Craig Wickham, who owns Exceptional Kangaroo Island, running wildlife tours, said the restrictions were a long time coming.

"It all seems to be fairly practical, well thought through and it's something which we're just going to have to deal with," he said.

"But I guess we're sort of in the space now where, you know, we've had fires, we've had COVID, we've had all sorts of things which have impacted on travellers and on experience, and so I think people have become fairly flexible in terms of 'OK, things happen'.

"We're not judged by what happens; it's how we respond to that and particularly around the communications."

Giovanna Paresxhi, from Brussels, arrived today on the island, and Seal Bay was her first stop. (Caroline Horn)

For Giovanna Paresxhi and her family, who had come from Brussels, arriving on Kangaroo Island today, Seal Bay was a priority first stop.

Though they were only recently informed that they would be unable to enjoy the beach tour, Ms Paresxhi and her family did not contemplate cancelling and instead wanted to do whatever was permitted.

"I mean, we came to see the nature because Australia is great in our minds, in our eyes, it's really great for nature," she said.

"We are very happy with what we have seen so far. We also could see a sea lion mum breastfeeding a little one, so this is amazing."

Giovanna Paresxhi and her family say even with the recent restrictions, Seal Bay is a must-see on any Kangaroo Island visit. (Caroline Horn)

Having now done the boardwalk tour, Ms Paresxhi said she was glad her family had not altered their plans.

"I think it's worth still not cancelling everything, but to come even for the boardwalk," she said.

"It's a must-see. We thought about that before [sic], but now it's confirmed that I would recommend to every person coming to Australia and to Kangaroo Island to do this little tour. It's really something."

World.title: Australia's Pacific climate meeting headed for 'disaster', officials warn
World.content:
Australia may be forced to drop its insistence that only prime ministers and presidents attend a high-profile climate meeting in Tuvalu as it struggles to convince them to fly to a United Nations gathering in the Pacific ahead of the main COP in Türkiye.

The federal government has been pressing leaders to attend the pre-COP meeting in early October, where officials, civil society and business representatives gather in Fiji, with a much smaller group of world leaders then flying on to the low-lying nation of Tuvalu, which is expected to be effectively inundated this century due to climate change.

The government won a commitment to hold the event with Pacific nations as part of its agreement with Türkiye.

Pacific countries to use Tuvalu's plight as example to world powers Fiji, Palau and Tuvalu look set to host world leaders and climate change ministers in the lead-up to COP31 in a bid to encourage larger countries to accelerate cuts to emissions.

Climate Minister Chris Bowen will take charge of global climate negotiations, while Türkiye retains the COP presidency and hosting rights for the main summit in November.

It has repeatedly spruiked the pre-COP as a chance to draw global attention to the Pacific's exposure to the ravages of climate change, while also driving greater climate ambition and mobilising funding for a key Pacific adaptation fund.

But multiple sources say Australia has not yet succeeded in convincing world leaders to attend the gathering, with several countries hesitating to commit.

'Difficult' to attract world leaders, foreign official warns

If the government fails to convince any leaders to join the meeting, it will be a severe diplomatic embarrassment for Australia, which has enjoyed several conspicuous foreign policy successes in the Pacific over the last few years.

"It has been very difficult for them," one diplomat told the ABC.

Funafuti, Tuvalu's most populous island. (Reuters: Kirsty Needham)

A second senior foreign official was scathing, saying they were worried the event was heading towards a "disaster" because Australia had spent months insisting that only leaders attend the gathering in Tuvalu.

The official said that bar was "far too high", and convincing leaders to make a long trip to the Pacific so close to the main COP event was never going to be easy, adding that several nations would prefer to send ministers or more junior representatives instead.

"They need to be more flexible, and more realistic," they said.

Other foreign officials were more sympathetic, saying Australia was facing serious headwinds, including uncertainty over pre-COP outcomes, scheduling clashes, the event's proximity to the main summit in Türkiye, and anxieties about political and energy security shocks from the ongoing chaos in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pacific Resilience Facility funding falling short

Australia has been keen for world leaders to use the pre-COP to commit additional money to the Pacific Resilience Facility (PRF), a Pacific-led financing mechanism for climate adaptation.

So far, countries have pledged $US172 million ($246 million) to the fund, well short of the initial capitalisation target of $US500 million by December this year.

The nation holding back the sea Tuvalu is building new land to hold back rising sea levels, but the majority of its people are applying to relocate to Australia. As they do, many are confronting a disturbing question.

But raising money for the PRF has been difficult in the current global economic climate, with several developed countries already moving to cut development assistance.

Some countries may also prefer to make any announcements about PRF contributions at the main COP summit in Türkiye rather than the pre-COP.

Tuvalu's high commissioner to Australia, Samuelu Laloniu, told a clean energy forum in Sydney on Wednesday that while he was not aware of any leaders who had committed to attend the meeting, Australian and Pacific officials were still working hard to convince them.

"We want them to see how we are coping, how we are adapting, and how we are building our resilience, how we, for example, are growing our food crops on lands that are frequently flooded with seawater," he said.

" Tuvalu has an opportunity to really showcase the need for immediate transformational changes in terms of how we adapt to the climate crisis. "

Australia may consider allowing ministers and political representatives to attend

The ABC has been told that Australia is now considering shifting course and allowing countries to send ministers or other political representatives instead, although it is expected to continue to pursue leaders as its top priority.

A spokesperson for the climate minister said Australia was "focused on bringing the world to the region to see climate impacts and solutions firsthand and deliver on Pacific priorities".

"That involves convening a range of actors and leaders, across government, industry and civil society," they said.

" Pre-COPs are critical to setting the main COPs up for success, and by bringing attention to the Pacific, we will be able to influence global negotiations to focus on our region. That's good for the Pacific and Australia. "

The spokesperson also declined to say whether any leaders had agreed to head to Tuvalu.

"Australia does not announce the travel plans of other nations," they said.

World.title: Social media pushing young adults towards 'DIY dentistry'
World.content:
Young Australians are delaying dental care because of the cost with many also performing "DIY dentistry" due to the influence of social media, a new national survey says.

The Australian Dental Association (ADA) has found 60 per cent of adults aged 18 to 25 are making decisions about how to manage their dental health through social media.

ADA vice president Angie Nilsson said that included getting veneers and aligners for cosmetic reasons and ordering whitening products that could damage teeth.

Dentist Angie Nilsson says young adults face a “concerning combination” of untreated dental problems, pressure from social media and preventable sports injuries. (Supplied: Australian Dental Association)

"It's not something that we recommend doing without a registered dental practitioner advising and ensuring that they're getting the right product, the right concentration and that it is actually in line with all the Australian regulations that we have to keep people safe," Dr Nilsson said.

University student Ava Veres said she had seen "whitening hacks" and ads for whitening strips online.

"Some of my friends have actually considered buying it recently," she said.

The business and drama student said she'd started getting pain from her wisdom teeth but could not afford to book a dental appointment for advice.

"I have been dreading even looking at that because it's just not really on the cards for me," she said.

Ava Veres says her wisdom teeth are causing her discomfort but she’s putting off seeing a dentist because of the cost. (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

"Now I'm living in a share house by myself in Brisbane so it's a little bit different [to living at home]. Expenses are on me now."

Wisdom tooth issues

The ADA's latest national consumer survey, released today, found 60 per cent of adults in the 18 to 25-year-old age bracket have had wisdom tooth-related issues such as pain, swelling, crowding, infection, and discomfort.

The number of respondents with wisdom tooth problems was higher in remote areas, at 65 per cent, than in metropolitan areas, at 59 per cent.

Dr Nilsson, who practises dentistry in public clinics in northern NSW, said wisdom teeth did not always need to be removed but it was "really important" to talk to a dentist about how to manage any problems.

"It can escalate, you can get infection, there can be issues involved with bone affecting other teeth — so it's important not just to let it go and hope that it gets better," she said.

The dentist said many young adults were "falling through the cracks" when it came to oral health care because they were at an age where they had moved out of home and sometimes come off their parents' private health insurance.

"Unfortunately, many are delaying dental visits until something goes wrong, and by then the problem is often more painful, more complex, and more expensive to treat," Dr Nilsson said.

Dr Nilsson said young people are "falling through the cracks" and delaying dental care due to the cost. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"If you catch things early on, it's going to be less painful in your pocket, less painful in your mouth."

She also said good daily oral health care could help prevent problems.

"Brushing twice a day for two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste is key. Spit don't rinse is a good one — because then you get a layer of the toothpaste on there," Dr Nilsson said.

Law student Ryan Quigley said while going to the dentist was something he had thought about, it was "not the highest priority" because of his other living expenses.

"It definitely needs to become more affordable, especially for young people making the transition, like myself, out of home, to make it more affordable, make it more accessible and then that'll improve overall dental health for everyone," he said.

Brisbane university students Maksim Krilov and Ryan Quigley say dental care is too expensive for young Australians. (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

Mr Quigley's friend, finance student Maksim Krilov, said general dental check-ups were too expensive for a lot of young people.

"Medicare, in general, I think needs to cover more," he said.

Calls for dental Medicare reform

Dental spokesperson for the Australian Greens, West Australian Senator Jordon Steele-John, said the party continued to push for "the mouth to be treated as part of the body" by including dental care in the publicly funded Medicare system.

"For decades dentists, experts, community advocates and The Greens have been calling for the reform that's needed, bringing dental care into Medicare and yet we've seen government after government fail to take the action that is needed," Senator Steele-John said.

"The Labor government just has not done enough in this area."

Senator Jordon Steele-John. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

In a statement, a spokesperson said the Albanese government "recognises that oral health is fundamental to overall health, wellbeing and quality of life".

"The government continues to make a significant funding contribution through the National Health Reform Agreement (NHRA) for public hospital services, including hospital-based dental treatment," the spokesperson said.

They said the Commonwealth was "working closely with states and territories" to develop a new National Oral Health Plan.

The use of mouthguards was another issue highlighted by the ADA survey which found only 38 per cent of young adults who played a high-impact sport were wearing the protective devices.

According to the survey, 13 per cent of young adults had experienced a sports-related injury involving their teeth or mouth.

"The damage that can be done by not having a custom-made mouth guard from a dental practitioner, it could be devastating," Dr Nilsson said.

The survey was conducted in November 2025 via focus groups, phone interviews and online surveys and had 25,000 respondents aged 18 and older.

Last year's survey focused on the oral health of children.

World.title: The ABC bureau that's older than the organisation itself celebrates 95 years
World.content:
Long before smartphones delivered footy scores in an instant, central Queenslanders tuned their radios to hear Terry Moore's familiar voice each weekend.

For more than two decades, the late rugby union correspondent was one of the many voices that became synonymous with ABC Capricornia, including on the station's Sports Show from the early 1980s.

"It was a unique program where rugby union, rugby league, Australian Rules [Football] and soccer [correspondents] all sat in the room together and basically chewed the fat," Terry's son, Tom Moore, reflected.

"It was an amazing show and it was predominantly local sport, which was fantastic."

Tom Moore with a framed service medal and letter presented to his late father Terry from then-ABC board chair Donald McDonald. (ABC Capricornia: Russel Talbot)

The show evolved in 1990 into the weekend institution known today as ABC Grandstand Sport.

As ABC Capricornia celebrates 95 years of storytelling this week, generations of dedicated staff and volunteers have reflected on the Rockhampton station's role in central Queensland life, including the Moore family.

"Saturday was rugby day for the Moore family and the whole day started here in the studios at ABC," Tom said.

"The rest of the day was spent at rugby, and if Terry Moore wasn't at Rugby Park on a Saturday afternoon then something was wrong."

A photo of engineers with the original microphones from 4RK in the 1930s. (ABC Capricornia: Jess Hinchliffe)

The stories, the crises, the community

From sharing the region's sporting triumphs and community milestones to serving as the trusted emergency broadcaster through floods, cyclones and bushfires, ABC Capricornia has been a constant for almost a century.

As one of regional Queensland's oldest radio stations it is, in fact, older than the ABC itself.

Known as 4RK in its humble beginnings, the privately-run Australian Broadcasting Company started the station at Gracemere on the outskirts of Rockhampton in 1931.

Loading...

The Australian Broadcasting Commission, later to become Corporation, was launched the following year.

The ABC took on 4RK, and the Rockhampton station became the fledgling national broadcaster's first regional Queensland radio station.

The station moved to its current location on Quay Street in 1963 into a building that was formerly Mount Morgan Gold Mining Company's head office and gold vaults.

The ABC Capricornia building on Quay Street was once the Mount Morgan Gold Mining Company office. (ABC Capricornia: Erin Semmler)

Legacy lives on through airwaves

Terry Moore's early involvement began with the ABC's classical music Concert Series in the late 1960s before becoming a much-loved contributor on the station's sports show, anchored by CQ's "voice of sport" Vince Pheely.

"Dad had probably close to 35 years involvement with the ABC," Tom said.

After a short battle with bowel cancer, the long-serving rugby union stalwart and one of the founding members of the sport in Rockhampton died in October 2001.

Some of the station's broadcast equipment used in the early days, alongside an old newspaper clipping calling for music auditions. (ABC Capricornia)

Six months before his death he was honoured with a letter of "special recognition" and a meritorious service medallion from then-ABC board chair Donald McDonald.

"Your regular reports on rugby union happenings on the ABC Capricornia Saturday sports program have helped give our regional service credibility and authority, and have been widely appreciated by the Queensland audience," Mr McDonald wrote.

"ABC regional radio wouldn't enjoy the standing it has in the community without the voluntary efforts of people like yourself who've been prepared to go above and beyond the call of duty to serve the people of central Queensland.

"You've not only kept the local community well informed on your chosen sport but have presented these reports with great warmth and good humour, endearing yourself to many of our listeners."

From the Queen's message to election results and Test cricket coverage, ABC radio and TV in its humble beginnings in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia)

Tom Moore, who followed in his father's footsteps behind the microphone on the Saturday sports program from the early 2000s, said the honour was a source of immense pride for his family.

"It was special recognition for what dad had done, and if we don't have volunteers like that then shows like that don't happen," he said.

"He was instrumental in forming and revitalising rugby [union] in Rockhampton back in those years."

ABC Capricornia was the first ABC station in regional Queensland. (ABC Capricornia)

Celebrating 95 years of Aunty

Central Queensland-based Nationals leader Matt Canavan said ABC Capricornia's 95-year history was a "pretty big innings" and testament to the station's deep roots in the community.

"It just emphasises how important Rockhampton has been to our state and country's development, with it being the first ABC radio station in regional Queensland," he said.

" It won't be long until it hits the big 100, and it's great to see that it's still continuing to provide important news to our region. "

The ABC Capricornia building on Quay Street in Rockhampton as it is today. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

Rockhampton Regional Council Mayor Tony Williams echoed those sentiments, also paying special tribute to the local emergency broadcaster.

"The ABC is the backbone of regional Queensland. From sharing local news, stories and events to preparing us and responding to natural disasters," he said.

" Our local station has been at the forefront of every major event that's happened in our region for the last 95 years. "

According to Member for Rockhampton Donna Kirkland, the "remarkable milestone of 95 years of serving central Queensland" showed its continued importance as a trusted source of news and information for the region.

"This anniversary is a testament to the dedication of its journalists, presenters, producers and staff, past and present, who have worked tirelessly to keep central Queensland informed."

World.title: ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple reports iPhone sales surge
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple reports iPhone sales surge Stan Choe Updated July 31, 2026 — 6:39am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A monster day for Microsoft’s stock following signals that its big spending on AI is translating into profits led a powerful rebound on Wall Street, while computer-chip companies regained some of their sharp recent losses. In the bond market, though, worries remained about inflation potentially remaining high for years. The S&P 500 rallied 1.7 per cent and more than recovered its drop from the day before, which was its worst in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 613 points, or 1.2 per cent. The Nasdaq composite, which is full of artificial-intelligence stocks, rallied 2.8 per cent a day after it fell 9.8 per cent below its record set last month. Technology stocks continue to drive the direction of Wall Street. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures pointing to a gain of 110 points, or 1.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.35¢. On Wall Street, Microsoft led the way and leaped 15.5 per cent for its best day in nearly 18 years after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Growth was strong for its Azure cloud business, and CEO Satya Nadella said it reflects how customers are using Microsoft to move into AI.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Perhaps just as importantly for Wall Street, Microsoft did not announce a big increase in how much it plans to spend on AI investments, something that several other Big Tech rivals have done. Worries are high that such spending is eating into companies’ cash flows and may not ultimately be worth it if AI does not produce as much productivity and profits as promised. Apple released its results after the closing bell, with sales and profits beating Wall Street expectations, fuelled by its customers snapping up iPhones and MacBooks amid price increases across the consumer electronics sector. Driving Apple’s results was a 21.7 per cent increase in iPhone sales to $US54.25 billion ($77.2 billion), above analyst estimates of $US53.86 billion, according to LSEG data. Those iPhone sales were Apple’s best-ever for a third quarter, when phone sales typically begin to slow as customers anticipate new models during the fall. Apple shares are 3.3 per cent lower in after-hours trade. Meta Platforms fell 8 per cent. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though it made slightly more in revenue than expected. It also raised the lower end of its forecasted range for spending on investments this year.



Companies involved in the making of the computer memory and processors that such “hyperscalers” are buying to power their AI efforts rose, recovering some of the big losses they’ve taken on worries their stock prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI. Micron Technology jumped 18.4 per cent, for example, to trim its loss for the week to 5 per cent. It was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500 after Microsoft. Lam Research, a supplier to the semiconductor industry, soared 18 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chip giant Advanced Micro Devices rallied 13 per cent. On the losing end of Wall Street was Jersey Mike’s Subs. The sandwich chain’s stock fell 6 per cent in its first day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange. All told, the S&P 500 rose 121.48 to 7,437.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 613.92 to 52,208.06, and the Nasdaq composite leaped 679.24 to 25,122.18.



In the bond market, longer-term Treasury yields held steadier following their sharp accelerations Wednesday. They had jumped after the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, gave few clues about what the central bank will do with interest rates to combat the painfully high inflation that continues to hurt the country. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they can also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury was 4.67 per cent, the same as late Wednesday. The 30-year Treasury yield ticked up to 5.22 per cent from 5.20 per cent, a day after it shot up from 5.09 per cent. Those yields move with investors’ expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years. Warsh reaffirmed on Wednesday the Fed wants to get inflation back to 2 per cent, even though the central bank decided not to raise interest rates despite inflation remaining higher than that. He also implied the bond market may already be doing some of the Fed’s work to restrain inflation, and he pointed to how yields have climbed since the central bank’s last meeting six weeks earlier. That leaves investors questioning whether the Fed is prepared to act if inflation worsens, or whether it is relying on financial markets to achieve the same outcome, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management.



“If investors conclude that the latter is true, the credibility of the Fed’s inflation-fighting commitment could come under increasing scrutiny. Arguably, it already is.” Related Article Opinion

Home loans Buckle up for the banks’ mortgage war! Home loans have fallen off a cliff Elizabeth Knight Business columnist President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates even though they could cause inflation to accelerate. Reports released Thursday suggested the U.S. economy’s growth slowed by more during the spring than economists expected. A measure of Inflation, meanwhile, remained worse last month than the Federal Reserve’s target, but it slowed from May’s level. In the oil market, prices eased. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.4 per cent to settle at $US86.88 per barrel.



It had swung as low as $US72 early this month and as high as $US102 last week on uncertainty about whether the United States and Iran could reach a deal to allow oil tankers to move freely again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. In stock markets worldwide, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. Seoul’s market has been at the centre of AI’s huge swings because it’s dominated by two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. After more than doubling through this year’s first six months, the Kospi has plunged 34 per cent so far in July. Its drop on Thursday came as Samsung Electronics dipped 0.7 per cent. The tech giant reported a record profit for the spring and said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply, but its earnings nevertheless fell shy of analysts’ high expectations. AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist
World.content:
SportCyclingCommonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist Billie Eder July 31, 2026 — 6:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was flicking through her local newspaper in Tasmania in 2021 when she saw an  for a cycling talent search. Bored at home during the COVID-19 pandemic, she thought, why not show up and give it a crack? Five years on, Wilson-Haffenden is a Commonwealth Games champion after motoring home to win gold in the women’s team pursuit alongside Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks and Alyssa Polites after only starting the sport in 2021. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory in the women’s team pursuit. Getty Images “I don’t think I can say this too loudly because COVID probably wasn’t great for a lot of people. But for me, it changed my life,” Wilson-Haffenden said.



“I can’t be grateful for COVID, but I can be grateful for the outcome, that’s for sure.” Wilson-Haffenden, who was a hockey player at the time, was lucky to make it at all – she had to call in a favour and delay her tryout. “I actually couldn’t make it on the talent ID date, and called saying ‘I really want to give this a crack’,” she said. Australia’s gold medal winning women’s pursuit team. Getty Images “So they made a little allowance for me, but I just think it’s a message to all young kids, if you’re interested, give it a crack because you never know where it’ll take you.”



She now spends most of the year in Girona – a cycling town in Catalonia, in the north-east of Spain – but said it was her formative cycling years in Tasmania that turned her into a champion. “I actually think it’s the cold mornings in Tassie that really build character – I think G [teammate Georgia Baker] will attest to it as well,” Wilson-Haffenden said. Tara Neyland broke a world record on her way to winning gold. Getty Images “It’s a pretty lonely sport. There are lots of times on the bike, you’re out there 6am, freezing cold, dodging wallabies down in Tassie, and it’s not glamorous, but I think that’s what builds champions. And we’ve got two Tasmanians right here winning a gold medal. It speaks for itself.” The Australian team’s victory continues its unbeaten run in the event at the Commonwealth Games. Since the team pursuit was introduced at the 2018 Games on the Gold Coast, Australia’s women have never lost.



The women’s pursuit was one of three gold medals Australia won at the Chris Hoy velodrome on day one of the cycling in Glasgow, along with Tara Neyland, who set a new world record on her way to gold in the women’s C4-C5 individual pursuit, and the men’s sprint team, who won without former teammate Matthew Richardson. Richardson represented Australia until 2024, when he defected to England following the Paris Olympics. The allegiance switch was a shock to the Australian cycling team, including Leigh Hoffman, who earlier this week said Richardson “went on a holiday and never came back”. But the Australian team of Hoffman, Ryan Elliott and Daniel James Barber managed to win without him – defeating England in the gold medal race. They didn’t, however, get the chance to race him. Richardson withdrew from the Games earlier this week after injuring himself in a crash during a world series race in Japan. Ryan Elliott, Daniel James Barber and Leigh Hoffman celebrate after winning gold. Getty Images



However, team officials told reporters Richardson wouldn’t have taken part in the team race anyway because he wouldn’t have arrived in Glasgow in time. Nevertheless, the Australian team said it was nice to get a win over England. Asked whether it was good to win without Richardson on the team, Hoffman said: “It would have been great if he stayed with Australia, but his heart was obviously never always in it. So, good riddance.” Australia and New Zealand collide in the second of three races for the women’s tandem B sprint gold medal. Getty Images Among Australia’s other cycling medallists were Jessica Gallagher and pilot Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr, who won silver in the women’s tandem B sprint finals after a crash in the second of their three finals races.



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Davies and Hull win gold and silver; Aussie cyclist sets world record; Kennedy, Lewis into 200m final; Diamonds complete demolition job Tandem riding is a para cycling event where a visually impaired athlete has a pilot at the front of the bike. The duo had a tyre failure, which caused the crash and forced them to rest before the Kiwis went on to win the final two races and clinch gold. “When that tyre pressure literally disappears, you’re riding on carbon rims,” Mengler-Mohr explained. “It’s like going from being on roller skates to ice skates, and just sliding and having no traction. There’s nothing we could have done.”

World.title: George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage Ardee Napolitano July 31, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paris: Hollywood actor George Clooney and his British wife Amal, an international human rights lawyer, have evacuated their luxury home in south-eastern France as a result of the wildfires blazing in the region. The star behind the Ocean’s Eleven franchise and other films made the statement on Thursday (France time) in a letter to Didier Bremond, the mayor of the town of Brignoles, about 90 kilometres east of Marseille, Clooney’s publicist Guido Gotz said in an email. George and Amal Clooney. Alberto Pezzali/Invision/AP Addressed “Dear Didier”, the letter said the Clooneys had “no idea whether our beautiful home makes it through this terrible moment”. But as they evacuate Brignoles they wanted to assure Bremond that, whatever happened to the community, “we’ll be part of making it whole”, the letter said.



The Clooneys bought their home on a vineyard in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur region in 2021 when it had an estimated value of about €9 million ($15 million). In an interview with Esquire last October, Clooney described their “farm in France” as their primary residence. Related Article Updated

Bushfires ‘Doing their best to survive’: Inside Bordeaux’s wildfire refugee centre The fire near Brignoles broke out Wednesday afternoon and burned some 100 hectares, local officials said. The blaze was far smaller than a vast inferno that has swept up the region around Bordeaux in southwestern France in recent days. About 700 residents from the areas near Brignoles had been evacuated, but were allowed to return to their homes on Thursday after the fire was brought under control, the officials said. Water-bombing helicopters remained deployed over the area after the evacuation order was lifted, the regional administration said. It said weather conditions remained unfavorable, with high temperatures and winds expected to pick up again in the afternoon.



The French government in December announced that the Clooneys along with their twins Ella and Alexander were awarded French citizenship. Related Article Celebrity life Clooney takes swipe at Trump after dig over French citizenship In the Esquire interview, Clooney said part of the impetus for the move to France was that he was “worried about raising our kids in LA, in the culture of Hollywood”. US President Donald Trump seemingly welcomed the news the pair had been granted French citizenship, calling them “two of the worst political prognosticators of all time” and claiming the actor was better known for his politics than his “totally mediocre movies”. But George Clooney hit back, saying he also wanted to “make America great again” – starting with the US midterm elections in November.



Europe is sweltering under an exceptionally hot and arid summer, creating tinderbox conditions for unprecedented fires that have flared from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean and forced hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate homes and vacation spots. Firefighters also battled flames in the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, Greece and Turkey on Thursday and were tamping down smouldering forests in southwest France where 224,000 people had been forced to flee. Romania shut down both reactors at its Cernavoda nuclear power plant due to low water levels in the Danube River used to cool them. A firefighting aircraft releases fire retardant in Lanton. Getty Images In the Bordeaux region, wildfire evacuees streamed back to nine localities that authorities now deem safe after round-the-clock combat with the huge fire that ignited last week.



“It’s the first somewhat optimistic day,” said Sophie Brocas, prefect of Bordeaux’s Gironde region who gave the go-ahead for nearly two-thirds of the 224,000 evacuees to go home, including 60,000 allowed back to three Bordeaux suburbs on Tuesday. Related Article Bushfires As south-west France burns, it’s not just the flames that have residents worried Authorities said the blaze is no longer growing beyond the 420 square kilometres already affected – an area four times that of Paris. A heat wave – France’s fourth of the year – gave way Thursday to cooler weather, higher humidity and even a little rain, helping the effort. World.title: Defending champ de Minaur beats Hewitt in first of ‘many battles to come’
World.content:
Updated SportTennisATP Tour Defending champ de Minaur beats Hewitt in first of ‘many battles to come’ Marc McGowan Updated July 31, 2026 — 5:34am ,first published 2:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cruz Hewitt was gasping for air with a towel over his head 15 minutes into his first official clash with Alex de Minaur in Washington on Friday. The scoreboard was sobering for the 17-year-old rising star: 5-0 to de Minaur, his friend and regular guest at the dinner table for Christmas. Hewitt had won only six points, while nervously spraying almost double as many errors. Alex de Minaur ended Cruz Hewitt’s breakout week in Washington. Getty Images None of this was surprising, given the decade difference in age and even wider gap in their resumes. De Minaur has routinely dispatched fellow Australians, and was never going to take it easy on the teenager, no matter how friendly they are off the court.



Related Article Wimbledon Cruz Hewitt fell agonisingly short at Wimbledon. His next dream is closer to home The world No.6 and defending champion finished the job with relative ease, 6-2, 6-3 in barely an hour over the Wimbledon junior boys’ finalist to book a quarter-final against Brandon Nakashima – but not before Hewitt showed glimpses of why he is so highly rated. Hewitt smiled as he walked to the net afterwards before embracing de Minaur, who offered his protege kind words, including wishing him “good luck for the next 10 years of your career”. “It was definitely weird,” de Minaur said post-match. “I would say that I knew I was going to play him on the tour someday, but I didn’t actually expect it to be this week. It was an amazing feeling. Even all the lead-up, seeing all the incredible pictures that we have together, and how we’ve grown up, both of us, and I’m ecstatic.



“I’m glad that I managed to get through, but I’m sure we’re going to have many, many battles in the years to come.” With Australian bands INXS, AC/DC and Midnight Oil fittingly blasting through the speakers at the change of ends, Hewitt shook off his error-strewn opening to illustrate why many good judges believe he has a bright future ahead. De Minaur and Hewitt embraced at the net afterwards. Getty Images It started with the son of former world No.1 Lleyton Hewitt coming out on top in a bruising extended rally to begin the sixth game of the match on de Minaur’s serve. Hewitt nailed a down-the-line backhand pass winner at full stretch for 0-30, and shortly after, a fluffed de Minaur drop shot attempt delivered Hewitt the break and his first game of the match. Hewitt pumped his fist, and the Washington crowd gave him a warm response.



Related Article Tennis Australia How a Portofino honeymoon and 13 days without tennis helped de Minaur move on from Wimbledon heartbreak It was relief as much as anything else, but Hewitt’s uptick in form was here to stay. He followed a clever chipped backhand low at de Minaur at the net with a more forceful backhand pass to leave the world No.6 at 30-all as he again tried to serve out the opening set. De Minaur dodged consecutive breaks by throttling a backhand winner off a short return, but the set ended far differently than it kicked off. Hewitt, who secured the first two top-100 victories of his fledgling career in Washington this week, is a polar opposite to his famous dad in playing style. He crushes first serves and forehands, which he demonstrated with a sizzling winner to go 1-0 up in the second set.



At that point, it was becoming pretty interesting. De Minaur limped to 30-all once more before knotting the set in what was suddenly a competitive contest. Unfortunately for Hewitt, that was a short-lived status. De Minaur is chasing back-to-back singles titles in Washington. Getty Images De Minaur pounced in the next game, punching an angled volley winner then benefiting from consecutive netted shots from his young rival to snatch another break of serve before quickly going 3-1 up. Impressively, Hewitt carved out back-to-back love holds in response, refusing to give up. But de Minaur made his move with the finish line in sight. Serving at 3-5, Hewitt’s errors returned as de Minaur’s dinking and dunking and off-pace balls confounded him.



There was one last highlight for Hewitt. Facing a second straight match point, he hung with de Minaur from the baseline then socked a forehand crosscourt winner that caught the sideline. The match was over a point later, but Hewitt – who is certain to score a wildcard into next year’s Australian Open – did enough to keep the hype going. “We’ve both hit with each other so often, and we’ve both practised and grown up with each other so often that we know each other’s games inside out,” de Minaur said. “It was probably about who could execute a little bit better, and I think I managed to do that today. The serve helped me out in a couple of big moments, and that was probably the key thing today.”



‘Like my older brother’: Protege Hewitt to face de Minaur in Washington The present and future of Australian tennis will collide in Washington DC early on Friday when newly married Alex de Minaur and his protege Cruz Hewitt face each other in the second round. Former world No.1 Lleyton Hewitt’s 17-year-old son made the most of his qualifying wildcard to reach the ATP 500 event’s main draw and then upset 85th-ranked American Marcos Giron to continue his steep rise after reaching the Wimbledon boys’ final last month. Cruz Hewitt and Alex de Minaur in 2018. They will play each other in the Washington Open. Getty But the much-anticipated clash – scheduled for 3am AEST on Friday – depended on de Minaur beating his nemesis Stefanos Tsitsipas for just the second time in 14 match-ups, which he achieved with a 6-4, 3-6, 6-3 victory on Thursday.



Davis Cup captain Lleyton Hewitt is a regular part of Team Demon, mostly at the grand slams, and that relationship has helped foster a close bond between de Minaur and Cruz Hewitt, too. They train together, support one another from courtside, and even spend Christmases at the same table. Hewitt describes de Minaur as “like my older brother”. “I think there’s got to be a lot of respect shown to [Cruz] because it’s definitely not easy being an ex-No.1 in the world’s son,” de Minaur said. “Ever since he started [and] picked up the racquet … the expectation, the eyeballs, the spotlight was already on him. It’s not easy when there is that kind of weight behind your surname.” Loading



De Minaur’s win followed closely behind being revealed this week as one of the six tennis stars competing at the invite-only Six Kings Slam, which offers a $US1.5 million ($2.2 million) appearance fee, plus $US6 million ($8.6 million) to the winner. Defending champion Jannik Sinner, 2025 runner-up Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev and Taylor Fritz round out the field. It has been a whirlwind period for de Minaur, who married British player Katie Boulter in an intimate legal ceremony in Leicestershire, England, followed by a larger celebration in Tuscany, Italy. They squeezed in a brief honeymoon in Portofino before de Minaur returned to defend his Washington Open title. The wedding helped the world No.6 brush off the devastation he felt in losing his fourth-round match at Wimbledon to Italy’s Flavio Cobolli, after which he said the circumstances of the defeat “breaks me inside”. “I don’t think it was warranted, as much as a lot of people – myself included – wanted to make a big deal out of it,” de Minaur said of the reaction to his post-match comments.



“It became a really big thing, but realistically, it took me a couple of days to get over it. They were just the same feelings and emotions that any athlete has after a tough loss. Now, I’m feeling great.” Related Article Wimbledon Ice-creams, selfies and the Federer twins: Cruz Hewitt hype is building at Wimbledon Hewitt’s own Wimbledon campaign, which was his last junior tournament, was a significant success despite losing the boys’ final in three sets to American rising star Jordan Lee. To many, inside and outside Australia, the result legitimised the teenager as a top-tier prospect and proved he was more than just the “son of”. Hewitt backing up his Wimbledon run by qualifying in Washington then upsetting Giron has only furthered that cause as he emerges from his dad’s sizeable shadow. “I try to deal with it as best I can,” Hewitt said of following in Lleyton’s footsteps.



“Obviously, there is still pressure, but I try to take the positive that comes with it as well. I’m happy with how I’m dealing with it so far.” Hewitt told this masthead at Wimbledon that he hoped to be inside the world’s top 300 by year’s end. His Washington breakout means his ranking is already guaranteed to surge into the 360s from outside the top 600. That will improve further if he can stun his mentor de Minaur, a seven-time major quarter-finalist. Alex de Minaur (right) will take on rising teen Cruz Hewitt, son of Lleyton, in Washington. Getty Images “He’s like my older brother. I’ve known him basically my whole life,” Hewitt said after his first-round win, before he knew whether he would play de Minaur.



“He’s stayed with us. We have Christmas together also. He’s taught me so much – I think that would be a pretty cool memory for us.” De Minaur won’t underestimate Hewitt, who stands about 190 centimetres and boasts a fearsome serve and forehand combination that is already proving problematic to rivals. “I think what he’s done an incredible job of is maturing, getting a good head on his shoulders and becoming his own player,” de Minaur said. “Having these results [shows] that he deserves to be where he is. I think he’s a great kid, he’s been doing great, and I think Lleyton has done an incredible job as his father and helping him out whenever he can. “They’ve created a great atmosphere, and that’s led to him being a very good tennis player.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.
