World.title: ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe David Crowe July 31, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thousands of migrants have rushed across the border from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in a startling move that was relayed on social media and triggered a political row about migration into Europe. One security official declared the border checkpoint had “totally collapsed” under pressure from the crowd, as young men spread instructions on social media on how to enter the Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa. Authorities said at least nine people had died trying to reach Ceuta from Morocco. Loading Some migrants swam from Moroccan territory to reach the Spanish enclave, while others walked around a breakwater and crossed the rocks in numbers that overwhelmed authorities. The political impact reached far beyond Spain because of the debate across Europe about migration, with British right-wing leader Nigel Farage sharing the dramatic videos online.



“It’s time to wake up everybody,” Farage declared. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez promised an “immediate response” to the situation, as his critics blamed his migration laws for encouraging people to seek asylum in Spain and gain work rights in the European Union. Thousands of people flood the border. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere “We are mobilising all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necessary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible,” Sanchez said. Spain’s government later said it would send the military to help the Civil Guard “to maintain security in the city of Ceuta”.



Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Civil Guard officers had to open the gates because they needed to prevent a bottleneck forming at the checkpoint. The rush follows a Supreme Court decision in Spain last month that protects migrants who are intercepted at sea while seeking to get to Ceuta, preventing them from being immediately returned to Morocco. Migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere That ruling is being blamed by some politicians for giving Moroccans an incentive to swim to Ceuta, a distance of about 2 kilometres across the water, or walk around the breakwater. Another source of debate is the Sanchez government’s decision this year to grant an amnesty to migrants who were already in the country, leading to more than 1.3 million people applying to stay permanently.



Ceuta, located roughly opposite Gibraltar in the western Mediterranean, has been a Spanish territory since 1580 and now has the status of an autonomous city of Spain, although it is surrounded by Moroccan territory. Rachid Sbihi, the head of the association that represents the Spanish Civil Guard officers in Ceuta, called for a national emergency to be declared in Madrid to stop the mass movement because the border had totally collapsed. Spanish police officers respond as migrants cross from Morocco. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere “The situation is absolute chaos,” he said. “It’s not possible to give precise numbers, but there are thousands of migrants crossing.” The Ministry of the Interior in Madrid has pushed back at the idea of a national emergency being declared.



Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is due to travel to Ceuta on Friday. The Mayor-President of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, said the influx had overwhelmed the city’s ⁠reception system and left hundreds of migrants sleeping outside. “We are facing a situation ​of absolute humanitarian and social emergency,” Vivas told radio station Cadena SER, adding that facilities for ​unaccompanied minors were operating at 2400 per cent of capacity. In comments to radio station Onda Cero, he described the situation as a national emergency and called for a “decisive, forceful, immediate and co-ordinated” response under a ​single command structure.



Arrivals were currently averaging about 300 people a day, according to Vivas. At that pace, he warned, Ceuta could face a situation comparable to the May 2021 migration crisis, when 10,000 people entered ​the enclave in mere ​days. Vivas also pointed ⁠to the human cost of the crossings, saying 60 bodies had been recovered at sea in recent months, and argued that ​stronger migration controls would help prevent further deaths. World.title: Historic Clifton Hill pub on the market after failed development bid
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCommercial real estate Historic Clifton Hill pub on the market after failed development bid Nicole Lindsay July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Capital Gain The Royal Hotel in Clifton Hill is on the market for the first time in four decades and nearly 10 years since the front bar was open. The move comes three years after its owners, the Gudic family, lost their bid to build a five-storey apartment project over the historic corner hotel. For sale: the Royal Hotel on the corner of Spensley and Berry streets, Clifton Hill. Built in 1889, the three-storey hotel at 35-41 Spensley Street is on a 736-square-metre corner site in the heart of the Clifton Hill village and includes 29 rented rooms on the top floors. A gin distillery currently occupies some of the space and operates the bottleshop, but the pub is ripe for a new publican prepared to revamp the historic site.



Neighbours were outraged in 2019 when the Gudics lodged a bid for a residential project above the once-loved but shuttered pub in the enclave east of Hoddle Street. Colliers agents Ben Baines and Lucas Soccio are running the September 10 auction campaign and expect a price in the mid-$5 million range. Related Article City life Spawned from inner-city muck, this suburb full of lawyers is getting younger “There’s nothing better than a corner hotel in a village setting,” Baines said. Records show the Gudic family bought the pub in 1985 from Carlton & United Breweries with “5000 class 52 redeemable preference shares”. If that sounds like a complex way to buy a pub, it’s worth remembering CUB was taken over by Elders IXL in 1983 during the heady “corporate raider” period of management heralded by the late John Elliot.



Stingo Down Hoddle Street into Collingwood, investor Joe Awad has snapped up the Yorkshire Stingo Hotel for $2.5 million, a deal which reflects a skinny 3.82 per cent yield. The City East Motel behind it fetched $3.5 million. It’s not quite the total $8 million result that was hoped for the two properties. The pub, at 40-48 Hoddle Street, and the motel, at 181 Langridge Street, were bought by the Freeman family in 1988 for $130,000. The Yorkshire Stingo, on the corner of Hoddle and Langridge streets. Both properties cover 1136 square metres of land and were earmarked for a development along with another 1121 square metres at the rear. Those three warehouses, at 197-203 Landgridge Street, were owned by Munro Shoes – one of the last remaining shoe manufacturers in Abbotsford – and sold for $3 million. Stonebridge’s Max Warren, Dylan Kilner, Nic Hage and Chao Zhang handled negotiations.



Chinatown Last month’s hot auction in Chinatown, where 172-176 Little Bourke Street sold for $6.11 million, has inspired a clutch of owners to test the market with their own long-held properties. First up is 179 Russell Street, which is going to auction on August 26. The 180-square-metre two-level building is on a 102-square-metre piece of the city and is expected to fetch more than $3 million. It’s got a new lease and fitout to Jin Noodle Restaurant, which pays $165,000 a year in rent. 179 Russell Street, in Melbourne’s Chinatown district. Records show it last sold in 1994 for $1.05 million. Savills agents Julian Heatherich and Tom O’Halloran, with the Di Petta Group’s Winnie Chow, are running the auction campaign.



On August 27, the loveliest of the lot, 107 Little Bourke Street goes under the hammer. Designed by one of Melbourne’s best architects, Nahum Barnett, in 1903, the three-storey building last changed hands in 1970 for $27,000. It’s on a 99-square-metre parcel of land and rented to Khao Soi Melbourne. Lemon Baxter’s Hans Fan expects it to sell for about $4.8 million, which equates to a yield of 4.1 per cent. 107 Little Bourke Street, in Melbourne’s Chinatown district. Next month, 218-220 Little Bourke Street will be up for auction after 70 years in the one family’s hands. The double-storey shop of 325 square metres is expected to sell for about $4 million on September 3.



The building has a 10-year lease, with a 10-year option to the Lost Bar, which pays just under $180,000 a year in rent. Records show a quarter-share in the building last changed hands in 2004 for $500,000 and in 1970, a half-stake was transferred for $32,000. Fitzroys’ Lewis Waddell, Ben Liu and David Bourke are running the auction. According to Fitzroys’ latest Walk the CBD report, Chinatown vacancies nearly halved in the past year to 3.5 per cent from 6.6 per cent. 218-220 Little Bourke Street, Melbourne. There are a clutch of cafes and restaurants for sale along the west end too but not at auction.



Brendan Sullivan is selling the freehold of the long-running Grain Store restaurant at 517 Flinders Lane. Sullivan has been progressively selling the office and retail complex on Flinders Lane, which he bought in 2011 from the Smorgon family for $16.35 million. CBRE’s Alex Brierley, Nathan Mufale and Jing Jun Heng have the listing and expect about $3 million. At 540 Little Collins Street, the freehold of the Five Points bagel outlet is also for sale and expected to sell for about $1 million through Fitzroys’ Waddell and Liu. The Grain Store at 517 Flinders Lane. Lemon Baxter’s Fans and Paul O’Sullivan are also selling the Jumbo Kebabs freehold at 200 Spencer Street, opposite Southern Cross Station. It has a $1.95 million price tag.



Sculptor The North Melbourne laneway studio of the renowned late sculptor Erwin Fabian is up for sale. Fabian, born in Berlin in 1915, travelled to Australia in the 1940s on the ship the Dunera after escaping Nazi Germany in 1938. He joined the Australian Army’s education unit during World War II before returning to London for 12 years. He came back to Australia as a sculptor working with found pieces of metal. Inside the North Melbourne studio of sculptor Erwin Fabian. Fabian, whose work was described as “conceptual illusionism” by art professor Sasha Grishin, died in 2020.



The studio of 117 square metres is off Arden Street at 3-5 Wylies Lane, in the central pocket between Curzon and Errol streets. It’s on 152 square metres of land and goes to auction on August 27. Simpsons agents Richard Simpson and Ariana McCarron expect between $900,000 and $990,000 for the property. “Artwork not included” is the disappointing postscript to the Simpsons ad. Armadale redux Armadale’s blue-chip High Street has another large property up for sale, a 1990s office building halfway between Glenferrie and Kooyong roads. Records show the vendors of 1113-1121 High Street paid $3.45 million in 1996 and are looking at a payday of about $13.5 million.



113-1121 High Street, Armadale The 1589-square-metre building has five shops at street level, four offices upstairs and 61 car spaces. It’s on a large site of 1363 square metres. It has three agents on the case: Cushman & Wakefield’s Oliver Hay, Maker Property’s George Davies and Gross Waddell ICR’s Alex Ham. Last week, 935-951 High Street, on 1373 square metres, hit the market with a price tag of about $15.5 million and a permit for an apartment project. World.title: We think our boss has become obsessed with a chatbot. What can we do?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion We think our boss has become obsessed with a chatbot. What can we do? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor July 31, 2026 — 5:01am

July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I used to have a strong professional relationship with my boss and I respected them. But they have changed recently. Once they were considerate and supportive – some colleagues even thought they were a bit too gentle. Now they are neither of those things. They are definitely not gentle. They have started talking about instituting a new regime based on the advice of a friend and business mentor. All the new policies and ideas seem severe. A small group of people who report to this boss (including me) have talked in private about who this “mentor” is and why they are telling our manager to be so harsh and punishing. Our team is performing well, and has for years. There is now a strong rumour that the friend is actually an AI chatbot. Surely, that can’t be true, can it? There could be any number of reasons for how this has come about. John Shakespeare It certainly seems extraordinary that a professional could become so attached to a chatbot that they would change their entire work style and personality based on its “opinion”. Extraordinary but not inconceivable. About three years ago, a reader wrote to me about a work problem that they had reported to their HR team. They had been rudely brushed off. When they experimentally asked a chatbot about the same problem, the AI response was infinitely more empathetic and sensitive.



Although we can put this down to the tendency of modern large language model (LLM) chatbots to validate and endorse the concerns or ideas of its user, partly as a way of keeping the conversation going, an unflattering term like “AI sycophancy” doesn’t change the experience of that reader. Or anyone who speaks with AI and finds “someone” who appears to genuinely listen. I’m not going to say I know for sure what is going on with your boss. They may not be consulting a chatbot at all (although I find the evidence proposed in your longer email, via your worried colleagues, compelling). But to answer your direct question: yes, it can absolutely be true. People today are anthropomorphising AI in all sorts of different ways – this is no longer a fringe practice. Some people develop what are known as parasocial relationships with this new generation of ultra-coherent AI models. “Parasocial interaction” is a term coined in the 1950s to describe, for example, the way a TV viewer might come to think of a media personality as their friend, despite the relationship being entirely one-way. Now, some experts in the field believe “parasocial” is not quite the right term to apply to profound relationships between humans and AI. Whereas in the ’50s a TV presenter might inadvertently (or at least perfunctorily) encourage parasocial intimacy by looking down the camera and talking directly to the audience, in the 2020s a chatbot mimics interest, understanding and even love in a highly sophisticated, often utterly earnest, way.



Let’s stick with the term for now, at any rate. Editor's pick Opinion

Work therapy My colleague is constantly negative. How can I make them cheer up? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor We know that people today are anthropomorphising AI in all sorts of different ways – this is no longer a fringe practice. They converse with their favourite chatbot as they might a human therapist, a companion, a “troubleshooter” and even a “work buddy”. If your boss is doing that, but has entered into a pathological version of parasocial engagement, it’s quite possible that they’re taking advice from this digital confidant in good faith, genuinely understanding it to be their intimate. And perhaps their teller of cold, hard truths. There could be any number of reasons for how this has come about. It might have been a conversational chain reaction, beginning with a benign question but branching, exchange by exchange, into something much more radical.



Or it may have been less accidental. Perhaps your boss, worried that they were seen as a soft touch, sought advice on changing this perception, and were given a menu of aggressive and ruthless management tactics. The change won’t have come out of nowhere. And while I think it’s sensible to be curious about, and even sympathetic to, what catalysed it, you don’t need to tolerate or excuse the cold-hearted turn. Your manager, of course, has the prerogative to make changes, and is under no obligation to be your friend, but if they’re taking dogmatic advice from a chatbot, I think they’re engaging in an ill-advised, even dangerous practice – and possibly stepping onto legally shaky ground. One day in the future consulting with robots as if they’re trustworthy humans might be entirely normal, and possibly beneficial. That day has not arrived. Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple reports iPhone sales surge
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple reports iPhone sales surge Stan Choe Updated July 31, 2026 — 6:39am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A monster day for Microsoft’s stock following signals that its big spending on AI is translating into profits led a powerful rebound on Wall Street, while computer-chip companies regained some of their sharp recent losses. In the bond market, though, worries remained about inflation potentially remaining high for years. The S&P 500 rallied 1.7 per cent and more than recovered its drop from the day before, which was its worst in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 613 points, or 1.2 per cent. The Nasdaq composite, which is full of artificial-intelligence stocks, rallied 2.8 per cent a day after it fell 9.8 per cent below its record set last month. Technology stocks continue to drive the direction of Wall Street. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures pointing to a gain of 110 points, or 1.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.35¢. On Wall Street, Microsoft led the way and leaped 15.5 per cent for its best day in nearly 18 years after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Growth was strong for its Azure cloud business, and CEO Satya Nadella said it reflects how customers are using Microsoft to move into AI.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Perhaps just as importantly for Wall Street, Microsoft did not announce a big increase in how much it plans to spend on AI investments, something that several other Big Tech rivals have done. Worries are high that such spending is eating into companies’ cash flows and may not ultimately be worth it if AI does not produce as much productivity and profits as promised. Apple released its results after the closing bell, with sales and profits beating Wall Street expectations, fuelled by its customers snapping up iPhones and MacBooks amid price increases across the consumer electronics sector. Driving Apple’s results was a 21.7 per cent increase in iPhone sales to $US54.25 billion ($77.2 billion), above analyst estimates of $US53.86 billion, according to LSEG data. Those iPhone sales were Apple’s best-ever for a third quarter, when phone sales typically begin to slow as customers anticipate new models during the fall. Apple shares are 3.3 per cent lower in after-hours trade. Meta Platforms fell 8 per cent. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though it made slightly more in revenue than expected. It also raised the lower end of its forecasted range for spending on investments this year.



Companies involved in the making of the computer memory and processors that such “hyperscalers” are buying to power their AI efforts rose, recovering some of the big losses they’ve taken on worries their stock prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI. Micron Technology jumped 18.4 per cent, for example, to trim its loss for the week to 5 per cent. It was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500 after Microsoft. Lam Research, a supplier to the semiconductor industry, soared 18 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chip giant Advanced Micro Devices rallied 13 per cent. On the losing end of Wall Street was Jersey Mike’s Subs. The sandwich chain’s stock fell 6 per cent in its first day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange. All told, the S&P 500 rose 121.48 to 7,437.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 613.92 to 52,208.06, and the Nasdaq composite leaped 679.24 to 25,122.18.



In the bond market, longer-term Treasury yields held steadier following their sharp accelerations Wednesday. They had jumped after the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, gave few clues about what the central bank will do with interest rates to combat the painfully high inflation that continues to hurt the country. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they can also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury was 4.67 per cent, the same as late Wednesday. The 30-year Treasury yield ticked up to 5.22 per cent from 5.20 per cent, a day after it shot up from 5.09 per cent. Those yields move with investors’ expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years. Warsh reaffirmed on Wednesday the Fed wants to get inflation back to 2 per cent, even though the central bank decided not to raise interest rates despite inflation remaining higher than that. He also implied the bond market may already be doing some of the Fed’s work to restrain inflation, and he pointed to how yields have climbed since the central bank’s last meeting six weeks earlier. That leaves investors questioning whether the Fed is prepared to act if inflation worsens, or whether it is relying on financial markets to achieve the same outcome, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management.



“If investors conclude that the latter is true, the credibility of the Fed’s inflation-fighting commitment could come under increasing scrutiny. Arguably, it already is.” Related Article Opinion

Home loans Buckle up for the banks’ mortgage war! Home loans have fallen off a cliff Elizabeth Knight Business columnist President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates even though they could cause inflation to accelerate. Reports released Thursday suggested the U.S. economy’s growth slowed by more during the spring than economists expected. A measure of Inflation, meanwhile, remained worse last month than the Federal Reserve’s target, but it slowed from May’s level. In the oil market, prices eased. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.4 per cent to settle at $US86.88 per barrel.



It had swung as low as $US72 early this month and as high as $US102 last week on uncertainty about whether the United States and Iran could reach a deal to allow oil tankers to move freely again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. In stock markets worldwide, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. Seoul’s market has been at the centre of AI’s huge swings because it’s dominated by two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. After more than doubling through this year’s first six months, the Kospi has plunged 34 per cent so far in July. Its drop on Thursday came as Samsung Electronics dipped 0.7 per cent. The tech giant reported a record profit for the spring and said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply, but its earnings nevertheless fell shy of analysts’ high expectations. World.title: Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist
World.content:
SportCyclingCommonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist Billie Eder July 31, 2026 — 6:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was flicking through her local newspaper in Tasmania in 2021 when she saw an  for a cycling talent search. Bored at home during the COVID-19 pandemic, she thought, why not show up and give it a crack? Five years on, Wilson-Haffenden is a Commonwealth Games champion after motoring home to win gold in the women’s team pursuit alongside Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks and Alyssa Polites after only starting the sport in 2021. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory in the women’s team pursuit. Getty Images “I don’t think I can say this too loudly because COVID probably wasn’t great for a lot of people. But for me, it changed my life,” Wilson-Haffenden said.



“I can’t be grateful for COVID, but I can be grateful for the outcome, that’s for sure.” Wilson-Haffenden, who was a hockey player at the time, was lucky to make it at all – she had to call in a favour and delay her tryout. “I actually couldn’t make it on the talent ID date, and called saying ‘I really want to give this a crack’,” she said. Australia’s gold medal winning women’s pursuit team. Getty Images “So they made a little allowance for me, but I just think it’s a message to all young kids, if you’re interested, give it a crack because you never know where it’ll take you.”



She now spends most of the year in Girona – a cycling town in Catalonia, in the north-east of Spain – but said it was her formative cycling years in Tasmania that turned her into a champion. “I actually think it’s the cold mornings in Tassie that really build character – I think G [teammate Georgia Baker] will attest to it as well,” Wilson-Haffenden said. Tara Neyland broke a world record on her way to winning gold. Getty Images “It’s a pretty lonely sport. There are lots of times on the bike, you’re out there 6am, freezing cold, dodging wallabies down in Tassie, and it’s not glamorous, but I think that’s what builds champions. And we’ve got two Tasmanians right here winning a gold medal. It speaks for itself.” The Australian team’s victory continues its unbeaten run in the event at the Commonwealth Games. Since the team pursuit was introduced at the 2018 Games on the Gold Coast, Australia’s women have never lost.



The women’s pursuit was one of three gold medals Australia won at the Chris Hoy velodrome on day one of the cycling in Glasgow, along with Tara Neyland, who set a new world record on her way to gold in the women’s C4-C5 individual pursuit, and the men’s sprint team, who won without former teammate Matthew Richardson. Richardson represented Australia until 2024, when he defected to England following the Paris Olympics. The allegiance switch was a shock to the Australian cycling team, including Leigh Hoffman, who earlier this week said Richardson “went on a holiday and never came back”. But the Australian team of Hoffman, Ryan Elliott and Daniel James Barber managed to win without him – defeating England in the gold medal race. They didn’t, however, get the chance to race him. Richardson withdrew from the Games earlier this week after injuring himself in a crash during a world series race in Japan. Ryan Elliott, Daniel James Barber and Leigh Hoffman celebrate after winning gold. Getty Images



However, team officials told reporters Richardson wouldn’t have taken part in the team race anyway because he wouldn’t have arrived in Glasgow in time. Nevertheless, the Australian team said it was nice to get a win over England. Asked whether it was good to win without Richardson on the team, Hoffman said: “It would have been great if he stayed with Australia, but his heart was obviously never always in it. So, good riddance.” Australia and New Zealand collide in the second of three races for the women’s tandem B sprint gold medal. Getty Images Among Australia’s other cycling medallists were Jessica Gallagher and pilot Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr, who won silver in the women’s tandem B sprint finals after a crash in the second of their three finals races.



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Davies and Hull win gold and silver; Aussie cyclist sets world record; Kennedy, Lewis into 200m final; Diamonds complete demolition job Tandem riding is a para cycling event where a visually impaired athlete has a pilot at the front of the bike. The duo had a tyre failure, which caused the crash and forced them to rest before the Kiwis went on to win the final two races and clinch gold. “When that tyre pressure literally disappears, you’re riding on carbon rims,” Mengler-Mohr explained. “It’s like going from being on roller skates to ice skates, and just sliding and having no traction. There’s nothing we could have done.”

World.title: George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage Ardee Napolitano July 31, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paris: Hollywood actor George Clooney and his British wife Amal, an international human rights lawyer, have evacuated their luxury home in south-eastern France as a result of the wildfires blazing in the region. The star behind the Ocean’s Eleven franchise and other films made the statement on Thursday (France time) in a letter to Didier Bremond, the mayor of the town of Brignoles, about 90 kilometres east of Marseille, Clooney’s publicist Guido Gotz said in an email. George and Amal Clooney. Alberto Pezzali/Invision/AP Addressed “Dear Didier”, the letter said the Clooneys had “no idea whether our beautiful home makes it through this terrible moment”. But as they evacuate Brignoles they wanted to assure Bremond that, whatever happened to the community, “we’ll be part of making it whole”, the letter said.



The Clooneys bought their home on a vineyard in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur region in 2021 when it had an estimated value of about €9 million ($15 million). In an interview with Esquire last October, Clooney described their “farm in France” as their primary residence. Related Article Updated

Bushfires ‘Doing their best to survive’: Inside Bordeaux’s wildfire refugee centre The fire near Brignoles broke out Wednesday afternoon and burned some 100 hectares, local officials said. The blaze was far smaller than a vast inferno that has swept up the region around Bordeaux in southwestern France in recent days. About 700 residents from the areas near Brignoles had been evacuated, but were allowed to return to their homes on Thursday after the fire was brought under control, the officials said. Water-bombing helicopters remained deployed over the area after the evacuation order was lifted, the regional administration said. It said weather conditions remained unfavorable, with high temperatures and winds expected to pick up again in the afternoon.



The French government in December announced that the Clooneys along with their twins Ella and Alexander were awarded French citizenship. Related Article Celebrity life Clooney takes swipe at Trump after dig over French citizenship In the Esquire interview, Clooney said part of the impetus for the move to France was that he was “worried about raising our kids in LA, in the culture of Hollywood”. US President Donald Trump seemingly welcomed the news the pair had been granted French citizenship, calling them “two of the worst political prognosticators of all time” and claiming the actor was better known for his politics than his “totally mediocre movies”. But George Clooney hit back, saying he also wanted to “make America great again” – starting with the US midterm elections in November.



Europe is sweltering under an exceptionally hot and arid summer, creating tinderbox conditions for unprecedented fires that have flared from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean and forced hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate homes and vacation spots. Firefighters also battled flames in the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, Greece and Turkey on Thursday and were tamping down smouldering forests in southwest France where 224,000 people had been forced to flee. Romania shut down both reactors at its Cernavoda nuclear power plant due to low water levels in the Danube River used to cool them. A firefighting aircraft releases fire retardant in Lanton. Getty Images In the Bordeaux region, wildfire evacuees streamed back to nine localities that authorities now deem safe after round-the-clock combat with the huge fire that ignited last week.



“It’s the first somewhat optimistic day,” said Sophie Brocas, prefect of Bordeaux’s Gironde region who gave the go-ahead for nearly two-thirds of the 224,000 evacuees to go home, including 60,000 allowed back to three Bordeaux suburbs on Tuesday. Related Article Bushfires As south-west France burns, it’s not just the flames that have residents worried Authorities said the blaze is no longer growing beyond the 420 square kilometres already affected – an area four times that of Paris. A heat wave – France’s fourth of the year – gave way Thursday to cooler weather, higher humidity and even a little rain, helping the effort. World.title: Defending champ de Minaur beats Hewitt in first of ‘many battles to come’
World.content:
Updated SportTennisATP Tour Defending champ de Minaur beats Hewitt in first of ‘many battles to come’ Marc McGowan Updated July 31, 2026 — 5:34am ,first published 2:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cruz Hewitt was gasping for air with a towel over his head 15 minutes into his first official clash with Alex de Minaur in Washington on Friday. The scoreboard was sobering for the 17-year-old rising star: 5-0 to de Minaur, his friend and regular guest at the dinner table for Christmas. Hewitt had won only six points, while nervously spraying almost double as many errors. Alex de Minaur ended Cruz Hewitt’s breakout week in Washington. Getty Images None of this was surprising, given the decade difference in age and even wider gap in their resumes. De Minaur has routinely dispatched fellow Australians, and was never going to take it easy on the teenager, no matter how friendly they are off the court.



Related Article Wimbledon Cruz Hewitt fell agonisingly short at Wimbledon. His next dream is closer to home The world No.6 and defending champion finished the job with relative ease, 6-2, 6-3 in barely an hour over the Wimbledon junior boys’ finalist to book a quarter-final against Brandon Nakashima – but not before Hewitt showed glimpses of why he is so highly rated. Hewitt smiled as he walked to the net afterwards before embracing de Minaur, who offered his protege kind words, including wishing him “good luck for the next 10 years of your career”. “It was definitely weird,” de Minaur said post-match. “I would say that I knew I was going to play him on the tour someday, but I didn’t actually expect it to be this week. It was an amazing feeling. Even all the lead-up, seeing all the incredible pictures that we have together, and how we’ve grown up, both of us, and I’m ecstatic.



“I’m glad that I managed to get through, but I’m sure we’re going to have many, many battles in the years to come.” With Australian bands INXS, AC/DC and Midnight Oil fittingly blasting through the speakers at the change of ends, Hewitt shook off his error-strewn opening to illustrate why many good judges believe he has a bright future ahead. De Minaur and Hewitt embraced at the net afterwards. Getty Images It started with the son of former world No.1 Lleyton Hewitt coming out on top in a bruising extended rally to begin the sixth game of the match on de Minaur’s serve. Hewitt nailed a down-the-line backhand pass winner at full stretch for 0-30, and shortly after, a fluffed de Minaur drop shot attempt delivered Hewitt the break and his first game of the match. Hewitt pumped his fist, and the Washington crowd gave him a warm response.



Related Article Tennis Australia How a Portofino honeymoon and 13 days without tennis helped de Minaur move on from Wimbledon heartbreak It was relief as much as anything else, but Hewitt’s uptick in form was here to stay. He followed a clever chipped backhand low at de Minaur at the net with a more forceful backhand pass to leave the world No.6 at 30-all as he again tried to serve out the opening set. De Minaur dodged consecutive breaks by throttling a backhand winner off a short return, but the set ended far differently than it kicked off. Hewitt, who secured the first two top-100 victories of his fledgling career in Washington this week, is a polar opposite to his famous dad in playing style. He crushes first serves and forehands, which he demonstrated with a sizzling winner to go 1-0 up in the second set.



At that point, it was becoming pretty interesting. De Minaur limped to 30-all once more before knotting the set in what was suddenly a competitive contest. Unfortunately for Hewitt, that was a short-lived status. De Minaur is chasing back-to-back singles titles in Washington. Getty Images De Minaur pounced in the next game, punching an angled volley winner then benefiting from consecutive netted shots from his young rival to snatch another break of serve before quickly going 3-1 up. Impressively, Hewitt carved out back-to-back love holds in response, refusing to give up. But de Minaur made his move with the finish line in sight. Serving at 3-5, Hewitt’s errors returned as de Minaur’s dinking and dunking and off-pace balls confounded him.



There was one last highlight for Hewitt. Facing a second straight match point, he hung with de Minaur from the baseline then socked a forehand crosscourt winner that caught the sideline. The match was over a point later, but Hewitt – who is certain to score a wildcard into next year’s Australian Open – did enough to keep the hype going. “We’ve both hit with each other so often, and we’ve both practised and grown up with each other so often that we know each other’s games inside out,” de Minaur said. “It was probably about who could execute a little bit better, and I think I managed to do that today. The serve helped me out in a couple of big moments, and that was probably the key thing today.”



‘Like my older brother’: Protege Hewitt to face de Minaur in Washington The present and future of Australian tennis will collide in Washington DC early on Friday when newly married Alex de Minaur and his protege Cruz Hewitt face each other in the second round. Former world No.1 Lleyton Hewitt’s 17-year-old son made the most of his qualifying wildcard to reach the ATP 500 event’s main draw and then upset 85th-ranked American Marcos Giron to continue his steep rise after reaching the Wimbledon boys’ final last month. Cruz Hewitt and Alex de Minaur in 2018. They will play each other in the Washington Open. Getty But the much-anticipated clash – scheduled for 3am AEST on Friday – depended on de Minaur beating his nemesis Stefanos Tsitsipas for just the second time in 14 match-ups, which he achieved with a 6-4, 3-6, 6-3 victory on Thursday.



Davis Cup captain Lleyton Hewitt is a regular part of Team Demon, mostly at the grand slams, and that relationship has helped foster a close bond between de Minaur and Cruz Hewitt, too. They train together, support one another from courtside, and even spend Christmases at the same table. Hewitt describes de Minaur as “like my older brother”. “I think there’s got to be a lot of respect shown to [Cruz] because it’s definitely not easy being an ex-No.1 in the world’s son,” de Minaur said. “Ever since he started [and] picked up the racquet … the expectation, the eyeballs, the spotlight was already on him. It’s not easy when there is that kind of weight behind your surname.” Loading



De Minaur’s win followed closely behind being revealed this week as one of the six tennis stars competing at the invite-only Six Kings Slam, which offers a $US1.5 million ($2.2 million) appearance fee, plus $US6 million ($8.6 million) to the winner. Defending champion Jannik Sinner, 2025 runner-up Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev and Taylor Fritz round out the field. It has been a whirlwind period for de Minaur, who married British player Katie Boulter in an intimate legal ceremony in Leicestershire, England, followed by a larger celebration in Tuscany, Italy. They squeezed in a brief honeymoon in Portofino before de Minaur returned to defend his Washington Open title. The wedding helped the world No.6 brush off the devastation he felt in losing his fourth-round match at Wimbledon to Italy’s Flavio Cobolli, after which he said the circumstances of the defeat “breaks me inside”. “I don’t think it was warranted, as much as a lot of people – myself included – wanted to make a big deal out of it,” de Minaur said of the reaction to his post-match comments.



“It became a really big thing, but realistically, it took me a couple of days to get over it. They were just the same feelings and emotions that any athlete has after a tough loss. Now, I’m feeling great.” Related Article Wimbledon Ice-creams, selfies and the Federer twins: Cruz Hewitt hype is building at Wimbledon Hewitt’s own Wimbledon campaign, which was his last junior tournament, was a significant success despite losing the boys’ final in three sets to American rising star Jordan Lee. To many, inside and outside Australia, the result legitimised the teenager as a top-tier prospect and proved he was more than just the “son of”. Hewitt backing up his Wimbledon run by qualifying in Washington then upsetting Giron has only furthered that cause as he emerges from his dad’s sizeable shadow. “I try to deal with it as best I can,” Hewitt said of following in Lleyton’s footsteps.



“Obviously, there is still pressure, but I try to take the positive that comes with it as well. I’m happy with how I’m dealing with it so far.” Hewitt told this masthead at Wimbledon that he hoped to be inside the world’s top 300 by year’s end. His Washington breakout means his ranking is already guaranteed to surge into the 360s from outside the top 600. That will improve further if he can stun his mentor de Minaur, a seven-time major quarter-finalist. Alex de Minaur (right) will take on rising teen Cruz Hewitt, son of Lleyton, in Washington. Getty Images “He’s like my older brother. I’ve known him basically my whole life,” Hewitt said after his first-round win, before he knew whether he would play de Minaur.



“He’s stayed with us. We have Christmas together also. He’s taught me so much – I think that would be a pretty cool memory for us.” De Minaur won’t underestimate Hewitt, who stands about 190 centimetres and boasts a fearsome serve and forehand combination that is already proving problematic to rivals. “I think what he’s done an incredible job of is maturing, getting a good head on his shoulders and becoming his own player,” de Minaur said. “Having these results [shows] that he deserves to be where he is. I think he’s a great kid, he’s been doing great, and I think Lleyton has done an incredible job as his father and helping him out whenever he can. “They’ve created a great atmosphere, and that’s led to him being a very good tennis player.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe David Crowe July 31, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thousands of migrants have rushed across the border from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in a startling move that was relayed on social media and triggered a political row about migration into Europe. One security official declared the border checkpoint had “totally collapsed” under pressure from the crowd, as young men spread instructions on social media on how to enter the Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa. Authorities said at least nine people had died trying to reach Ceuta from Morocco. Loading Some migrants swam from Moroccan territory to reach the Spanish enclave, while others walked around a breakwater and crossed the rocks in numbers that overwhelmed authorities. The political impact reached far beyond Spain because of the debate across Europe about migration, with British right-wing leader Nigel Farage sharing the dramatic videos online.



“It’s time to wake up everybody,” Farage declared. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez promised an “immediate response” to the situation, as his critics blamed his migration laws for encouraging people to seek asylum in Spain and gain work rights in the European Union. Thousands of people flood the border. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere “We are mobilising all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necessary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible,” Sanchez said. Spain’s government later said it would send the military to help the Civil Guard “to maintain security in the city of Ceuta”.



Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Civil Guard officers had to open the gates because they needed to prevent a bottleneck forming at the checkpoint. The rush follows a Supreme Court decision in Spain last month that protects migrants who are intercepted at sea while seeking to get to Ceuta, preventing them from being immediately returned to Morocco. Migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere That ruling is being blamed by some politicians for giving Moroccans an incentive to swim to Ceuta, a distance of about 2 kilometres across the water, or walk around the breakwater. Another source of debate is the Sanchez government’s decision this year to grant an amnesty to migrants who were already in the country, leading to more than 1.3 million people applying to stay permanently.



Ceuta, located roughly opposite Gibraltar in the western Mediterranean, has been a Spanish territory since 1580 and now has the status of an autonomous city of Spain, although it is surrounded by Moroccan territory. Rachid Sbihi, the head of the association that represents the Spanish Civil Guard officers in Ceuta, called for a national emergency to be declared in Madrid to stop the mass movement because the border had totally collapsed. Spanish police officers respond as migrants cross from Morocco. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere “The situation is absolute chaos,” he said. “It’s not possible to give precise numbers, but there are thousands of migrants crossing.” The Ministry of the Interior in Madrid has pushed back at the idea of a national emergency being declared.



Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is due to travel to Ceuta on Friday. The Mayor-President of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, said the influx had overwhelmed the city’s ⁠reception system and left hundreds of migrants sleeping outside. “We are facing a situation ​of absolute humanitarian and social emergency,” Vivas told radio station Cadena SER, adding that facilities for ​unaccompanied minors were operating at 2400 per cent of capacity. In comments to radio station Onda Cero, he described the situation as a national emergency and called for a “decisive, forceful, immediate and co-ordinated” response under a ​single command structure.



Arrivals were currently averaging about 300 people a day, according to Vivas. At that pace, he warned, Ceuta could face a situation comparable to the May 2021 migration crisis, when 10,000 people entered ​the enclave in mere ​days. Vivas also pointed ⁠to the human cost of the crossings, saying 60 bodies had been recovered at sea in recent months, and argued that ​stronger migration controls would help prevent further deaths. World.title: Historic Clifton Hill pub on the market after failed development bid
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCommercial real estate Historic Clifton Hill pub on the market after failed development bid Nicole Lindsay July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Capital Gain The Royal Hotel in Clifton Hill is on the market for the first time in four decades and nearly 10 years since the front bar was open. The move comes three years after its owners, the Gudic family, lost their bid to build a five-storey apartment project over the historic corner hotel. For sale: the Royal Hotel on the corner of Spensley and Berry streets, Clifton Hill. Built in 1889, the three-storey hotel at 35-41 Spensley Street is on a 736-square-metre corner site in the heart of the Clifton Hill village and includes 29 rented rooms on the top floors. A gin distillery currently occupies some of the space and operates the bottleshop, but the pub is ripe for a new publican prepared to revamp the historic site.



Neighbours were outraged in 2019 when the Gudics lodged a bid for a residential project above the once-loved but shuttered pub in the enclave east of Hoddle Street. Colliers agents Ben Baines and Lucas Soccio are running the September 10 auction campaign and expect a price in the mid-$5 million range. Related Article City life Spawned from inner-city muck, this suburb full of lawyers is getting younger “There’s nothing better than a corner hotel in a village setting,” Baines said. Records show the Gudic family bought the pub in 1985 from Carlton & United Breweries with “5000 class 52 redeemable preference shares”. If that sounds like a complex way to buy a pub, it’s worth remembering CUB was taken over by Elders IXL in 1983 during the heady “corporate raider” period of management heralded by the late John Elliot.



Stingo Down Hoddle Street into Collingwood, investor Joe Awad has snapped up the Yorkshire Stingo Hotel for $2.5 million, a deal which reflects a skinny 3.82 per cent yield. The City East Motel behind it fetched $3.5 million. It’s not quite the total $8 million result that was hoped for the two properties. The pub, at 40-48 Hoddle Street, and the motel, at 181 Langridge Street, were bought by the Freeman family in 1988 for $130,000. The Yorkshire Stingo, on the corner of Hoddle and Langridge streets. Both properties cover 1136 square metres of land and were earmarked for a development along with another 1121 square metres at the rear. Those three warehouses, at 197-203 Landgridge Street, were owned by Munro Shoes – one of the last remaining shoe manufacturers in Abbotsford – and sold for $3 million. Stonebridge’s Max Warren, Dylan Kilner, Nic Hage and Chao Zhang handled negotiations.



Chinatown Last month’s hot auction in Chinatown, where 172-176 Little Bourke Street sold for $6.11 million, has inspired a clutch of owners to test the market with their own long-held properties. First up is 179 Russell Street, which is going to auction on August 26. The 180-square-metre two-level building is on a 102-square-metre piece of the city and is expected to fetch more than $3 million. It’s got a new lease and fitout to Jin Noodle Restaurant, which pays $165,000 a year in rent. 179 Russell Street, in Melbourne’s Chinatown district. Records show it last sold in 1994 for $1.05 million. Savills agents Julian Heatherich and Tom O’Halloran, with the Di Petta Group’s Winnie Chow, are running the auction campaign.



On August 27, the loveliest of the lot, 107 Little Bourke Street goes under the hammer. Designed by one of Melbourne’s best architects, Nahum Barnett, in 1903, the three-storey building last changed hands in 1970 for $27,000. It’s on a 99-square-metre parcel of land and rented to Khao Soi Melbourne. Lemon Baxter’s Hans Fan expects it to sell for about $4.8 million, which equates to a yield of 4.1 per cent. 107 Little Bourke Street, in Melbourne’s Chinatown district. Next month, 218-220 Little Bourke Street will be up for auction after 70 years in the one family’s hands. The double-storey shop of 325 square metres is expected to sell for about $4 million on September 3.



The building has a 10-year lease, with a 10-year option to the Lost Bar, which pays just under $180,000 a year in rent. Records show a quarter-share in the building last changed hands in 2004 for $500,000 and in 1970, a half-stake was transferred for $32,000. Fitzroys’ Lewis Waddell, Ben Liu and David Bourke are running the auction. According to Fitzroys’ latest Walk the CBD report, Chinatown vacancies nearly halved in the past year to 3.5 per cent from 6.6 per cent. 218-220 Little Bourke Street, Melbourne. There are a clutch of cafes and restaurants for sale along the west end too but not at auction.



Brendan Sullivan is selling the freehold of the long-running Grain Store restaurant at 517 Flinders Lane. Sullivan has been progressively selling the office and retail complex on Flinders Lane, which he bought in 2011 from the Smorgon family for $16.35 million. CBRE’s Alex Brierley, Nathan Mufale and Jing Jun Heng have the listing and expect about $3 million. At 540 Little Collins Street, the freehold of the Five Points bagel outlet is also for sale and expected to sell for about $1 million through Fitzroys’ Waddell and Liu. The Grain Store at 517 Flinders Lane. Lemon Baxter’s Fans and Paul O’Sullivan are also selling the Jumbo Kebabs freehold at 200 Spencer Street, opposite Southern Cross Station. It has a $1.95 million price tag.



Sculptor The North Melbourne laneway studio of the renowned late sculptor Erwin Fabian is up for sale. Fabian, born in Berlin in 1915, travelled to Australia in the 1940s on the ship the Dunera after escaping Nazi Germany in 1938. He joined the Australian Army’s education unit during World War II before returning to London for 12 years. He came back to Australia as a sculptor working with found pieces of metal. Inside the North Melbourne studio of sculptor Erwin Fabian. Fabian, whose work was described as “conceptual illusionism” by art professor Sasha Grishin, died in 2020.



The studio of 117 square metres is off Arden Street at 3-5 Wylies Lane, in the central pocket between Curzon and Errol streets. It’s on 152 square metres of land and goes to auction on August 27. Simpsons agents Richard Simpson and Ariana McCarron expect between $900,000 and $990,000 for the property. “Artwork not included” is the disappointing postscript to the Simpsons ad. Armadale redux Armadale’s blue-chip High Street has another large property up for sale, a 1990s office building halfway between Glenferrie and Kooyong roads. Records show the vendors of 1113-1121 High Street paid $3.45 million in 1996 and are looking at a payday of about $13.5 million.



113-1121 High Street, Armadale The 1589-square-metre building has five shops at street level, four offices upstairs and 61 car spaces. It’s on a large site of 1363 square metres. It has three agents on the case: Cushman & Wakefield’s Oliver Hay, Maker Property’s George Davies and Gross Waddell ICR’s Alex Ham. Last week, 935-951 High Street, on 1373 square metres, hit the market with a price tag of about $15.5 million and a permit for an apartment project. World.title: We think our boss has become obsessed with a chatbot. What can we do?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion We think our boss has become obsessed with a chatbot. What can we do? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor July 31, 2026 — 5:01am

I used to have a strong professional relationship with my boss and I respected them. But they have changed recently. Once they were considerate and supportive – some colleagues even thought they were a bit too gentle. Now they are neither of those things. They are definitely not gentle. They have started talking about instituting a new regime based on the advice of a friend and business mentor. All the new policies and ideas seem severe. A small group of people who report to this boss (including me) have talked in private about who this “mentor” is and why they are telling our manager to be so harsh and punishing. Our team is performing well, and has for years. There is now a strong rumour that the friend is actually an AI chatbot. Surely, that can’t be true, can it? There could be any number of reasons for how this has come about. John Shakespeare It certainly seems extraordinary that a professional could become so attached to a chatbot that they would change their entire work style and personality based on its “opinion”. Extraordinary but not inconceivable. About three years ago, a reader wrote to me about a work problem that they had reported to their HR team. They had been rudely brushed off. When they experimentally asked a chatbot about the same problem, the AI response was infinitely more empathetic and sensitive.



Although we can put this down to the tendency of modern large language model (LLM) chatbots to validate and endorse the concerns or ideas of its user, partly as a way of keeping the conversation going, an unflattering term like “AI sycophancy” doesn’t change the experience of that reader. Or anyone who speaks with AI and finds “someone” who appears to genuinely listen. I’m not going to say I know for sure what is going on with your boss. They may not be consulting a chatbot at all (although I find the evidence proposed in your longer email, via your worried colleagues, compelling). But to answer your direct question: yes, it can absolutely be true. People today are anthropomorphising AI in all sorts of different ways – this is no longer a fringe practice. Some people develop what are known as parasocial relationships with this new generation of ultra-coherent AI models. “Parasocial interaction” is a term coined in the 1950s to describe, for example, the way a TV viewer might come to think of a media personality as their friend, despite the relationship being entirely one-way. Now, some experts in the field believe “parasocial” is not quite the right term to apply to profound relationships between humans and AI. Whereas in the ’50s a TV presenter might inadvertently (or at least perfunctorily) encourage parasocial intimacy by looking down the camera and talking directly to the audience, in the 2020s a chatbot mimics interest, understanding and even love in a highly sophisticated, often utterly earnest, way.



Let’s stick with the term for now, at any rate. Editor's pick Opinion

Work therapy My colleague is constantly negative. How can I make them cheer up? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor We know that people today are anthropomorphising AI in all sorts of different ways – this is no longer a fringe practice. They converse with their favourite chatbot as they might a human therapist, a companion, a “troubleshooter” and even a “work buddy”. If your boss is doing that, but has entered into a pathological version of parasocial engagement, it’s quite possible that they’re taking advice from this digital confidant in good faith, genuinely understanding it to be their intimate. And perhaps their teller of cold, hard truths. There could be any number of reasons for how this has come about. It might have been a conversational chain reaction, beginning with a benign question but branching, exchange by exchange, into something much more radical.



Or it may have been less accidental. Perhaps your boss, worried that they were seen as a soft touch, sought advice on changing this perception, and were given a menu of aggressive and ruthless management tactics. The change won’t have come out of nowhere. And while I think it’s sensible to be curious about, and even sympathetic to, what catalysed it, you don’t need to tolerate or excuse the cold-hearted turn. Your manager, of course, has the prerogative to make changes, and is under no obligation to be your friend, but if they’re taking dogmatic advice from a chatbot, I think they’re engaging in an ill-advised, even dangerous practice – and possibly stepping onto legally shaky ground. One day in the future consulting with robots as if they’re trustworthy humans might be entirely normal, and possibly beneficial. That day has not arrived. Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: Golden sheen for weightlifter David Liti in Glasgow
World.content:
David Liti is a Commonwealth Games champion again.

Liti has won the +110kg class in Glasgow with a strong strategic move by his team in the clean and jerk phase.

He sat second behind Lovepreet Singh, of India, after the snatch and remained in that position until his second to last lift.

Liti told RNZ he enjoyed what in the end turned out to be a one-on-one battle with Singh.

"To be better we need to compete against each other, we're friends who just want to be the best they can be. Today I have the gold and maybe next time he would."

Liti said he got pumped up by the noisy crowd.

"It's the best feeling, the crowd was crazy, such a good crowd. I didn't think any crowd could match Gold Coast it helped a lot with the confidence and the adrenaline to get up on the platform.

"I think we had more Kiwis than Scots there today, so very very proud."

Liti achieved 220kg with his first clean and jerk lift to put the pressure on Singh who had a 10kg lead after the snatch.

The Kiwi then decided to nominate 223kg for his second lift meaning the Indian had to make 217kg to match him, but he failed.

Liti then successfully lifted 223kg on his first attempt to win gold.

The Aucklander finished with a games record combined weight of 389kg.

He admitted afterwards that he wasn't happy with his snatch but felt he could overcome his opponent in the clean and jerk.

Liti and coach Tina Ball embraced in front of the crowd and New Zealand supporters afterwards.

Ball is the only coach Liti has ever had.

"I thank her for everything I do, I'm very proud of her for looking after me and my emotions," Liti said.

The 30 year old won gold at the 2018 games and then silver four years ago.

He was also the flagbearer for the New Zealand team at the opening ceremony a week ago.

Tuʿi-Alofa Patolo finished fourth in the women's +86kg class.
