World.title: Weekend weather: Snow warnings and strong wind watches as chilly days ahead
World.content:
The country is set to face a chilly weekend as subantarctic winds move up the country, MetService says.

In the South Island, temperatures will start to drop in the south on Friday morning as the southerly pushes through Otago, and then into Canterbury this afternoon, with colder temperatures expected overnight Friday and Saturday.

MetService has road snowfall warnings in place for South Island mountain passes on Friday and the Desert Road on Saturday.

The mountain passes include Crown Range Road, Lindis Pass, Milford Road, Arthur's, Porters and Lewis Pass.

Meanwhile, the northern Cook Strait and the North Taranaki Bight have experienced thunderstorms.

Strong wind watches are also in place for parts of the South Island.

Coastal Otago's watch is in place from noon to 10pm on Friday, where southwest winds may approach severe gale in exposed places.

A watch for Christchurch, Banks Peninsula and the Canterbury Plains kicks off from 5pm Friday until 1am Saturday.

The watch for coastal Southland and southern Fiordland kicked in late Thursday and continues until 5pm Friday.

All watches have a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning.

MetService said subantarctic air was being dragged north by southerly winds - resulting in "bitterly cold conditions".

It would make temperatures feel close to -2C in Invercargill on Friday afternoon "and even colder for higher elevations".

The cold weather would move up to the North Island during Saturday, it said, "with the wind chill cooling things to a feels-like temperature of just 1C in Wellington".

For those running or on the sidelines at the Taupō marathon, meteorologist Braydon While suggested dressing warm.

"Those preparing for the marathon, whether competing or cheering on the sidelines, will want to wrap up warm and bring a cosy jacket in case a few showers manage to sneak over the hills."

Sunday would bring clear skies for most of the country, MetService said, and "widespread frosts".

World.title: Samoa face World Rugby ban over prime minister's 'political madness', opposition warns
World.content:
Samoa's opposition leader Tuilaepa Sa'ilele Malielegaoi says the country faces suspension by World Rugby today because of "a dirty political move" by the government.

Tuilaepa's spoke to RNZ Pacific after the government announced that it was pulling its support of Lakapi Samoa due to "unresolved internal issues and division" at the national rugby union.

"The government does not provide the Samoa Rugby Union with any financial assistance, there are no internal issues, it's political madness on the part of the prime minister, " Tuilaepa, who is a former Samoan PM and the leader of the Human Rights Protection Party (HRPP), said.

World Rugby has given the Samoan government until Friday to accept a review of its decision to withdraw recognition and financial support of the rugby union.

Failure to accept the review or respond by the deadline could result in Samoa being suspended from international rugby for four years, the news outlet reported.

It added that the development follows a meeting between the Lakapi Samoa and World Rugby representatives on Thursday.

RNZ Pacific has contacted World Rugby, Lakapi Samoa and the Samoan government's press secretariat for a response to Tuilaepa's comments.

Tuilaepa, who stepped down as chairman of Lakapi Samoa in March, told RNZ Pacific he was not interested in whether the country faced suspension from international rugby.

"I was chairman (of Lakapi Samoa). I've done all that is possible for the good of rugby. If the new government comes in and doesn't support it, that's it," the former long-time prime minister said.

"I am not worried (about Samoa being suspended), if World Rugby wants to do that, that is the proper thing to do. Our people chose the government and therefore if our people suffer, that is what our country wants.

"World Rugby should not bend to a country where its leadership is so stupid it becomes involved in political decisions that are hurtful to the young people of our country," he said.

Tuilaepa added: "If the majority of Samoans end up regretting that young rugby players are banned at a world level, they should go and talk to the prime minister they voted for."

In February, Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa (La'auli) Leuatea Schmidt said the sport had been "politicised" and the status of the game in Samoa was poor.

"At this stage, our rugby is very impoverished ... we are at a level that Samoa has never been before, because of what? Because of management," Laauli said.

"We're coming in to clear out all the politicians inside our rugby union," he said at the time.

Tuilaepa stepped down as chairman of the Samoa Rugby Union a month later after his political stand-off with La'auli threatened to stall a new funding programme for the Pacific's three top rugby unions.

Laauli had refused to sign any new agreement with the Fijian and Tongan rugby unions until Tuilaepa and his board resigned and made way for new appointments.

The prime minister added that his government would set up a rival union to govern the sport in the country, if the entire Lakapi Samoa board did not resign.

World.title: Is Australia losing its shine?
World.content:
What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

A promise of a better life in Australia has drawn many New Zealanders across the Tasman in recent years. But economists say the tide may be about to turn.

As the economy slowed after the post-Covid boom, the number of New Zealanders migrating to Australia picked up. There was a net migration loss of 28,500 people to Australia in the year to December last year, smaller than the 31,100 in 2024 but much higher than the 3000 a year that was normal between 2014 and 2019.

The record was a loss of 43,700 in the year to March 2012.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said people were drawn to Australia because the country was richer and had become steadily more so than New Zealand for the last 40 years.

Australia's GDP per person started to diverge from New Zealand's in the 1970s and is now significantly higher.

Eaqub said that was partly because of their commodity prices and a better terms of trade but it was not only mining that helped. New Zealanders were earning less on average and spending more of their income on housing.

But he said where New Zealand's house price relative to GDP per person, and rents relative to GDP had been higher for a long time, they were starting to converge.

"For a long time, New Zealand's housing market has just been really terrible in terms of how unaffordable it is, both in terms of house prices and rents… we spend a lot more of our income on housing compared to Australia, everything else is much the same.

Susan Edmunds on the Australia migration trend Morning Report Download MP3 2m

"Ours has got a little bit better and theirs has got a lot worse."

Eaqub said the current slowdown in Australia's housing market could change the picture again but New Zealand had made more progress with its conversation about public policy and housing in recent years than Australia had.

"I'm not saying we're perfect but I think it's far more mature here than it is over there."

He said Australia's economy also had headwinds and unemployment rising, which might discourage people from moving there if their access to welfare was likely to be limited. Australia also has higher central bank interest rates with similar levels of inflation.

A comparison of house prices relative to GDP per capita in Australia and New Zealand from 1995 until 2025. Supplied / Simplicity

There was a net migration loss of 28,500 people to Australia in the year to December last year, Supplied / Qantas

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones agreed there were signs that "some of those economic relativities are starting to tilt more towards New Zealand".

"Probably more so from the Australian side as the Aussie economy slows down. Household spending growth there is entering a softer patch alongside falling house prices and a likely further rise in unemployment. As an example, New Zealand job ads have been, tentatively, rising against a flat-to-lower trend in Australia. That's historically quite a good indicator to suggest some narrowing in the big gap between New Zealand and Aussie unemployment rates is likely. That subtle shift in labour market relativities is I think one of the key reasons why New Zealand departures to Australia have slowed up a little."

He said he would still frame it more as New Zealand catching up rather than overtaking.

"Australia's economy starts from an outright stronger position in nearly all areas. Our forecasts do have New Zealand growth catching up and eventually overtaking that of Australia over the next 12-18 months, but it could be quite a while before New Zealand's unemployment rate falls down to where Australia's resides in the mid-to-late 4s."

ANZ senior economist Miles Workman said the two economies had been on different paths for a while.and New Zealand had more of a "boom-bust" Covid experience than Australia.

"That's likely to remain the case for a while yet, with New Zealand starting from a weaker position than Australia in terms of economic momentum, meaning the hurdle to growth in New Zealand should be a bit lower. The starting point for the respective housing markets is a similar story.

"The difference in unemployment rates between Australia and New Zealand helps explain the trans-Tasman migration cycle. Our forecasts have that gap narrowing from late this year, which should reduce some of the incentive to move purely for cyclical labour market reasons.

"However, it will take more than a few years of business cycle divergence to address the more structural income differential between the two countries. Even if New Zealand's economy outperforms Australia's for a period, skilled workers will likely still be able to earn materially more in Australia doing similar work. Australia's labour market is also larger, with more major cities, industries and career opportunities to choose from."

He said it was possible New Zealand would start to look more attractive over the next little while, because it was coming off a weaker base.

"Closing the gap with Australia in a more structural sense would require stronger productivity growth over the long run, which is what ultimately drives higher incomes. A cyclical upswing alone is unlikely to be enough."

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod last year argued that New Zealand's economic growth was likely to outpace Australia's.

World.title: Solar recommendations could speed up installations, lower household bills - industry
World.content:
Regulation ministry urges government to legalise plug-in solar Morning Report Download MP3 3m

New recommendations for solar power could speed up installations and lower household bills, the industry says.

Minister for Regulation David Seymour laid out 15 recommendations to streamline solar uptake in a review published on Thursday.

He also advised legalising plug-in solar, which is currently illegal in the country due to concerns over electricity and fire risks.

"You may have heard people say in Australia you can go to Kmart, buy a plug-in solar panel, plug it in and be going just as though you'd bought a PS2 or a Sega Megastation, or any other device for that matter.

"However, this is much better for the environment and you actually make money instead of wasting your childhood," said Seymour.

Electrification advocates Rewiring Aotearoa welcomed the recommendations.

Its policy director Dave Karl said the suggestions addressed the challenges stopping households from taking up solar: delays and unnecessary added costs.

"I think absolutely solar's day has come in New Zealand and I think the commitments from almost every party around the finance through the ratepayers assistance scheme, will absolutely unlock the choice for more than 90 percent of households to get solar on board."

Rewiring Aotearoa policy director Dave Karl. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said the review cut through red tape without sacrificing safety: accredited installers employing properly certified electricians would still be required.

"I do see it as a job creation opportunity in the medium to long run, and I really hope some parties come out with good policies around building that workforce domestically," he said.

He said legalising plug-in solar would make it very popular with renters.

"And I think more so than just plug-in solar, we'll be seeing lots of people also pairing that with plug-in batteries, enabling them to capture cheap electricity overnight and use that a little bit during the day as well.

"So I think it'll be, I mean, not as game-changing for power bills as rooftop solar can be, but shaving 50 bucks, 20 bucks - everything counts these days for a lot of families."

Future Energy co-founder Heath Coleman agreed this was a positive direction for the industry.

"I think we're all very supportive to see the removal, making solar easier and faster for homeowners to get solar, ultimately, at the end of the day," he said.

But he said the biggest challenge was the workforce.

"What we're facing at the moment is that there's a long process to get registered and solar installers to have the micro credentials that they need in order to sign off and install a solar system."

A home powered by solar. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said apprentices in his team of 80 would have to wait an extended period of time after their qualifications before being allowed to install solar.

"We're really struggling to find people that have the right skill sets there because it's still a very new and emerging industry. So, we have to train people up constantly and that takes time and obviously a lot of cost in there as well."

He said he wanted to see the certification process speed up.

However, he said he thought the upfront costs would still be a major deterrent - even with rate payers assistance schemes announced by several political parties.

"I think financially all the numbers do tend to stack up'" he said.

'Significant savings'

But Consumer NZ's power switch manager Paul Fuge said solar installations typically took less than a decade to pay themselves back.

"The other way to look at it is in terms of the unit price.

"So currently the average price in New Zealand is around 35 cents to 40 cents a kWh, depending on where you live. And solar is coming in around 15 cents, including the cost of capital.

"So there's significant savings in terms of the cost of the electricity that's coming off a solar system compared to buying it from the grid."

Consumer NZ' power switchmanager Paul Fuge. Supplied / Consumer NZ

The consumer champion said the perceived hassle and expense of solar deterred consumers.

"I mean, this review is really about removing unnecessary barriers. And if these reforms make solar quicker and easier to install without compromising safety, that's a win for consumers," he said.

He also welcomed legalising plug-in solar, as renters would be able to reap the benefits too.

"But what we'd say is installation is only half the story," he warned.

Fuge said he wanted to see more oversight of buy-back rates - the price of selling electricity back to the grid.

"Consumers also need to get fair pricing and fair returns from the electricity they generate from their solar systems."

James Scott from Electrify the Hutt, a community-led initiative to promote electrification, said allowing solar panel companies to sign off on an installation without an inspection would help speed up the process, but there was also a need for more installers to meet the demand.

The Ministry for Regulation said a small-scale solar system could involve up to six different sign-offs and five site visits from four different entities before it could be switched on.

James Scott from Electrify the Hutt. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Scott said his daughter and son-in-law had to wait around seven weeks due to the amount of red tape.

However, Scott added that he was able to be connected within 48 hours as his installer had done the preparatory work.

"I think that the regulatory review is one part of it, and taking away some of those things will help," he said.

"I think the other thing... is we need a good supply of trained and competent installers who know what they're doing."

Scott said some solar panel companies had more business than they could cope with.

World.title: Water bills in Auckland and Wellington to climb as investment is made in infrastructure
World.content:
Water bills climbing as infrastructure costs mount Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Water bills in Auckland and Wellington are about to climb, as water companies try to catch up on decades of under-investment.

In Auckland, Watercare revealed on Thursday an average household's water bill would go up about $8 per month, as part of a $15.2 billion investment in the city's water infrastructure.

Meanwhile in Wellington, people would pay 13.3 percent more as new water agency Tiaki Wai invested in ageing infrastructure.

A wastewater leak in Wellington's CBD in October 2024. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Auckland has been plagued by problems with its ageing water infrastructure, including in 2023 when a huge sinkhole in Parnell meant millions of litres of sewage a day were pumped into the Waitemata harbour.

Deputy Mayor Desley Simpson said Watercare's $15b investment would prevent those kind of problems in the future.

"It means that we're going to get investment that we've been crying out for ages, below the ground to improve water quality... and actually finally gets us an Auckland that we can swim at our beaches with no black flags."

Auckland Deputy Mayor Desley Simpson. RNZ / Nick Monro

Separating Watercare from Auckland Council, with its own balance sheet, had meant it could take on more debt to fund the infrastructure, Simpson said.

Watercare has also put up water prices, by about $8 per month for the average Auckland household, to help pay for it.

"And that's painful. It's a tough economic time. But I suppose one of the advantages we have in Auckland is we can, as households, monitor how much we spend. You know, if you have shorter showers," Simpson said.

Aucklanders RNZ spoke to agreed the increase would be painful.

"Well it affects everyone doesn't it? To a degree. I think I could afford $8, but a lot of people can't," said one.

"For lower-income people, it probably would be a challenge for them, so I feel sorry for them in that regard," said another.

But many felt the extra cost was worth it, if it meant fewer issues with the water network in the future.

"I sometimes go to Mission Bay and you can't swim there because there's some warning sign saying that it's contaminated. So I definitely look forward to that."

"It's heartbreaking really, we're supposed to be this clean, green country and summer after summer not being able to go to the beach."

A sign warns of a sewage leak at an Auckland beach. RNZ / Nikki Mandow

In Wellington, council organisation Tiaki Wai has taken over management of water services, and sent out its first new bills on Wednesday.

Water bills in the city would increase by 13.3 percent on average this year.

Wellingtonian Charlotte Murphy felt there hadn't been enough communication that the new bills were coming.

"I haven't seen a lot of information as a ratepayer about it, and I know that there are a lot of questions around it from people in, for example, my apartment complex."

Back in Auckland, Watercare chief executive Jamie Sinclair told Checkpoint the infrastructure work it was doing was urgently needed.

"We've got significant underinvestment in the assets that we own. The 20,000 kilometres of pipe or so that we maintain at the moment. We also need to build resilence into our network as we're dealing with more extreme weather events and also increasing demand."

World.title: Tom Walsh settles for Commonwealth Games silver as three-peat bid falls short
World.content:
Tom Walsh has fallen just short of a third consecutive Commonwealth Games title, claiming silver in the men's shotput final in Glasgow.

The reigning indoor world champion was edged for gold by Nigeria's Chukwuebuka Enekwechi, with Scott Lincoln, of England, winning the bronze.

It was New Zealand's second medal from the track and field events on Friday, after three-time Paralympic champion Anna Grimaldi won bronze in the T47 100m final earlier in the evening.

Seeking to become the first man to win three straight Commonwealth shotput gold medals, Walsh led the final through the first four rounds after firing an opening round throw of 21.03m.

Despite the early lead, Walsh struggled to find his rhythm in the circle, recording no throws in the third and fourth rounds.

Enekwechi overtook Walsh with a fifth-round throw of 21.07m, putting the pressure on the Kiwi in the final rounds.

Walsh looked to find good distance in his fifth round throw, but it landed outside the sector, taking out a television microphone in the process.

While he managed to record a throw in the final round, it was not enough to reclaim the lead from the Nigerian.

Fellow Kiwi Nick Plamer finished sixth in the final in what was his first Commonwealth Games.

Anna Grimaldi PHOTOSPORT

In other action, Grimaldi won bronze in the women's T47 100m, claiming New Zealand's second sprint medal on the track following Zoe Hobbs' gold medal heroics on Wednesday.

World.title: Ex-MAFS star Ridge Barredo sticking to weightlifting despite ugly injury
World.content:
Ridge Barredo's description of the knee injury that ended his Commonwealth Games weightlifting campaign is enough to turn most of us off even watching the sport for good.

"I heard it pop on the third attempt, I tried to give it my all and I heard it pop [out] and pop back in," he said of his failed third snatch attempt in the men's 110kg class.

"Just to feel it was a little bit scary. Initial pain was an eight or nine out of 10."

Barredo said it was the first time he had ever experienced an injury like that, sustained as he tried to throw 162 kilograms over his head.

Loading Instagram content

By the time he spoke to media, having been helped off the Armadillo stage, he said he was just "a little bit uncomfortable" and described the pain as down to a six or seven out of 10.

This was his third Commonwealth Games and the 30-year-old vowed to be back at Amdavad in four years.

"It's not the end. I'm still relatively young, still hungry for it, still want to be the best in Australia," he said.

"I'm not done yet, no way. Not a chance. I'll be back for sure. Four times, watch, mark my words."

And he said this difficult and painful journey is still preferable to a return to the scene that made his descriptor on Google not "athlete" or "weightlifter", but "internet personality".

That's thanks to his turn on reality TV show Married At First Sight three years ago.

One of only a handful of successful couples from the program, Barredo and wife Jade are still together.

Loading Instagram content

Jade and daughter Victoria were in the crowd watching as he suffered his injury.

And while the program worked out for him, Barredo says his TV days are over.

"My TV career is definitely done, I've found my partner. I'm off reality TV. Wouldn't recommend it," he said.

"If you want to have some fun in a toxic environment, go for it, but personally I wouldn't be going back."

He's not the only Games athlete shunning the reality TV scene (for now) with Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan revealing she had to make a choice to continue swimming or go on Love Island last year.

'If you've got a lane, you've got a chance' An unexpected source kicks off another record-breaking night for Australian swimming as we get implicit and explicit reminders that we shouldn't take this for granted.

Shanahan opted not to enter the villa, ultimately winning silver in the women's 200m backstroke on the first night of the Glasgow swimming program.

"I'm the biggest Love Island fan ever. I've watched every season," Shanahan told BBC Scotland.

"Last year the producers asked me and [English swimmer] Abbie Wood if we would be interested in doing it.

"I couldn't go on, though, because [I was] focusing on the swimming, but who knows in the future?

"I was a bit tempted but the swimming had to come first."

World.title: 'Try not to die': Why Glasgow's gales hit different for hurdlers
World.content:
After rain blighted the first six days of the Commonwealth Games, Glasgow dialled up the dimmer on Thursday morning.

But a gorgeous, sunny, slightly brisk morning turned blustery and bleak by the time athletics competition was in full swing at Scotstoun Stadium.

It mercifully stayed dry as day seven's heats and qualifiers kicked off, but the wind was wreaking havoc across the track and field.

Australian javelin thrower Cameron McEntyre was launching into a mighty headwind that saw none of the 17 throwers reach the qualification standard of 84 metres.

The temperature plummeted as clouds rolled over Scotstoun. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

McEntyre got through on his 78.91m effort, but Kenya's Julius Yego, boasting the fourth longest throw in the Commonwealth this year, missed out on qualifying for the final as he finished in 13th spot.

"Everyone struggled with the wind and the temperature as well. Hopefully better conditions tomorrow and then push for a podium [but] everyone's in the same boat," McEntyre said, crediting his thorough preparation at training for keeping him ready for a day like today.

"If it's pissing down with rain or huge headwinds, whatever the conditions are, we just deal with it because we know one day there's gonna be a competition that's exactly the same."

And while hurling a spear into a breeze that's trying to throw it back at you might sound like the more dangerous prospect, Michelle Jenneke said her 100m hurdles with the wind at her back is a frightening experience.

Michelle Jenneke said the tailwind can mess up hurdlers' all-important stride patterns. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I get pretty jealous when I see the sprinters because you get a tailwind and you run fast, we get a tailwind and we're like 'let's try not to die today'. The hurdles were really coming at us," Jenneke said.

"I am just really really grateful we knew that was going to be a possibility and we really trained for it. It was tough today, towards the end I was really struggling to make sure I was hitting my stride pattern. But I think I did it really well, I did really safe and still managed to run quite fast."

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

Jenneke clocked a time of 12.72 seconds, 0.05 of a second outside her personal best from two years ago, but this time with an illegal +4.3 metres per second tailwind.

"The wind was really pushing us onto the hurdles, it was a good time, though," she said after progressing to the evening's final as the sixth-fastest qualifier.

"Hopefully a little less windy [in the final] but I did really prepare for that tailwind and I think I handled it better than some of the other athletes."

Adeyah Brewster (background) went down at the final hurdle. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

She certainly did, with Barbados's Adeyah Brewster clipping the final hurdle and falling flat on her belly barely 6 metres short of the finish line.

National 400m champion Reece Holder experienced both sides of the coin in his single-lap semifinal, saying it was exactly what they expected when coming to Glasgow.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

"Everyone's running in the same conditions, so can't really complain because everyone's showing up to show out," he said.

Holder, who suffered a hamstring injury in mid-May, missed the 400m final while teammate Tom Reynolds won his semifinal to progress.

"I actually only just put spikes on two weeks ago from May," he said.

"So to come out here and run 45s, just be thankful for that and push forward for the future.

"I just don't think I'm race fit. Big ups to everyone else out there putting on a show for everyone in these conditions, but I just don't think I was there."

World.title: Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years
World.content:
Sydney Roosters sent a warning to the rest of the NRL about their premiership credentials with a 82-12 whipping of North Queensland in Townsville, the most points by a winning team in 91 years.

Halfback Sam Walker, in the midst of a multi-million dollar contract negotiation, showed why Roosters supremo Nick Politis wants to keep him at the club for life in a masterclass display.

This was a muscle flex of epic proportions as the visitors scored the equal most first half points in premiership history to lead 48-6 after 40 minutes.

The Roosters scored eight first half tries with fullback James Tedesco and Walker both crossing twice. Walker's 24 points in the first half, including eight goals from as many attempts, was also the equal most points by an individual in an opening 40 minutes.

The team total of 82 was the most by a team since the Roosters beat Canterbury 87-7 in 1935. It was also the third-highest in premiership history.

Walker finished with 36 individual points and a hat-trick of tries, as did unstoppable winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

Tedesco left the field at halftime with an ankle injury in a concern for the Tricolours.

North Queensland were helpless before the Tricolour onslaught. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock )

The Roosters temporarily joined Penrith on 34 competition points at the top of the table in their most complete performance of the season.

It was their sixth win in a row and a sign that come September they will be in prime position to challenge their bogey team Penrith.

The Cowboys are hanging on in eighth position but will drop back to ninth if Canterbury beat Melbourne away on Friday night.

The nature of the thrashing will test Cowboys coach Todd Payten's ability to get an appropriate response

Captain Tedesco, fresh from a hat-trick of tries last week, started and finished the opening try and it was carnage from that moment.

Roosters forwards Naufahu Whyte and Salesi Foketi monstered the hosts early and the spine of Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans, Walker and Reece Robson ran riot.

Tedesco, also the NSW custodian, is making a compelling case to oust Reece Walsh from the fullback position for Australia at the World Cup later in the year.

The Cowboys levelled at six-all when halves Jake Clifford and Jaxon Purdue combined to put Braidon Burns over but that was the only moment the match was in the balance.

A brilliant interchange of passing between halfback Walker and Tedesco led to the No.7 slicing over.

Tedesco then laid on a try for centre Hugo Savala with a left-foot grubber and it was clear which way the match was heading. . Walker's left foot step on the last tackle to score his second was elite.

The dazzling half set up runaway Foketi for a 40m rampage to the line.

The last try of the match, scored by replacement fullback Cody Ramsey, featured Walker grubbering and then kicking the ball over the head of the last dismal line of Cowboys defence.

AAP

World.title: Tomic continues resurgence, de Minaur sets up clash with Hewitt
World.content:
Born-again Bernard Tomic has continued his extraordinary renaissance with another stunning victory to surge into his first ATP quarterfinal in seven years.

A day after notching the fastest win on the tour all year, Tomic claimed the prized scalp of dual grand slam semifinalist Karen Khachanov in a straight-sets blitz in Mexico on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

And rounding out a banner day for Australian tennis less than a month out from the US Open, world number six Alex de Minaur has beaten his old nemesis Stefanos Tsitsipas to set up an intriguing showdown with Cruz Hewitt in Washington.

The day, though, belonged to the resurgent Tomic.

The one-time world number 17 crushed fourth-seeded Khachanov — the big-serving Russian who ousted Nick Kyrgios to reach the 2022 US Open semifinals — 6-2, 6-4 to continue his spectacular comeback from the brink of retirement.

The 33-year-old hinted he was considering hanging up his racquet before snaring the Lincoln Challenger this month.

"I'll be as honest as I can, about 10 days ago I hit a bit of a brick wall, maybe two weeks ago," Tomic said in the aftermath of his biggest breakthrough since 2018.

"I said this was going to be my last year, so I guess I have to reassess a few things now. Now that I won, I'm going to have to go back to the table. I'm probably going to play another 20 years."

Twenty more years may be a stretch, but Tomic is playing some vintage tennis.

The former teenage Wimbledon quarter-finalist only made the main draw in Mexico as a qualifying lucky loser.

Now he is three wins away from hoisting the trophy in Los Cabos, having earlier needed just 46 minutes to take down Alex Hernandez 6-1, 6-0 in the first round.

Currently ranked 171st, Tomic will climb even further and potentially to as high as number 132 if he wins a most unexpected fifth ATP title.

Next up will be either British fifth seed Cam Norrie or fellow Australian James Duckworth in Tomic's first ATP quarterfinal since losing to de Minaur in Atlanta in 2019.

De Minaur, meanwhile, is celebrating his own big victory, after downing Tsitsipas for only the second time in 14 meetings to reach the last 16 in the US capital.

The 6-4, 3-6, 6-3 win earned the top seed and defending champion a first-time encounter with 17-year-old Hewitt, de Minaur's understudy and son of Australian Davis Cup captain and mentor Lleyton.

After winning his first ATP match on Wednesday, Hewitt said it would be a "dream" to square off against de Minaur, who he likened to a big brother.

"I've known him basically my whole life," said Hewitt, who made the Wimbledon boys' final two weeks ago.

"​He's stayed with us and we have Christmas together, also. He's taught me so ​much. I think that ⁠would be a pretty cool memory for us."

AAP

World.title: Last-minute race to deliver marathon medals after shipping delays
World.content:
A last-minute logistical scramble has ensured thousands of runners at a major Queensland marathon festival will receive their medals.

A record number of more than 16,000 people will descend on the Sunshine Coast as the region hosts the event on Sunday.

But participants received an email late on Wednesday informing them they might not get a medal for crossing the line.

A medal from last year's Sunshine Coast Marathon Festival. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Event director Jason Crowther told the ABC a container full of T-shirts and medals arrived at the Port of Brisbane on Tuesday, but was stranded on the dock.

Mr Crowther said the merchandise was ordered months ago and was due to arrive on July 3, with the shipping company blaming point-of-origin delays and a typhoon for the late arrival.

"This is something you just don't want to happen," he said.

"To not get a finisher medal is not acceptable from our point of view.

"We don't take this lightly."

The Sunshine Coast Marathon Festival is a popular event, which attracts runners from around the country. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Marathon)

Port mobilises to solve crisis

When the Port of Brisbane was made aware of the issue following a media enquiry, officials rolled up their sleeves.

Executive general manager Brendan Connell said he was "really pleased" to help.

"We've been able to identify the container, get it moving and get it onto the Sunshine Coast so that all those hard-running marathoners, very worthy recipients, can get their medals on the weekend," he said.

"As soon as we found out … we wanted to do everything we could to help.

"We made a couple of phone calls, some senior people made some decisions, and in fact they disrupted their own days to ensure that we could identify this container.

"A few other things were put on the backburner to make that happen, but ultimately, everybody was able to come together and get to a really good outcome."

The event provides a much-needed tourism boost for the region over the winter months. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Marathon)

Mr Crowther said he was grateful to port officials for helping get the medals and merchandise released.

"They've moved heaven and earth to make it happen so a big thank you to them," he said.

" I've had a week of sleepless nights; it was something that was meant to arrive a long time ago. "

For anyone considering calling the port to get their parcel delivered faster, Mr Connell has bad news.

"It is a really complex series of events that moves freight around the world," he said.

"This isn't a scenario we could repeat every day, it isn't something that we can ordinarily influence.

"But certainly when there's a massive event like this going on … we wanted to make sure we could come together and do what we could to find those medals and get them on their way."

Last year, tourism officials estimated the Sunshine Coast race weekend generated about $10.5 million for the local economy.

World.title: Final frontiers drive Hazlewood in twilight years
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has more boxes to tick in a stellar career after returning to peak fitness following several injury impacted years.

The 35-year-old Australia paceman, veteran of 76 Tests, has never won a series in India or England, two classic confrontations that loom large in the 20 Tests at least the team are set to play in the next 12 months.

Australia have not won an away Ashes series since 2001, while 2004 was the last triumph in India — well before any of the current squad were playing Tests.

Australian men's Tests in 2026/27 August 12-26: Two Tests vs Bangladesh

Two Tests vs Bangladesh October 9-31: Three Tests in South Africa

Three Tests in South Africa December 9-January 7: Four Tests vs New Zealand

Four Tests vs New Zealand January 21-February 23, 2027: Five Tests in India

Five Tests in India March 11-15, 2027: One Test vs England

One Test vs England June, 2027: World Test Championship final (potential)

World Test Championship final (potential) June-July, 2027: Five Tests in England

"The big series are obviously England and India. I haven't won in South Africa either, so there are a few boxes to tick off there, not just me, but this whole playing group," Hazlewood said.

"That's been a driving factor during this prep, it is in the back of your head, and in the months leading into it. They're real big Test series, all away against tough competition. Hopefully we get the job done."

Hazlewood's most recent setback in the Test sphere came when Achilles tendon and hamstring injuries cruelled any involvement in last summer's Ashes series.

Since then he has returned to the bowling crease with a bang, helping Royal Challengers Bengaluru win back-to-back IPL titles.

Hazlewood has been preparing with other members of the Australia squad at the National Cricket Centre in Brisbane ahead of two Tests against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay next month.

He said the "big days" of training in one location and without other playing commitments had been ideal.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

"Leading into other Test series and Test matches, you're playing T20, you're playing one-dayers, you're travelling, so it's tough to fit those bowling sessions in," he said.

"It's just trying to replicate a day in the field of Test cricket. It's bowling multiple spells in a day. It's bowling back-to-back days."

"This has been tailor-made for a Test match, which I think should work out well."

Hazlewood said it would be "tough" for any of the quicks in the squad to play every Test in the next year.

"Maybe a spinner," he quipped.

Hazlewood, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Scott Boland, Brendan Doggett and Michael Neser will all be vying for games.

Boland, who has been in sensational Test form, has been mostly overlooked when Hazlewood was previously available, but it need not be an either/or proposition.

"I think we've only played one game together … in England at Edgbaston, which was nice. I'd love to play more with Scotty," Hazlewood said.

"We're obviously a little bit similar, but there are still a lot of differences in our bowling. Every time he's come in, he's done unbelievably well. His career just keeps getting better and better the older he gets.

"I think there are enough opportunities in the next 12 to 18 months for us to play a lot of cricket, hopefully, together. We've got Ness (Neser) and Doggy (Doggett) there as well, so I think we'll have to lean on all six at some point in the next 18 months."

Hazlewood's most recent injuries have coincided with home Tests, but he is not sweating over what transpired in the past.

"We've got a nice lead-in this time. We've got Test matches abroad, so hopefully we hit the ground running again in Australia," he said.

"I've been lucky enough to play 70-odd Test matches now, which is quite a lot in terms of Aussie quicks. Hopefully I can tick a few more off."

AAP

Tech.title: LinkedIn actually adds a ‘seems like AI slop’ button
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A lot of content on LinkedIn might seem like AI slop, and now, you’ll be able to report those posts. As part of a series of updates to reduce the volume of AI slop on the platform, LinkedIn is introducing an actual button that lets you flag a post as something that “Seems like AI slop.”

The new feature is part of a broader push to reduce the volume of apparent AI slop on the platform. AI detector Pangram recently found that 41 percent of longform LinkedIn posts were flagged as being completely generated by AI, as reported by 404Media.

“AI slop is a top priority for all of us,” chief product officer Hari Srinivasan says in a post. “We really care about this.” In addition to the button to report a post as seemingly being AI-generated, LinkedIn is also ramping up new classifiers to identify “if a post is AI-slop or generally low-quality content,” which will “reduce the amount of AI slop you might see in suggested content and content from outside your network.”

I’m currently seeing the new report button in the three-dots menu on posts. When I click it, LinkedIn hides the post and shows a message thanking me for my feedback.

The new button will help LinkedIn “tune our models and make better feeds,” Srinivasan says. The company is also testing a way to show people that other users feel their posts come across as inauthentic or that they include heavy use of AI.

In addition, LinkedIn is removing a feature that used AI to “enhance” a post and will replace it with a “feature that proofreads your words, but does not change your voice,” according to Srinivasan.

Tech.title: Govee’s portable smart lamp is down to one of its best prices to date
Tech.content:
Buying multiple lamps for different rooms can get expensive. Govee’s rechargeable Table Lamp Classic gives you one lamp you can use throughout your home instead of getting one for every room, and right now it’s down to $59 ($21 off) at Amazon. That’s just $4 shy of the all-time low set during Prime Day, and the smart lamp’s second-best price to date.

Because it’s cordless, the lamp is surprisingly versatile. You can use it to brighten your desk during the day, keep it by your bedside at night, and even carry it to the patio for dinner (just don’t forget to bring it back inside if it’s expected to rain, as the lamp isn’t weather-resistant). A built-in 4,800mAh battery powers the lamp for up to 30 hours with colored lighting enabled, or about five hours when using bright white light, so you don’t need to worry about staying near an outlet.

Despite being small and light enough to carry from room to room, the Table Lamp Classic offers many of the same smart lighting features found on Govee’s bigger lamps. It lets you tweak the color temperature, cycle through 72 preset scenes, and sync the lighting to your music, making it easy to match the mood whether you’re studying, unwinding, or enjoying a date night. If you have something more specific in mind, Govee’s app can even generate a custom effect from a short text prompt. Since it supports Matter, you won’t have to reach for the Govee app every time you move the lamp to a different room, either. Instead, you can control it with your voice through your favorite smart home platform.

Tech.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover found a ‘sea of polygons’ on Mars
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The latest discovery from NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover is a field of honeycomb-shaped polygons covering a Martian valley called Valle Grande. As Gizmodo reports, Curiosity has snapped pictures of the unusual terrain texture before, called polygonal fractures, each about 1.5 to 3 inches wide, but NASA says it’s previously only found them in small patches, “nothing on the scale discovered in Valle Grande.”

Curiosity captured a 360-degree panorama of the “sea of polygons” on June 19th and 20th (Martian sols 4,930 and 4,931) that shows the texture spreading out in all directions. Project scientist Ashwin Vasavada says the Curiosity team “measured their shapes and chemistry carefully and are hopeful there are clues in the data as to how these features formed.”

NASA says billions of years ago, “lakes and streams dappled the lower foothills of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014.” This terrain could also indicate there was once water in Valle Grande, based on previous polygon patches:

Some of the polygons that the mission has spotted in the past clearly formed as mud cracks, though a variety of processes can contribute to their honeycomb textures, including cycles of warm and cold temperatures or compression that squeezed water out of the sediment when the surface was buried.

Tech.title: Google DeepMind’s new AI model can control a robot’s entire body
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google DeepMind says the latest version of its Gemini Robotics AI model can “control entire humanoid robots.” While the previous model focused on controlling a humanoid robot’s upper body, Gemini Robotics 2 now supports “whole-body motions” ranging from its feet to fingertips, according to an announcement on Thursday.

The new model will allow humanoid robots to perform a wider range of actions, as it allows them to walk, crouch, stretch, and manipulate objects. Videos shared by Google show how Apptronik’s Apollo 2 robot can bend over to pick up a watering can, as well as find and take specific items off a shelf.

Though Google DeepMind notes that its robots “have more to advance in movement speed,” it adds that this update “is an important step towards the skills needed to complete more complex, real-world tasks that require whole-body coordination.”

Additionally, Gemini Robotics 2 supports better dexterity, as it can now control more complex, five-fingered hands. That enables robots to perform tasks like sealing a Ziploc, tying a trash bag, or unscrewing a lightbulb.

Google DeepMind is updating Gemini Robotics ER (embodied reasoning) as well, a vision-language model that helps robots to analyze their surroundings, process instructions, and perform multi-step tasks. Gemini Robotics ER 2 is better at completing tasks over an extended period of time and “now understands when tasks begin and end.”

Google DeepMind says this update also allows multiple robots of different types to work together and complete tasks, with one video showing how Apollo 2 instructs Google’s dual-arm robot to put tools inside a bin while cleaning the garage.

The company notes Gemini Robotics ER 2 is its “safest robotics model to date,” as it can “better detect when humans are nearby, trigger safety tool calls and bring the robot to a safe stop if someone approaches too closely.”

Meanwhile, Google DeepMind has brought improvements to its Gemini Robotics On-Device Model, which can run locally on a robot without an internet connection. This model can now adapt to new embodiments faster, including those with “drastically different shapes, sensors and degrees of freedom.”

Tech.title: ABC demands FCC drop its ‘punitive’ early license renewal of its stations
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ABC filed its formal opposition to the Federal Communications Commission’s effort to force it to submit to an early renewal of its broadcast station licenses, calling it an effort to chill the speech of broadcasters across the country.

In a new filing with the FCC, ABC charges that the agency’s willingness to pursue the early renewal of eight of its licenses far before they expire is “extraordinary and unprecedented.” The company alleges the FCC “has spent the last 18 months searching for some pretext for revoking the Stations’ licenses,” but charges that the agency’s real motivations for pursuing these licenses are clear: “Each is owned by ABC, and the Administration has openly and repeatedly called for the revocation of ABC’s licenses, because it dislikes the content and viewpoints expressed on ABC network programs.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The FCC ordered ABC to file for early license renewal for the stations in April, noting that it had been investigating the company for potential violations of the law and FCC rules, “including the agency’s prohibition on unlawful discrimination,” an apparent reference to its probe into ABC and owner Disney’s Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) programs.

“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country”

The station license fight has led to an outpouring of support for ABC, including from viewers it urged with on-air ads to file public comments. More than 153,000 comments have been left on the FCC docket, including from a bipartisan group of former FCC chairs and officials who slammed the agency’s action as part of a “broader pattern” in a “campaign to punish speech disfavored by the Trump administration.”

The FCC under Republican Chair Brendan Carr has repeatedly targeted ABC for actions he claims violate their obligation as a publicly licensed broadcaster to serve the public interest. That included threatening the company’s licenses over a joke late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel made on air after conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s killing, and attempting to penalize “The View” for platforming a Democratic candidate, positing it could be subject to equal time rules the agency previously ruled it was exempt from. Some of these actions have earned Carr criticism even from administration allies like Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), who likened the chair to a “mafioso” over his threat over the Kimmel comments.

“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: accommodate the Administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price,” ABC wrote in its latest filing. “The tools vary; the objective does not: a media industry too fearful of official reprisal to report the news freely.”

Tech.title: Google is working on Chrome updates that don’t require restarts
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is working on a way to apply Chrome updates without requiring you to restart your browser. In a post on Thursday, Google outlines its approach to bug fixes in the age of AI, while noting that it’s trying to make updates less disruptive by “investing in ‘dynamic patching’ that will eliminate the need for a full browser restart.”

According to Google, AI-powered security tools have already helped the company find and fix dozens of bugs. Chrome 149 and 150, for example, contained 1,072 bug fixes, exceeding the number of patches in the past 23 major releases combined. That’s part of the reason why Chrome is switching to a two-week release cycle starting in September with security updates in between. However, Google says it’s considering introducing two weekly security updates to counter “fast-moving AI-powered attacks.”

To make these updates go more smoothly, Google is trying to “shift the burden away” from users, who could be at risk of “N-day” attacks, which occur when hackers exploit newly released bug fixes that haven’t yet been downloaded on a user’s device.

Along with working on dynamic patching, Google is also trying to find “opportune moments to restart automatically, when we can guarantee a seamless session restore.” Google has already launched a version of this in Chrome 150 on macOS, as the browser takes advantage of a state “where applications typically continue running in the background even after all windows are closed.” Chrome will automatically restart if it detects an update in this windowless state, Google says.

“Our long-term vision is a browser that is always up-to-date — continuously and dynamically patched, and automatically restarted during opportune periods of minimal disruption,” Google writes.
